| [LNK-F-0002](#lnk-f-0002) | A stalled Redis stretches a link edit to about nine seconds | Measured while building LNK-M-0018, against a TCP proxy that accepts the connection and then never answers — which is what a stalled Redis looks like, as opposed to a refused connection, which fails in 264ms. `InvalidateAlias` took **9.07s** with the publish removed, so the time is the delete path alone: it makes three attempts, each given `RedisTimeout` (50ms in the test), and go-redis does not honour that context when it has to establish a connection to a server that never speaks. The measurement is in the transcript for LNK-M-0018; the same shape is reproducible with `redisProxy.blackholed(true)` in `test/integration/invalidation_test.go`. Predates LNK-M-0018 — the retry loop is LNK-M-0003's — and LNK-M-0018's own publish was made fire-and-forget so it adds nothing to this. | closed |
| [LNK-F-0003](#lnk-f-0003) | Dark mode has no effect on the UI: the light tokens are unlayered and beat every dark rule | Owner report, 2026-07-31, and confirmed by construction rather than inferred from the symptom. The light `:root` block sits at the top level of the file; both dark blocks sit inside `@layer base`. CSS cascade layers give **unlayered** normal declarations priority over layered ones regardless of specificity, so `:root { --t-surface: #f8fafc }` unconditionally beats `:root[data-theme="dark"] { --t-surface: #0f172a }`. Walking the built `app.css` top level confirms it survives the build: the dark override is inside the `@layer base { … }` construct, and `:root { color-scheme: light; … }` is emitted after `@layer utilities` closes, as its own unlayered top-level rule. Both dark paths are dead, the explicit override and the `prefers-color-scheme` one, which is why `color-scheme: dark` never takes either — matching "changing to Dark Mode does nothing". The server side is *correct* and is not implicated: the demo serves `data-theme="dark"`, `data-theme="light"` and no attribute across the three cookie states. **The milestone's own enforcement cannot catch this**: `TestTemplatesUseThemeTokensOnly` asserts templates name tokens, and the AA contrast figures are recorded in comments, so nothing tests that a token's *value* ever changes. A fix wants a test that fails on this specific cascade, not more contrast arithmetic. | closed |

| [LNK-F-0008](#lnk-f-0008) | The rate limiter's comment blames a stalled Redis on connection establishment, which measurement contradicts | Measured for LNK-M-0025 on 2026-07-31. The context is not honoured on a stalled read whether or not a connection has to be established: a client with `ReadTimeout` 400ms took 401ms to fail a command carrying a 50ms context both against a server that never answered the handshake *and* down a connection established beforehand and then left to go quiet mid-command. What bounds the wait is the client's own `ReadTimeout`; connection establishment has nothing to do with it, and a dial in isolation does honour the deadline (8s dial timeout, 50ms context, 50ms elapsed). The comment's conclusion — enforce the deadline from outside the call — is correct and the code is correct; only the stated reason is wrong, which makes it the kind of comment that misleads the next person deciding whether the same defence is needed somewhere else. | closed |
| [LNK-F-0009](#lnk-f-0009) | An uncached redirect pays `REDIS_READ_TIMEOUT` twice while Redis is stalled, not once | Measured for LNK-M-0025 on 2026-07-31, against `redisProxy.blackholed(true)` with a client built the way `internal/platform/redis.Open` builds one (`DialTimeout` 1s, `ReadTimeout` 50ms). A cold `Resolve` took **108ms**; the two following resolves took 0s, because the in-process tier was populated. The 108ms is 50ms of failed lookup, plus the Postgres query, plus 50ms of `Set` against a server that will not answer it either. Both calls are bounded and neither retries, so this is not the compounding LNK-M-0025 was scheduled for — that was the invalidation path's three-attempt loop, now bounded — but the `redis.go` comment claiming a stalled Redis "costs a little latency" was written about one call and there are two. | closed |

| [LNK-F-0011](#lnk-f-0011) | `TestInvalidationReachesAnotherReplica` is flaky | Observed 2026-08-01 while running LNK-M-0027's gates. | [LNK-F-0012](#lnk-f-0012) | D18's text does not describe the map it governs, in two ways: applied literally its two limbs would make an irreversible permission delegable, and its *"either direction"* sentence promises a disarmi… | Found while recording `org.delete`'s delegability, which m28.5.md required be named against D18. D18 says a permission is non-delegable "when reading it exposes an actor's identity tied to network data, **or** when holding it lets a key widen its own reach. Everything else is delegable." `org.delete` does neither — it discloses nothing and removes tenancy rather than granting any — yet it has been in `NonDelegableScopes` since Phase 1's `00700_seed.sql`, on irreversibility. The map's own comment states the wider rule explicitly: "the rule this map encodes is now 'escalating, irreversible, or disclosing' rather than only the first two." So the code and the decision text disagree about what the rule *is*, and the code is the one that has been right since before D18 was written (2026-07-31). **Folded in from F56 (LNK-M-0036), 2026-08-04:** the same decision's other sentence is wrong the other way. D18 says *"Flipping a permission in **either direction** stays a one-line map edit"*, and it does not: adding an already-granted permission to `NonDelegableScopes` would not disarm keys already issued, because `Authenticate` restricts the identity to the **row's** stored scopes and never consults the map. Never exploitable — `git log -S` confirms all the entries landed in the same commit as the migration creating their permission (`a0f23ff` for `audit.read`/00900, `e8a6b1c` for `destinations.review`/01600, the Phase-1 seed for the rest), so no key has ever held a scope that later became non-delegable. F56's own "only enforcement" reading is now **one site out of date** and is corrected here rather than carried forward: LNK-M-0049's rotation added a second check, `narrowScopes` at `apikey_rotation.go:328-338`, which refuses to carry a now-non-delegable scope into a successor. Mint and rotate are covered; request time is not. F56's cited claim at `apikey.go:147-149` was an over-read — that comment is about the *deleting* direction and is true there. | closed |
| [LNK-F-0013](#lnk-f-0013) | Registration answers whether an address already has an account, which on an open instance is a public enumeration oracle | Reachable without any credential once the effective mode is `open`: `POST /api/v1/auth/register` with a known address answers `409 conflict`, an unknown one answers `202 verification_sent`, and the browser form makes the same distinction in words. Rate limiting slows a sweep but does not remove the signal. The behaviour is not new — the endpoint has answered `409` for a taken address since Phase 1 — but until LNK-M-0029 the endpoint was API-only and there was no browser form; opening self-serve signup is what makes it a surface a stranger reaches. LNK-M-0026 deliberately spent argon2 work to stop redemption answering the same question (D27), so the product already treats this as something worth not disclosing, and the two surfaces now disagree. | closed |
| [LNK-F-0014](#lnk-f-0014) | Anyone who can create a link can now write audit rows at will, because every refused destination is recorded | Built into LNK-M-0030 by its own bullet: *every blocked attempt writes an audit event with `ip_prefix` and the attempted URL stored as evidence*. Confirmed by `TestEveryDestinationSurfaceRunsTheFullTierCheck`, which asserts exactly one `destination.blocked` row per refusal. The caller needs `links.create` or `links.update`, so this is not reachable anonymously — but on an instance with open signup (LNK-M-0029) or many members, a holder of an ordinary editor role can loop `POST /api/v1/links` with `http://127.0.0.1/` and add a row per request, each carrying a metadata blob and up to 2 KiB of defanged URL. Nothing rate-limits the write beyond `LINKCTRL_API_RATE_PER_MIN` (600/min by default), and unlike the other eleven audit actions this one records something that did *not* happen, so there is no successful state change bounding how often it can be provoked. | closed |
| [LNK-F-0015](#lnk-f-0015) | Every organization owner on an instance can read every dispute filed on it, and lift a blocklist entry for everybody | Built into LNK-M-0032 by the shape of what it governs, and confirmed by `TestTheQueueIsGatedOnTheNewPermission`: the queue query has no `organization_id` filter, and `DeleteBlockedDestination` removes a row from a table 01500 makes instance-wide on purpose. So on an instance with two organizations, A's owner sees that somebody in B tried to link to a given host, sees their address in `filed_by`, and can delete the entry that refuses it for both. With `LINKCTRL_SIGNUP_MODE=open` (LNK-M-0029) that reach is one registration away, because registering provisions an organization and makes the registrant its owner. The queue *cannot* honestly be narrower than the decision — a per-organization view over an instance-wide effect would hide rows the same reader is deciding for — so this is the tenancy model showing through rather than a scoping mistake. | closed |
| [LNK-F-0016](#lnk-f-0016) | Most dashboard pages are counted as redirects in the HTTP metrics, because the surface classifier's prefix list stopped being updated after Phase 1 | Noticed while adding `/feeds` and finding there was no list to add it to that anybody had been maintaining. `webPrefixes` holds eight entries — `/login`, `/logout`, `/setup`, `/dashboard`, `/docs`, `/links`, `/keys`, `/account` — and `ClassifySurface` labels everything else that is not `/api/`, `/static/` or an ops endpoint as `redirect`. | [LNK-F-0017](#lnk-f-0017) | `docs/SECURITY.md`'s paragraph on what the audit log records is wrong in both directions — it under-reports what is recorded, over-promises what is coming, and contradicts itself | Found by LNK-M-0036's documentation-truth dimension. **Limb one, under-reporting** (`:301-304`): the paragraph says "The events recorded today are" — present tense, no as-of scoping — and lists the root redirect, the invitation lifecycle and LNK-M-0027's membership, workspace and organization changes. | [LNK-F-0020](#lnk-f-0020) | `/workspaces` and `/members` return 500 on a plain GET once an organization has more than one workspace | Reproduced live on the test instance and confirmed by the server's own log: `render failed … page=workspaces error="ui: render page workspaces: template: nav.html:30:61: executing \"workspace_switch\" at <.OrganizationName>: can't evaluate field OrganizationName in type team.Workspace"`, and an identical line for `page=members`. Creation itself succeeds — the POST 303s and the row is in Postgres; the page you land on is what fails. **The trigger is >1 workspace in the CURRENT organization, not >1 overall**: an adversarial verifier held a user with six workspaces across two orgs and got 200 while acting in the one-workspace org, 500 on switching back, because `team.Service.Workspaces` filters on `actor.OrgID` (`internal/team/workspace.go:60`). A regression test written from the looser wording would pass without the fix. Two further symptoms: the switcher is silently **absent** from both pages rather than merely broken, so the two pages most about workspaces are the two you cannot switch from; and `renderWorkspacesError` re-renders the same broken page, so a duplicate workspace name answers 500 instead of 422 and validation messages on that page are unreachable. Every other authenticated GET route was swept and is unaffected. `/members` additionally needs `members.write`, so a read-only member sees no error at all | closed |
| [LNK-F-0021](#lnk-f-0021) | Picking a workspace in the header dropdown does nothing until **Switch** is pressed, and any navigation silently discards the choice | Found by adversarial verification of two owner reports that a selection *resets* between pages and that the links page *does not update*. Both are this: the store-level switch is sound (`POST /workspace/switch` persists `users.last_workspace_id` and survives new sessions, 500 pages, API calls and short-link hits), but the UI never sends that POST unless the button is pressed, so the next render re-emits `selected` at the workspace the user is actually in and their pick vanishes. The template's own comment records what it believed was the cause — an auto-submitting select needs a change handler and the CSP forbids inline script — so this reads as a deliberate design whose affordance misleads, not an oversight. It is what the owner actually experienced. **That justification is false, and the tree falsifies it** (checked 2026-08-02, draining the queue): the CSP forbids *inline* script and always did, but htmx has been served from `internal/ui/static/js/htmx.min.js` since LNK-M-0006 (`13fb0f6`), is loaded by `layout.html:9` on every page, and runs under `script-src 'self'` — `internal/httpx/middleware.go:266-270` says so in as many words. `internal/ui/templates/pages/links.html:56` already ships **exactly** the control this finding says was impossible: `<select name="status" hx-get="/links" hx-trigger="change">`, needing no inline script and no CSP waiver. So the two-step was never forced by the CSP; it was a change handler nobody wired | closed |

| [LNK-F-0023](#lnk-f-0023) | Aliases are global across workspaces, so the create form leaks the existence of another workspace's aliases | Reproduced: creating a link in Sales with an alias already used in Marketing answers `409 alias "vmk2" is already in use`. Two costs: the same alias cannot be used in two workspaces, and a 409 tells a member of one workspace that an alias exists in another they may not be able to see. **Re-derived 2026-08-04 (LNK-M-0052) against the tree LNK-M-0044 and LNK-M-0045 left**, because this row's own evidence pointed forward to them: the query comment it quoted (*"Phase 2 gives a workspace its own and this gains a filter"*) has been discharged — `GetWorkspaceDefaultDomain` now takes the workspace and prefers its own verified hostname, then an organization-owned one, then the instance default, and says so at `links.sql:354-357`. So the collision is no longer instance-wide by construction: it is bounded to workspaces that **share** a domain, which means every workspace still on the instance default, and the workspaces of one organization sharing an organization-owned hostname | closed |
| [LNK-F-0024](#lnk-f-0024) | The dashboard shows two different numbers for the same link's clicks, side by side | Found while adversarially verifying that the dashboard scopes by workspace (it does). With 7 human and 2 bot clicks on one link, the row read 9 and the tile read 7, on the same page for the same workspace. | [LNK-F-0025](#lnk-f-0025) | `ResolveWorkspaceForUser` does not check the organization's `deleted_at` while `ListWorkspacesForUser` does | Verified by reading both queries. So either F71's stated cause is incomplete or there is a second one; what is *not* plausible is that LNK-M-0046 caused it, because the seeder's click generation runs before `demoSeeder.run` and is untouched by this milestone, and disabling LNK-M-0046's seeding entirely was one of the runs that passed. **Observed a third time on 2026-08-04, during LNK-M-0052**, on a tree whose only change was this file: 34746 on the first run and 34898 on the second and third — a **152-click** delta, reported by both `demo_coverage_test.go:744` and `:778`, with logged seeder runtimes of 3.435s, 3.382s and 3.446s. Green on an immediate `GOFLAGS=-count=1` re-run. Two independent observations now sit two orders of magnitude above F71's mechanism, and the deltas are unequal (252, then 152), so whatever the second cause is, it is not a fixed quantity | closed |
| [LNK-F-0075](#lnk-f-0075) | Revoking an API key is scoped to the key's id and its **owner**, with no organization check, while listing keys is scoped to the owner *and* the organization — so the two disagree about which keys an… | Read from the two statements, not reproduced. Both keys are that user's own, so nothing crosses a tenancy boundary and no key is destroyed that its owner could not have destroyed by switching organization first. What it does give is a weak existence oracle — `204` versus `404` distinguishes *my key, elsewhere* from *not mine* — against ids the caller would have to guess. Not touched by LNK-M-0049: rotation adds no revoke path, and the milestone's org-wide keys are still revoked by their own owner | closed |

DNS and certificates for those names already exist | closed |
| [LNK-F-0077](#lnk-f-0077) | A host spelled with Unicode label separators or fullwidth characters walks past every destination tier, and is stored and served | **Reproduced live against the current build.** `POST /api/v1/links` accepted and stored `http://169。254。169。254/latest/meta-data/`, `http://１６９.２５４.１６９.２５４/`, `http://ｌｏｃａｌｈｏｓｔ/`, `http://metadata。google。internal/computeMetadata/v1/` and `http://127。0。0。1/admin`, each percent-escaped into storage, while the control `http://169.254.169.254/` was refused 422. So the defect is one missing deadline and not a missing mechanism. Log flood measured at **3697 lines / 14.7 MiB in 2 s**. Every attack on it failed — a non-superuser alters its own per-database settings with no grant, since these are USERSET; there is no `SET ROLE` escape hatch because `addons.go:417-418` logs the pool in **as** the role, which is why startup applies the rows; `pin` (`addons.go:1195-1197`) pins only `search_path` and `statement_timeout`, and replaying inside that transaction still reads 4GB. **Wider than first filed**: `IN DATABASE <any name>` is accepted including databases the role cannot connect to, so a one-database repair is also incomplete, and no `DROP ROLE` path exists anywhere in the product, so the rows outlive uninstall. **The test that guards this is structurally blind** — `test/integration/addon_storage_test.go:1432` sets the plain variant and its verifier `roleConfig` at `:1484` reads only `pg_roles` | closed |

## HRD-F-0001

**Valheim's catalog root is the whole IronGate folder, and Steam Cloud is on by default**

finding · 2026-09-13

w: [HRD-W-0001](work-units/HRD-W-0001.md#hrd-w-0001)

The Ludusavi catalog roots Valheim at <xdgConfig>/unity3d/IronGate/Valheim on Linux and <home>/AppData/LocalLow/IronGate/Valheim on Windows, with cloud_steam true (hoard-manifest/data/ludusavi-catalog.json.zst, slug valheim). Worlds sit under worlds_local and characters under characters_local, so a Hoard save of that root ships characters with the world. With Steam Cloud enabled Valheim keeps worlds in worlds rather than worlds_local and Steam syncs them, so a shared world needs Steam Cloud off for Valheim on every member's machine, or Hoard tracking worlds_local only. Documentation for members, and a check the client could make.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Consequence | world scope needs a file subset; members disable Steam Cloud for Valheim |

## HRD-F-0002

**Valheim most likely does not hold the world file open, which makes file evidence a late backstop**

finding · 2026-09-13

w: [HRD-W-0001](work-units/HRD-W-0001.md#hrd-w-0001)

Unverified on a real install; from what I know of the game: the world is read at load and written by autosave (default every 30 minutes, -saveinterval) and on exit as <name>.db.new renamed over <name>.db, with the previous copy kept as .db.old. If so, /proc/<pid>/fd (agent.rs:4837) and the Windows sharing-violation probe (locks.rs) see the file only for the moment of load, which a 2 s poll catches by luck, and the first write can be 30 minutes in. The claim prompt becomes the primary signal and the design's item 3 the backstop. To verify before phase 2: inotifywait on worlds_local during a session on Linux, Process Monitor on Windows, noting open, write and rename events and whether .fwl is rewritten at load.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Status | claim to verify; owner has the game, this VM does not |

## HRD-F-0005

**The desktop app's connection test passes on a plain-http address behind Cloudflare, and sign-in then fails with no useful message**

finding · 2026-09-13

q: [HRD-Q-0009](questions.md#hrd-q-0009)

w: [HRD-W-0001](work-units/HRD-W-0001.md#hrd-w-0001)

Cloudflare answers http://hoard.killerofpie.com with a 301 to https. The app's Test connection is an unauthenticated GET /v1/health, which reqwest follows across the redirect, so it reports the server reached. Sign-in calls /v1/auth/whoami with a bearer token; reqwest drops the Authorization header when a redirect changes the origin, and the server answers 401 without a database lookup, so nothing shows in its log and the app shows the 401 as the key being refused. Pie hit exactly this on 2026-09-13 and it cost a token-format investigation. normalizeUrl in ServerSetup.svelte already picks https for a public hostname; the trap is a typed http:// prefix, which it keeps verbatim (ServerSetup.svelte:36). Fix candidates for the fork, later: have the health check report the final URL after redirects and reflect it into the field, or warn when a typed http address answered through an https redirect.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Status | defect noted, not fixed; upstream-relevant |

## HRD-F-0008

**The self-hosted event stream is read by the desktop, not the engine, so lease frames need an engine-side listener**

finding · 2026-09-13

w: [HRD-W-0001](work-units/HRD-W-0001.md#hrd-w-0001)

The only consumer of GET /v1/events is hoard-desktop/src/commands/selfhosted_events.rs (connect_once :157, handle_event :220), which turns a save frame into an IPC ForceRestore. hoard-agent has no SSE client; its cloud counterpart is cloud_live.rs (WebSocket). A lease frame that only the desktop sees never reaches the engine that must hold the lease, and a CLI-only machine sees none. Phase 2 therefore adds an SSE loop in hoard-agent beside cloud_live.rs that handles lease frames and, for now, ignores save frames, leaving the desktop loop as it is; folding the save frame into the engine loop and retiring the desktop one is a later cleanup. Also noted from the map: AgentEvent has no serde(other) catch-all (ipc/events.rs:45), so a client older than its daemon fails to read new event kinds; the fork ships all three binaries together, so this only matters for mixed installs.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Consequence | phase 2 gains hoard-agent/src/selfhosted_live.rs; plan.md updated when phase 2 is briefed |

## HRD-F-0009

**Review of PR 1 found ten confirmed defects in the server half, three of them data loss**

finding · 2026-09-13

w: [HRD-W-0001](work-units/HRD-W-0001.md#hrd-w-0001)

Posted as inline comments on https://github.com/DevOfPie/hoard/pull/1 at 278d887 on 2026-09-13. (1) store.rs:511 purge_owned_groups on owner deletion deletes every object in the group, including saves other members shared in, which then point at keys that no longer exist. (2) cas.rs:660, snapshots create, share.rs:214: the namespace is resolved before the transaction, so a share racing a push lands a version in the wrong namespace; unshare then 500s forever. (3) cleanup.rs:307 purge_trash resolves the namespace outside its transaction and skips a None decref, so a racing share skews refcounts either way, up to deleting a blob another save still uses. (4) saves.rs:360 deleting a shared save cascades without touching group refcounts or the owner's charge; groups.rs:241 group delete never purges objects. (5) admin.rs:626 deleting a member who shared into someone else's group leaves the group's refcounts and charge behind. (6) 0022_groups.sql:34,37 group_invites.created_by and used_by reference users with no ON DELETE, so deleting a user who redeemed an invite fails on the foreign key after the object purge already ran. (7) groups.rs:405 removing a member leaves their shared_saves row: the group owner keeps paying, cannot unshare, cannot delete the group, and the removed member can still push. (8) same site: the departing member's live lease is not ended. (9) groups.rs:358 invite redemption checks used_at outside the transaction and the UPDATE has no used_at IS NULL guard, so two concurrent redeemers both join. (10) leases.rs:258 acquire uses a deferred transaction, so two concurrent acquires give one a 500 instead of 409 held; BEGIN IMMEDIATE fixes it and require_host at cas.rs:905 has the same race. Fixes follow on the same branch, then a second PR comment.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Severity | three data-loss (1, 3, 4), two lockouts (6, 7), two races (9, 10) |

## HRD-F-0011

**Moving the demo from a branch to the v1.1.7 release took it down: the database was ahead of the binary's migrations**

finding · 2026-09-13

d: [HRD-D-0015](decisions.md#hrd-d-0015)

w: [HRD-W-0001](work-units/HRD-W-0001.md#hrd-w-0001)

2026-09-13 08:01: after the first release-following deploy, hoard-server 1.1.7 refused to start with 'migration 22 was previously applied but is missing in the resolved migrations', restarting nine times. The demo had run the sharing branches, whose migrations 0022 to 0027 were applied to its database; the release knows 0001 to 0021. Fix applied: service stopped, database backed up (data/hoard.db.bak-branch-*), the six sharing tables dropped and the _sqlx_migrations rows for 22 to 27 deleted, service started; users and tokens untouched. Guard added to deploy.sh: it refuses a ref whose migration count is below the database's applied maximum. Rule that follows: while the demo follows releases, a branch with new migrations is deployed to it only if the roll-back is accepted in advance.

| --- | --- |
| Downtime | about 20 minutes |
| Status | resolved 2026-09-13 08:3x by HRD-D-0017; total downtime about 35 minutes |

Posted on https://github.com/DevOfPie/hoard/pull/7 at 7dd2c31 on 2026-09-13 from six review angles. Correctness: remember_save drops a shared row's include list; adopt seeds an empty list when the server errs and seats the slot unscoped; a restore with a destination override builds its safety copy and gate from an empty list; share_save loads state.json before its HTTP calls and clobbers hoardd's writes; share and unshare resume a paused row; a local failure after the server succeeded reports an error with the server already moved; the server never enforces include_json on a push; the include grammar cannot name a per-world directory and is a persisted format. Structure: SharedRef should carry include; one RestoreGate::for_row; LiveReseat instead of a second reseat path. Efficiency: per-file allocations in included, no directory pruning, blocking IO on the IPC task. The reviews of PR 4 and PR 8 died on the session's API limit (resets 11:10 UTC) and rerun after it.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Severity | one design change (server-side enforcement plus prefix grammar) before any row exists |

finding · 2026-09-13

## IDW-F-0004

**The sub-agent drawer can be dragged wider on a desktop screen**

finding · 2026-08-26

Superseded by: [MUS-F-0047](#mus-f-0047)

Filed by the owner: the drawer takes more space than it needs on a laptop, and being able to drag it wider would be nice when wanted.

Built. A grip on the drawer's leading edge, above 60rem only — on a phone the drawer is already most of the screen and there is nothing to widen into. It is a button with a separator role rather than a decorated edge, so it is focusable and moves on the arrow keys: a drag handle that answers only a pointer is one that some people cannot move at all.

Only --drawer-w is set. Everything that has to move with it already reads that variable — the drawer's width, and the min() the reading column and the composer share — so the composer narrows in step without the resize code knowing the composer exists.

The width is remembered per browser; the drawer's open state deliberately is not (MUS-Q-0057). Those are different kinds of thing: shut by default is a statement about what is happening, and a width is how this screen suits this person. Re-dragging it every load would be the annoyance the request exists to remove. Stated as an assumption rather than asked, because it is one line either way.

This record stayed in the idea inbox. Correcting its routing is blocked on MUS-Q-0058, because the identifier prefix is the routing and there is no way to change one without deciding what happens to the other.

| Where | internal/web/sessions.go, internal/web/assets/session.js |

At 390x844 the grip is absent entirely. |

## LNK-F-0001

**Release-notes extraction sweeps up the changelog's link-reference block**

finding · 2026-07-31

cites: [LNK-M-0052](milestones.md#lnk-m-0052)

Release-notes extraction sweeps up the changelog's link-reference block

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | 0.1.0 release |
| Where | `.github/workflows/release.yml`, the "Extract this version's changelog section" step |
| Evidence | The `awk` runs from `## [<version>]` to the next `## [` heading. The newest version is always the last section in `CHANGELOG.md`, so the trailing reference definitions are inside that range: the published v0.1.0 body carries `[Unreleased]: …` and `[0.1.0]: …` immediately before the `### Container image` section. Confirmed against the live release body, not inferred. |
| Severity | Cosmetic. Markdown renders link *definitions* as nothing, so a reader sees no artefact; the cruft is in the raw body only. It will recur on every release, because the newest section is last every time. |
| Reviewed | Yes — owner approved 2026-07-31, scheduled as LNK-M-0052, which is the only milestone it can sit in: the extraction runs solely inside the release workflow, so the fix has to be checked against CHANGELOG.md as it will be at 0.2.0 before the tag exists rather than confirmed by publishing. **Fix written and verified 2026-08-06, waiting on the owner to apply it.** It lands in `.github/workflows/release.yml`, which the agent's token may not push — see W29 and `ci/proposed/release.yml`. The row stays **open** rather than closed on a written fix: the extraction that runs at the 0.2.0 tag is the live workflow, not the proposal, so until it is applied the release body carries the link definitions exactly as v0.1.0's does. **Corrected 2026-08-06, and it lowers the urgency I claimed.** The defect bites only the section that is *last* in `CHANGELOG.md`, because that is the only one whose range runs off the end into the reference block. v0.1.0 was hit because it was the first release and therefore last in the file. Once `[0.2.0]` was cut, `[0.1.0]` sits beneath it — and both the old program and the new one extract 0.2.0 with **zero** reference definitions, measured against the real file. So this does **not** block the 0.2.0 release, and my earlier statement that the release body would carry them was wrong. The fix stays proposed and worth applying: it is defensive against a future release that becomes last, and against anyone reordering the file. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-06, applied by the owner as `447095c` — the fix is in `.github/workflows/release.yml` and the row closes on the live workflow rather than on the proposal, which is the distinction it stayed open for. Verified against the real `CHANGELOG.md` by running the live program over **both** released sections: 0.2.0 gives 1802 lines and 0.1.0 gives 164, each with zero stray reference definitions and no trailing blank. **The urgency I claimed was wrong and is corrected above**: the defect bites only whichever section is last in the file, so 0.2.0 was never going to carry them and this was defensive rather than blocking. One flaw surfaced on the way in and is **not** fixed here: the proposal was a whole-file copy with a `# PROPOSAL` header, so applying it put that header on the live workflow, which now opens by telling a reader to apply a file they are already reading. Removing it is itself a workflow change the token cannot push — W30, proposed. It is cosmetic and F1 closes without it, because what F1 asserts is what the `awk` extracts. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F1 |

## LNK-F-0002

**A stalled Redis stretches a link edit to about nine seconds**

finding · 2026-07-31

cites: [LNK-M-0018](milestones.md#lnk-m-0018)

cites: [LNK-M-0003](milestones.md#lnk-m-0003)

cites: [LNK-M-0025](milestones.md#lnk-m-0025)

cites: [LNK-D-0026](decisions.md#lnk-d-0026)

A stalled Redis stretches a link edit to about nine seconds

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0018 |
| Where | `internal/redirect/resolver.go`, `deleteFromRedis` |
| Evidence | Measured while building LNK-M-0018, against a TCP proxy that accepts the connection and then never answers — which is what a stalled Redis looks like, as opposed to a refused connection, which fails in 264ms. `InvalidateAlias` took **9.07s** with the publish removed, so the time is the delete path alone: it makes three attempts, each given `RedisTimeout` (50ms in the test), and go-redis does not honour that context when it has to establish a connection to a server that never speaks. The measurement is in the transcript for LNK-M-0018; the same shape is reproducible with `redisProxy.blackholed(true)` in `test/integration/invalidation_test.go`. Predates LNK-M-0018 — the retry loop is LNK-M-0003's — and LNK-M-0018's own publish was made fire-and-forget so it adds nothing to this. |
| Severity | Moderate. Not data loss: the edit completes, the local tier is cleared, and correctness is unaffected. But `HTTP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` is 15s, so an edit made while Redis is stalled comes within a few seconds of timing out, and a Redis stall is exactly when an operator is most likely to be changing things. |
| Reviewed | Yes — owner approved 2026-07-31, scheduled as LNK-M-0025. That milestone corrects this row's attribution: the cause is two retry layers multiplying (the outer 3-attempt loop times go-redis's unset `MaxRetries` default of 3, over a 1s dial budget) rather than a context go-redis fails to honour. 3 × 3 × 1s matches the 9.07s measured. |
| Closed by | LNK-M-0025, 2026-07-31. Closed by bounding the whole retry loop with one budget (`REDIS_INVALIDATE_BUDGET`, 250ms, D26) rather than by lowering a timeout. This row's evidence is right and is left as written: go-redis really does ignore the context on a stalled read, and the *Reviewed* cell's correction of it — two retry layers multiplying over a 1s dial budget — is wrong on both counts. Measured for LNK-M-0025: `MaxRetries` does not multiply a read that timed out, and `REDIS_DIAL_TIMEOUT` is not involved at all against a server that accepts the connection. The arithmetic is 3 outer attempts x the client's `ReadTimeout`, and the 3s in that product was go-redis's own default in `redisProxy.client`, which sets no timeouts. The shipped client sets 50ms from `REDIS_READ_TIMEOUT`, so the same stall cost a deployment **215ms, not 9.07s** — the severity above was measured through a client no deployment runs, and the edit was never near `HTTP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT`. What was genuinely broken is that a documented, operator-tunable knob was multiplied by three on a path an operator waits on. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F2 |

## LNK-F-0003

**Dark mode has no effect on the UI: the light tokens are unlayered and beat every dark rule**

finding · 2026-07-31

cites: [LNK-M-0020](milestones.md#lnk-m-0020)

cites: [LNK-M-0022](milestones.md#lnk-m-0022)

cites: [LNK-M-0032](milestones.md#lnk-m-0032)

cites: [LNK-M-0042](milestones.md#lnk-m-0042)

cites: [LNK-M-0043](milestones.md#lnk-m-0043)

cites: [LNK-M-0046](milestones.md#lnk-m-0046)

cites: [LNK-M-0048](milestones.md#lnk-m-0048)

cites: [LNK-M-0049](milestones.md#lnk-m-0049)

Dark mode has no effect on the UI: the light tokens are unlayered and beat every dark rule

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0020 |
| Where | `internal/ui/static/css/input.css` — light `:root` block at line 88, dark rules at lines 139–178 (`@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`) and 182 (`:root[data-theme="dark"]`) |
| Evidence | Owner report, 2026-07-31, and confirmed by construction rather than inferred from the symptom. The light `:root` block sits at the top level of the file; both dark blocks sit inside `@layer base`. CSS cascade layers give **unlayered** normal declarations priority over layered ones regardless of specificity, so `:root { --t-surface: #f8fafc }` unconditionally beats `:root[data-theme="dark"] { --t-surface: #0f172a }`. Walking the built `app.css` top level confirms it survives the build: the dark override is inside the `@layer base { … }` construct, and `:root { color-scheme: light; … }` is emitted after `@layer utilities` closes, as its own unlayered top-level rule. Both dark paths are dead, the explicit override and the `prefers-color-scheme` one, which is why `color-scheme: dark` never takes either — matching "changing to Dark Mode does nothing". The server side is *correct* and is not implicated: the demo serves `data-theme="dark"`, `data-theme="light"` and no attribute across the three cookie states. **The milestone's own enforcement cannot catch this**: `TestTemplatesUseThemeTokensOnly` asserts templates name tokens, and the AA contrast figures are recorded in comments, so nothing tests that a token's *value* ever changes. A fix wants a test that fails on this specific cascade, not more contrast arithmetic. |
| Severity | **Critical.** LNK-M-0020's headline claim — every dashboard page follows `prefers-color-scheme`, and an explicit override renders in the chosen theme — is false in the shipped build. The milestone was reopened rather than corrected by a successor, so the status row now reads `in progress (reopened)` and no longer asserts something untrue. The AA contrast claim is false by consequence: the dark figures describe values no browser applies. LNK-M-0020 was placed before LNK-M-0022, LNK-M-0032, LNK-M-0042, LNK-M-0043, LNK-M-0046, LNK-M-0048 and LNK-M-0049 precisely so those build inside a working theme; every UI milestone landing before this is fixed is written and reviewed against a dark theme that cannot be seen, which is the retrofit the ordering existed to avoid. |
| Reviewed | Yes — owner-reported; folded into reopened LNK-M-0020, 2026-07-31 |
| Closed by | LNK-M-0020, 2026-07-31. Every `--t-*` block is now unlayered, so the dark selectors win on specificity and source order; `TestThemeTokensShareOneCascadeLayer` was shown failing against the stylesheet built from `b289a39` before it counted, and the live check now resolves the cascade against the composed stack rather than confirming the attribute. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F3 |

## LNK-F-0008

**The rate limiter's comment blames a stalled Redis on connection establishment, which measurement contradicts**

finding · 2026-07-31

cites: [LNK-M-0025](milestones.md#lnk-m-0025)

cites: [LNK-M-0019](milestones.md#lnk-m-0019)

cites: [LNK-F-0002](#lnk-f-0002)

cites: [LNK-M-0052](milestones.md#lnk-m-0052)

cites: [LNK-F-0138](#lnk-f-0138)

The rate limiter's comment blames a stalled Redis on connection establishment, which measurement contradicts

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0025 |
| Where | `internal/ratelimit/shared.go:143`–`:144`, in `take`'s doc comment: "does not honour the context deadline go-redis is handed **when it has to establish a connection**" |
| Evidence | Measured for LNK-M-0025 on 2026-07-31. The context is not honoured on a stalled read whether or not a connection has to be established: a client with `ReadTimeout` 400ms took 401ms to fail a command carrying a 50ms context both against a server that never answered the handshake *and* down a connection established beforehand and then left to go quiet mid-command. What bounds the wait is the client's own `ReadTimeout`; connection establishment has nothing to do with it, and a dial in isolation does honour the deadline (8s dial timeout, 50ms context, 50ms elapsed). The comment's conclusion — enforce the deadline from outside the call — is correct and the code is correct; only the stated reason is wrong, which makes it the kind of comment that misleads the next person deciding whether the same defence is needed somewhere else. |
| Severity | Cosmetic, and comment-only. No behaviour is affected and LNK-M-0019's mechanism is the right one. It is recorded rather than corrected in place because LNK-M-0025's bullets reach the invalidation path, the redirect path and F2's row, and none of them reach `internal/ratelimit` — a comment correction there is out of spec, and this repository's rule is that a shipped milestone's claim is reopened by the owner's scheduling, not by the worker who noticed. |
| Reviewed | Approved as work 2026-08-04 — LNK-M-0052's triage, the cheap comment sweep. Fixed under **LNK-M-0052's own number**: m45.md's Findings bullet is this work, so no milestone is reopened. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, `internal/ratelimit/shared.go` — `take`'s doc keeps its conclusion and loses its reason. Re-measured at the pinned go-redis **v9.21.0** rather than taken from this row: a command carrying a 50ms context against a server that accepts and never answers cost **401ms** with `ReadTimeout` 400ms, on a connection established beforehand and then left to go quiet as well as on one still being made, while a bare dial under the same context cost 50ms. The mechanism turned out to be nameable, which the row could not say: `baseClient.context` (`redis.go:1033-1038`) hands the socket deadline `context.Background()` unless `Options.ContextTimeoutEnabled` is set, and `internal/platform/redis` does not set it — setting it in the probe brought the same stall to 50ms. So the comment now says `ReadTimeout` bounds the wait and points at `internal/platform/redis`, whose own comment has carried the measurement since LNK-M-0025. F2's *multiple seconds* is deliberately not carried forward: F2's own Closed cell corrects that to 215ms through the shipped client. The option this uncovered is F138, not a change here. |

## LNK-F-0009

**An uncached redirect pays `REDIS_READ_TIMEOUT` twice while Redis is stalled, not once**

finding · 2026-07-31

cites: [LNK-M-0025](milestones.md#lnk-m-0025)

cites: [LNK-M-0052](milestones.md#lnk-m-0052)

cites: [LNK-F-0098](#lnk-f-0098)

An uncached redirect pays `REDIS_READ_TIMEOUT` twice while Redis is stalled, not once

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0025 |
| Where | `internal/redirect/resolver.go` — `fromRedis` (the failed `Get`) and `store` (the `Set` that repopulates), both reached synchronously from `Resolve` |
| Evidence | Measured for LNK-M-0025 on 2026-07-31, against `redisProxy.blackholed(true)` with a client built the way `internal/platform/redis.Open` builds one (`DialTimeout` 1s, `ReadTimeout` 50ms). A cold `Resolve` took **108ms**; the two following resolves took 0s, because the in-process tier was populated. The 108ms is 50ms of failed lookup, plus the Postgres query, plus 50ms of `Set` against a server that will not answer it either. Both calls are bounded and neither retries, so this is not the compounding LNK-M-0025 was scheduled for — that was the invalidation path's three-attempt loop, now bounded — but the `redis.go` comment claiming a stalled Redis "costs a little latency" was written about one call and there are two. |
| Severity | Minor. Nothing is wrong, only slow, and only while Redis is stalled: the redirect is still served from Postgres. The documented uncached target is 100ms and a stalled cache puts a cold redirect just past it, so the cost is an SLO the operator cannot meet during a Redis stall rather than a failure. The obvious fix — skip the repopulating `Set` when the lookup just timed out — is a change to the redirect path and therefore owes the k6 re-run, which is why it is not taken inside a milestone that deliberately left that path alone. |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 4, minor — redirect path and cache. The batch owes one k6 re-run, not six. Deliberately **not merged** with F98 by LNK-M-0052's queue hygiene, 2026-08-04. Same class — a stalled Redis costing `REDIS_READ_TIMEOUT` on the redirect path, against a document that says it costs nothing — but different call sites (`resolver.go`'s failed `Get` and repopulating `Set` versus `analytics/returning.go`'s `SISMEMBER`), different cache tiers, different SLOs (100ms uncached, 20ms cached), different false sentences, and incompatible fixes: this row's is to skip the repopulating `Set`, and F98's own note rules out both of the obvious ones. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05. The repopulating `Set` is skipped when the lookup that led to it just failed for any reason other than the key being absent — a server that will not answer a `Get` will not usefully answer the `Set`. Recorded on the resolver rather than threaded through the call, because the stall is a property of the server and the write happens inside a singleflight whose leader may be a different request than the one that saw it; the window is `DBTimeout`, one uncached resolve, which is exactly the span between the failed read and the write it provokes. **Deliberately not a circuit breaker**: reads are never skipped, because a read is how the cache recovers. The in-process tier is still populated, so skipping costs only that the shared tier stays cold for a window in which it was cold anyway. `TestAStalledRedisIsPaidForOncePerResolve` runs against a listener that accepts and never answers, at a 400ms timeout so the two outcomes are hundreds of milliseconds apart rather than tens; shown red by removing the skip, at *400.869753ms*. A second test asserts the suppression lapses, so one transient stall does not stop the shared tier being written to for the life of the process. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F9 |

## LNK-F-0011

finding · 2026-08-01

cites: [LNK-D-0020](decisions.md#lnk-d-0020)

`TestInvalidationReachesAnotherReplica` is flaky

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0027 |
| Where | `test/integration/invalidation_test.go:276` — "the second replica did not cache the alias in process" |
| Evidence | Observed 2026-08-01 while running LNK-M-0027's gates. Two consecutive uncached full runs (`GOFLAGS=-count=1 make test-integration`) of the same tree: the first failed on this assertion, the second passed, and three earlier full runs of the same tree during the milestone passed. Nothing in LNK-M-0027 touches the redirect path, the resolver, Redis or the invalidation subscriber — the milestone's diff is `internal/team`, `internal/httpx`, `internal/ui`, `internal/auth`'s provisioning helper and one migration — so the change under test is not a plausible cause. The assertion is that a *second* replica has populated its in-process tier, which is reached by a prior request whose caching is asynchronous relative to the assertion; that is the shape a timing-dependent assertion has. |
| Severity | Minor, and test-only — no product behaviour is implicated. The cost is a gate that fails for the wrong reason, which is expensive in a loop that treats a failing gate as a stop condition: a flake here reads identically to a real regression in whatever milestone happens to be in flight, and the next person will spend the same run re-running it to find out which. |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 5, minor — one-edit corrections. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05. The test warms the second replica's cache without waiting for the subscriber it started in a goroutine, and every establishment — including the first — flushes both in-process tiers, which is D20 and is correct. So the warm-up was racing a flush it had no way to see, which is why one run in five failed on a tree that never touched the redirect path. It now waits on `PUBSUB NUMSUB` for the channel before warming: Redis is asked, because there is no readiness hook and a test-only row is not where one gets added to the product. The barrier also makes the invalidation half prove itself — without it the publish could beat the subscription, the message be missed, and the establishment flush drop the entry anyway, so the test passed while demonstrating nothing about the thing it exists for. Eight consecutive runs green; sabotaged by publishing to a dead channel, which times it out. |

finding · 2026-07-31

cites: [LNK-D-0018](decisions.md#lnk-d-0018)

cites: [LNK-F-0104](#lnk-f-0104)

D18's text does not describe the map it governs, in two ways: applied literally its two limbs would make an irreversible permission delegable, and its *"either direction"* sentence promises a disarming the code never performs

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0028 |
| Where | Plan.md's D18 row, against `auth.NonDelegableScopes` at `internal/auth/apikey.go:186` and the comment stating the wider rule at `:131-143`; enforcement at `resolveScopes` (`internal/auth/apikey.go:607`, the mint path) and `narrowScopes` (`internal/auth/apikey_rotation.go:320-338`, the rotation path), against `Authenticate` (`:515-598`), whose `identity.restrictTo(row.Scopes)` at `:589` re-filters on the owner's role and nothing else |
| Evidence | Found while recording `org.delete`'s delegability, which m28.5.md required be named against D18. D18 says a permission is non-delegable "when reading it exposes an actor's identity tied to network data, **or** when holding it lets a key widen its own reach. Everything else is delegable." `org.delete` does neither — it discloses nothing and removes tenancy rather than granting any — yet it has been in `NonDelegableScopes` since Phase 1's `00700_seed.sql`, on irreversibility. The map's own comment states the wider rule explicitly: "the rule this map encodes is now 'escalating, irreversible, or disclosing' rather than only the first two." So the code and the decision text disagree about what the rule *is*, and the code is the one that has been right since before D18 was written (2026-07-31). **Folded in from F56 (LNK-M-0036), 2026-08-04:** the same decision's other sentence is wrong the other way. D18 says *"Flipping a permission in **either direction** stays a one-line map edit"*, and it does not: adding an already-granted permission to `NonDelegableScopes` would not disarm keys already issued, because `Authenticate` restricts the identity to the **row's** stored scopes and never consults the map. Never exploitable — `git log -S` confirms all the entries landed in the same commit as the migration creating their permission (`a0f23ff` for `audit.read`/00900, `e8a6b1c` for `destinations.review`/01600, the Phase-1 seed for the rest), so no key has ever held a scope that later became non-delegable. F56's own "only enforcement" reading is now **one site out of date** and is corrected here rather than carried forward: LNK-M-0049's rotation added a second check, `narrowScopes` at `apikey_rotation.go:328-338`, which refuses to carry a now-non-delegable scope into a successor. Mint and rotate are covered; request time is not. F56's cited claim at `apikey.go:147-149` was an over-read — that comment is about the *deleting* direction and is true there. |
| Severity | Minor today, and latent rather than active: no permission is mis-classified in the tree, and `org.delete` is correctly non-delegable. The cost is the next milestone that adds an irreversible permission — LNK-M-0049's rotation scopes are the near candidate — applying D18's two limbs as written, finding neither matches, and concluding the scope is delegable. Correcting it means rewording a decision, which is the owner's, and D18 is referenced by name from six milestone files. Absorbs F56's limb, which was filed **Note / informational** and stays that: no defect in shipped behaviour, and the fix is either an accurate one-line correction to D18 or an `isNonDelegable` filter in `restrictTo` as belt-and-braces — the helper already exists at `internal/auth/apikey.go:675-678` and is called from the two write paths but not from the read one. Both limbs are corrections to the same decision's text, which is why they are one row. |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 5, minor — one-edit corrections. **F56 (LNK-M-0036) was merged into this row** by LNK-M-0052's queue hygiene, 2026-08-04: both convict D18's wording against the same map, and one reword answers both. **F104 was deliberately not merged** although it calls itself *"F12's shape a second time"* — same shape, different rule, different file, different code: correcting D18 does nothing for `phase-details/README.md:75`, and merging on shape alone would put two unrelated repairs behind one disposition. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05, owner-answered. **The text is corrected and the map is untouched**, which is the direction this row argued for: the code has been right since before D18 was written. Limb one now reads *escalating, irreversible, or disclosing* — the three-limb rule `NonDelegableScopes`'s own comment has stated all along — so `org.delete` is described by the rule that has governed it since Phase 1. Limb two is **narrowed rather than deleted**: adding a scope to the map binds keys minted and rotated afterwards and does not disarm one already issued, because `Authenticate` restricts to the row's stored scopes and never consults the map. The request-time gap is **documented and left open**, with the price of closing it stated — an `isNonDelegable` filter in `restrictTo` is a check on every authenticated request for a state no key has ever been in. Both corrections are marked in place in the D18 row rather than replacing it, and the near miss is recorded at the map too: the next milestone to add an irreversible permission is the one that would have applied the two limbs, found neither matched, and shipped it delegable. Absorbs F56's limb. No `D` number: decisions.md is append-only and a later entry correcting an earlier one is what it is for. |
| Status | closed |

**Registration answers whether an address already has an account, which on an open instance is a public enumeration oracle**

finding · 2026-08-04

cites: [LNK-M-0029](milestones.md#lnk-m-0029)

cites: [LNK-M-0026](milestones.md#lnk-m-0026)

cites: [LNK-D-0027](decisions.md#lnk-d-0027)

cites: [LNK-M-0052](milestones.md#lnk-m-0052)

cites: [LNK-F-0141](#lnk-f-0141)

Registration answers whether an address already has an account, which on an open instance is a public enumeration oracle

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0029 |
| Where | `internal/signup/signup.go` — `Register`'s `CountUsersByEmail` check, surfaced as `409` by `WriteError`'s `auth.ErrEmailTaken` case in `internal/httpx/problem.go:137` and as "That email address is already registered." by `SignupSubmit` |
| Evidence | Reachable without any credential once the effective mode is `open`: `POST /api/v1/auth/register` with a known address answers `409 conflict`, an unknown one answers `202 verification_sent`, and the browser form makes the same distinction in words. Rate limiting slows a sweep but does not remove the signal. The behaviour is not new — the endpoint has answered `409` for a taken address since Phase 1 — but until LNK-M-0029 the endpoint was API-only and there was no browser form; opening self-serve signup is what makes it a surface a stranger reaches. LNK-M-0026 deliberately spent argon2 work to stop redemption answering the same question (D27), so the product already treats this as something worth not disclosing, and the two surfaces now disagree. |
| Severity | Minor, and bounded by the mode: on a `closed` or `invite` instance the endpoint refuses before it looks anything up, and the shipped default is `closed`. On a deliberately open instance it lets somebody test a leaked address list for membership. The honest fix is to answer `202` either way and mail "you already have an account" to a taken address, which is a behaviour change to a documented status code and a second mail template — scope, not a detail, which is why it is deferred rather than taken inside LNK-M-0029. |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 3, minor — a principal can act on it, in scope by the 2026-08-04 standing rule. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05. A taken address now gets the same `202`, the same body and the same argon2 cost as a free one, and the answer goes to the address by mail — `account-exists`, a fourth template — rather than to whoever typed it into the form. The hash is computed **before** the lookup, deliberately: argon2 is this request by two orders of magnitude, so branching first would have left the timing carrying what the status code stopped carrying. Nothing is written for a taken address, which also closes a smaller thing the row did not name — a pending registration would have superseded whatever the real owner had outstanding, so a stranger could invalidate their link by typing their address in. `TestRegistrationCannotBeAskedWhetherAnAddressIsTaken` compares whole response bodies with only the echoed address and the clock normalized out, **and that is what caught the residue**: the taken branch returned Go's nanosecond clock where the free one returned a value Postgres had truncated to a microsecond, so the fractional digits answered the question. Truncated to match. The 409 is gone from `api/openapi.yaml`, and the unreachable branch in `web_signup.go` is deleted rather than left asserting the opposite of the behaviour — its text also offered a password reset this product has never had (F141). |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F13 |

## LNK-F-0014

**Anyone who can create a link can now write audit rows at will, because every refused destination is recorded**

finding · 2026-08-04

cites: [LNK-M-0030](milestones.md#lnk-m-0030)

cites: [LNK-M-0029](milestones.md#lnk-m-0029)

cites: [LNK-M-0016](milestones.md#lnk-m-0016)

cites: [LNK-D-0005](decisions.md#lnk-d-0005)

cites: [LNK-M-0052](milestones.md#lnk-m-0052)

Anyone who can create a link can now write audit rows at will, because every refused destination is recorded

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0030 |
| Where | `internal/link/blocking.go` — `Service.recordBlocked`, reached from `checkDestination` on every tiered refusal, on all three destination-writing surfaces |
| Evidence | Built into LNK-M-0030 by its own bullet: *every blocked attempt writes an audit event with `ip_prefix` and the attempted URL stored as evidence*. Confirmed by `TestEveryDestinationSurfaceRunsTheFullTierCheck`, which asserts exactly one `destination.blocked` row per refusal. The caller needs `links.create` or `links.update`, so this is not reachable anonymously — but on an instance with open signup (LNK-M-0029) or many members, a holder of an ordinary editor role can loop `POST /api/v1/links` with `http://127.0.0.1/` and add a row per request, each carrying a metadata blob and up to 2 KiB of defanged URL. Nothing rate-limits the write beyond `LINKCTRL_API_RATE_PER_MIN` (600/min by default), and unlike the other eleven audit actions this one records something that did *not* happen, so there is no successful state change bounding how often it can be provoked. |
| Severity | Minor, and bounded rather than unbounded: LNK-M-0016 shipped `LINKCTRL_AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS` and `LINKCTRL_AUDIT_SIZE_WARN_BYTES`, so growth is trimmed and an operator is warned — but retention defaults to `0` (keep forever, D5), which is the configuration where this costs disk indefinitely. The trail is worth more than the risk, which is why the bullet is right and this is a row rather than a design change; the candidate fixes — a per-actor rate on the record, or collapsing repeated identical refusals into one row with a count — are both behaviour changes to a shipped audit contract and belong to whoever schedules them. |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 3, minor — a principal can act on it, in scope by the 2026-08-04 standing rule. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05. `recordBlocked` is bounded per actor **and per refusal code**, ten a minute (`BlockedAuditRatePerMin`), through the same limiter set every other limit is built in — shared via Redis so the bound means one thing across replicas, falling back to local buckets, which errs toward more rows rather than fewer. **The per-code half is the fix, not a refinement**: a per-actor budget would be a suppression tool, because the attacker picks the noise and could bury the refusal that mattered under a flood of a different one. A code nobody has provoked before is always recorded. The bound is on the *row* and never on the block — a destination is refused identically whether or not its audit row is written, and the test asserts that too. Of the two candidates this row named, collapsing repeats into one row with a count was rejected: `audit_logs` is append-only by design and mutating a written row is a larger break of that contract than declining to add one. **LNK-M-0030's bullet is amended, not silently falsified** — it read *Every blocked attempt writes an audit event*, and the amendment carries the bullet as it stood, as amended, and the tree fact. `docs/SECURITY.md`'s audit row says the same in operator terms. Sabotaged twice: keying per actor alone fails the burying assertion, and removing the bound writes twelve rows for twelve identical refusals. |
| Status | closed |

Every organization owner on an instance can read every dispute filed on it, and lift a blocklist entry for everybody

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0032 |
| Where | `internal/store/migrations/01600_destination_disputes.sql` — the grant of `destinations.review` to the owner role; `internal/dispute/dispute.go` — `List` and `decide`, both scoped by the permission and by nothing else; `internal/store/query/disputes.sql` — `ListDestinationDisputes`, which carries no organization predicate |
| Evidence | Built into LNK-M-0032 by the shape of what it governs, and confirmed by `TestTheQueueIsGatedOnTheNewPermission`: the queue query has no `organization_id` filter, and `DeleteBlockedDestination` removes a row from a table 01500 makes instance-wide on purpose. So on an instance with two organizations, A's owner sees that somebody in B tried to link to a given host, sees their address in `filed_by`, and can delete the entry that refuses it for both. With `LINKCTRL_SIGNUP_MODE=open` (LNK-M-0029) that reach is one registration away, because registering provisions an organization and makes the registrant its owner. The queue *cannot* honestly be narrower than the decision — a per-organization view over an instance-wide effect would hide rows the same reader is deciding for — so this is the tenancy model showing through rather than a scoping mistake. |
| Severity | Moderate, and the same shape as something already shipped rather than new: `domains.write` has been granted to owner and admin since 00800 and changes where the link domain's root sends every workspace's stray visitors. This is one degree wider because it decides what every workspace may link to, and because LNK-M-0032 adds a cross-organization *read* that `domains.write` does not have. The root cause is D38's finding that this product has no instance-level principal, so "the instance owner" is not a thing the permission system can name; every fix — an instance-owner flag, an environment-named moderator, or scoping the blocklist per organization and giving up 01500's reasoning — is a design decision rather than a correction. Bounded meanwhile by the shipped signup default (`closed`) and by admins deliberately not holding the permission. |
| Reviewed | Approved as work 2026-08-04 — LNK-M-0052's triage, which took F15, F31 and F36 together and recorded that the shape was blocked on a design fork the owner had not been asked. That fork is D98. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-04 (`docs/build-notes/decisions.md`, *LNK-M-0052, building the principal D98 authorized*). Closed by **D98**, the owner's choice among the four shapes this row's severity column enumerates: the instance-level principal D38 said did not exist. `03400` adds `instance_grants` — a permission held by a **person** over the whole instance, keyed on `user_id` rather than on an organization, because binding instance-wide authority to a founding organization is what D38 refused. The migration **removes** `destinations.review` from the owner role and confers the four instance scopes on the earliest surviving account, which on any instance that went through `/auth/setup` is the setup account; the direction only ever narrows, from a set that grows with every registration to one person. `Register(IsFirstUser)` confers the same four in the transaction that claims a fresh instance, and ordinary registration confers nothing — which is the half that would rebuild this row in one line. The permission **splits**: `destinations.review` reads the queue and **leaves** `NonDelegableScopes`, `destinations.decide` acts on one and enters it, so *"read it with a token, change it with a person"* is the map rather than a branch on credential type the inherited rule forbids. The principal may appoint reviewers (`/disputes`, `POST /api/v1/instance/reviewers`) and **a reviewer may not**: `instance.admin` is not in `auth.InstanceGrantable`, so no grant produces another grantor. What this row records as the *reach* is real and unchanged in kind — that account and its appointees read every dispute on the instance — and the Plan.md limitation row says so. Deliberately untouched: `domains.write` (F70), and `notify.EveryOwner`, so a filing still notifies every organization owner (F49, F137). Six sabotages across the four new tests, each red then counter-edited back. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F15 |

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0033 |
| Where | `internal/observability/metrics.go` — `webPrefixes`, and `ClassifySurface`'s fall-through, which returns `SurfaceRedirect` for anything it does not recognise |
| Evidence | Noticed while adding `/feeds` and finding there was no list to add it to that anybody had been maintaining. `webPrefixes` holds eight entries — `/login`, `/logout`, `/setup`, `/dashboard`, `/docs`, `/links`, `/keys`, `/account` — and `ClassifySurface` labels everything else that is not `/api/`, `/static/` or an ops endpoint as `redirect`. Every dashboard route added since Phase 1 is therefore mislabelled: `/notifications` (LNK-M-0017), `/workspaces` and `/members` (LNK-M-0022, LNK-M-0027), `/invites` and `/invite/` (LNK-M-0026), `/organizations` (LNK-M-0027), `/signup` and `/verify/` (LNK-M-0029), `/disputes` (LNK-M-0032), `/theme` and `/workspace/` — and `/feeds` would be the twelfth. `dashboardPatterns` in `internal/httpx/router.go` is the list that *is* maintained, and the two have silently diverged. |
| Severity | Minor, and observability-only — no request is served differently. The cost lands on the numbers an operator reads: `linkctrl_http_requests_total{surface="redirect"}` and `linkctrl_http_request_duration_seconds{surface="redirect"}` mix short-link traffic with dashboard page loads whose budget is 250ms rather than 20ms, so the redirect surface's own figures are inflated by whatever the dashboard is doing. The SLO itself is unaffected — that is measured by `linkctrl_redirect_duration_seconds`, which the redirect handler records directly and which this does not touch — so the claim in docs/slo.md stands. Not fixed here because adding `/feeds` alone would make the list wrong in a new way, and the honest fix is to derive the classifier from `dashboardPatterns` rather than to extend a second hand-written copy of it, which is a change to a shipped metric's labels. |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 5, minor — one-edit corrections. **Remedy pointer corrected 2026-08-04, F85's fix:** this row's evidence names `dashboardPatterns` in `internal/httpx/router.go` as "the list that *is* maintained" and proposes deriving the classifier from it. That slice no longer exists — F85 deleted it, because it had fallen behind the registrations it sat beside. The source this row asks for is now `(*appMux).mounts()`, which is derived from what the application mux was actually handed rather than hand-written, so it is a better one than the row could have had. The finding itself is unchanged and still open. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05. The classifier is **derived, not extended**. `observability.SetWebPaths` is called at boot with `(*appMux).mounts()` — what the application mux was actually handed — so the dashboard set cannot fall behind the routes again. The row proposed deriving it from `dashboardPatterns`, which F85 had since deleted for having fallen behind in exactly this way; `mounts()` is the better source it could not have known about, and its own Reviewed cell had already recorded that correction. Adding `/feeds` to the hand-written list would have made the list wrong in a new way, which is why the row refused to do it. `TestEveryDashboardRouteIsCountedAsTheDashboard` drives its assertion from `mounts()` too, so the test cannot drift either — a list checked against a copy of itself is what this finding was. Shown red by removing the boot call: nine routes reported `surface="redirect"`, `/automation` and `/campaigns` and `/disputes` among them. |

So this is NOT a live defect and no user is currently misled. What remains is that D7's rule has two implementations, and the page's copy bypasses the effective-mode logic entirely — if `Effective()` ever gains a case yielding `closed`, the invitation page would invite somebody to register while redemption refuses them. |

The fixture serves the dashboard tree now. The test sets the two answers apart deliberately, which `cmd/linkctrl` cannot produce because it derives one from the other; that is the point, since what is asserted is that the page *cannot* disagree with the enforcer rather than that today's wiring keeps them equal. Sabotaged by restoring the second derivation. |

Picking a workspace in the header dropdown does nothing until **Switch** is pressed, and any navigation silently discards the choice

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0022 |
| Where | `internal/ui/templates/partials/nav.html:23`–`:35` — a bare `<select>` and a separate submit button, with no change handler |
| Evidence | Found by adversarial verification of two owner reports that a selection *resets* between pages and that the links page *does not update*. Both are this: the store-level switch is sound (`POST /workspace/switch` persists `users.last_workspace_id` and survives new sessions, 500 pages, API calls and short-link hits), but the UI never sends that POST unless the button is pressed, so the next render re-emits `selected` at the workspace the user is actually in and their pick vanishes. The template's own comment records what it believed was the cause — an auto-submitting select needs a change handler and the CSP forbids inline script — so this reads as a deliberate design whose affordance misleads, not an oversight. It is what the owner actually experienced. **That justification is false, and the tree falsifies it** (checked 2026-08-02, draining the queue): the CSP forbids *inline* script and always did, but htmx has been served from `internal/ui/static/js/htmx.min.js` since LNK-M-0006 (`13fb0f6`), is loaded by `layout.html:9` on every page, and runs under `script-src 'self'` — `internal/httpx/middleware.go:266-270` says so in as many words. `internal/ui/templates/pages/links.html:56` already ships **exactly** the control this finding says was impossible: `<select name="status" hx-get="/links" hx-trigger="change">`, needing no inline script and no CSP waiver. So the two-step was never forced by the CSP; it was a change handler nobody wired |
| Severity | Moderate. Nothing is broken or lost, and D22's persistence holds — but a claim *is* false, which is new: `nav.html`'s comment asserts a constraint the same codebase disproves one directory over, and that comment is what would stop the next reader from fixing this. The cost is that the control looks like it changed something and did not, which is indistinguishable from a bug to the person using it |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 1, moderate and above. The owner directed the fix's shape on 2026-08-02; what it still waits on is the no-JavaScript question in upcoming-decisions.md. but the **owner has directed the shape of the fix** (2026-08-02, via `/note`): the dropdown performs the switch on change, and *"a separate button to switch can't stay"*. The one thing that leaves open — what a browser without JavaScript gets once the button is gone — is in upcoming-decisions.md. Approval to schedule the work is still the owner's and has not been given |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05, under **D103**. The select carries `hx-post`, `hx-trigger="change"` and `hx-include="closest form"`, and the **Switch** button is gone — the owner's 2026-08-02 directive carried literally. No `<noscript>` fallback: the owner settled the stance instead, so the dashboard requires JavaScript and that is written down rather than defended in markup. **Nothing was added to make it work.** htmx is already served on every page under `script-src 'self'` and already does this on the links page, and `seeOther` already answers an htmx request with `HX-Redirect`, so the switch performs a full navigation whichever way it was submitted and the handler is untouched. `nav.html`'s comment — *a plain form: a select and a button, no JavaScript*, justified by a CSP that forbids inline script — went with the button: the premise was false, since none of this needs inline script, so the two-step control was defending a constraint that did not exist. Asserted on the markup, because everything past the emitted attributes belongs to htmx and the browser; sabotaged by removing the wiring, which fails on all three attributes. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F21 |

| Evidence | Reproduced: creating a link in Sales with an alias already used in Marketing answers `409 alias "vmk2" is already in use`. Two costs: the same alias cannot be used in two workspaces, and a 409 tells a member of one workspace that an alias exists in another they may not be able to see. **Re-derived 2026-08-04 (LNK-M-0052) against the tree LNK-M-0044 and LNK-M-0045 left**, because this row's own evidence pointed forward to them: the query comment it quoted (*"Phase 2 gives a workspace its own and this gains a filter"*) has been discharged — `GetWorkspaceDefaultDomain` now takes the workspace and prefers its own verified hostname, then an organization-owned one, then the instance default, and says so at `links.sql:354-357`. So the collision is no longer instance-wide by construction: it is bounded to workspaces that **share** a domain, which means every workspace still on the instance default, and the workspaces of one organization sharing an organization-owned hostname |
| Severity | **Minor**, restated 2026-08-04 (LNK-M-0052) from *"Minor to moderate, depending on whether workspaces are meant to be isolated from each other"*. That condition has been answered by the tree rather than by a decision: LNK-M-0044 and LNK-M-0045 shipped a supported way for a workspace to get its own alias namespace, so what remains is that workspaces sharing a domain share its namespace — which is what a shared domain means — and the disclosure is bounded to that set. It is not nothing: the instance default is the state of every workspace that has not registered a hostname, so on a single-domain instance the original behaviour is unchanged |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 3, minor — a principal can act on it, in scope by the 2026-08-04 standing rule. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05. **The disclosure is not removable and was not removed**: a `409` and a `201` are distinguishable whatever either says, and alias uniqueness is per domain by construction. What is fixed is the silence around it. `aliasTakenError` replaces three identical literals at the three collision sites — the sites already said one message for all three *causes*, and this makes that structural rather than three strings that agree today — and the message names the namespace: which hostname, that uniqueness is per domain, who shares it, and that registering a domain for the workspace gives it a namespace of its own. **Scoped, not blanket.** LNK-M-0044 and LNK-M-0045 shipped that supported way out, so a collision on a workspace's own verified hostname really is its own business and the shared-namespace sentence would be false there; the wording branches on the domain's scope, and `targetDomain` and `GetWorkspaceDefaultDomain` carry `organization_id` and `workspace_id` so it can. The test asserts both cases, and **it caught a real bug in the fix**: the first implementation left the scope fields unset on the named-domain path, so a private hostname got the shared warning. Sabotaged by collapsing back to the flat message. |

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0036 |
| Where | `internal/link/destination.go:198` (`looksNumeric` returns false on the empty last label), `:169` (the `localhost` equality test), and `internal/link/blocking.go:218` (a bare `embeddedHosts[host]` lookup) |
| Evidence | Reproduced live on :8081 through the real handler: `POST /api/v1/links` answered **201** for `http://169.254.169.254./latest/meta-data/` and **422 `unappealable.private_address`** for the dotless control; `PATCH` is affected identically; the stored value is 302'd verbatim at serve time and **no `destination.blocked` audit row is written** for any dotted attempt. A second verifier, working the design angle, established the correction that matters: **LinkCtrl never fetches a destination server-side** — the only two `http.Client`s in the tree are the opt-in feed and the container healthcheck — so this is a stored **open redirect**, not SSRF, and the attacker cannot read the response.
