Canonicalized rather than refused, as this row's *Reviewed* cell required: `https://example.com./path` is accepted and **stored** as `https://example.com/path`, so the value a visitor is later handed is the value the tiers judged. This row's evidence is right on every point and is left as written, including its four `Where` sites. One correction, and it is the reason the fix is not the one-liner the row validated: `strings.TrimSuffix` trims a single dot, and `http://127.0.0.1../` has an empty last label after one trim just as `http://127.0.0.1./` does before any — measured, by running the row's proposed fix against the new test, which accepted it. `strings.TrimRight` is what closes the spelling as well as the character. `looksNumeric`'s empty-label branch, which this row correctly names as the mechanism at `destination.go:198`, now answers true rather than false; nothing reaches it once the fold is in, so it changes no behaviour and exists so the helper fails closed if a third caller appears. The test gap the row exposes is closed too: `TestUnappealableTierHasNoOverrideSwitch` guarded a promise about what may be *accepted* with a reflection walk over `DestinationPolicy`'s *fields*, so it never tried a host. `TestATrailingDotDoesNotDefeatAnyTier` (`internal/link/blocking_test.go`) feeds each dotted spelling against its dotless control through all four mechanisms and the embedded list, and `TestATrailingDotIsRefusedAndRecorded` (`test/integration/blocking_test.go`) holds the consequence this row found and the unit tests cannot see — the refusal now writes its `destination.blocked` row, on create and on update, where before there was no refusal and therefore no record. ## LNK-F-0027

LNK-M-0027's workspace-scoped memberships confer **organization-wide** authority: a workspace-scoped admin can grant themselves into any workspace, re-role and remove org-wide members, issue org-wide invitations, and — with no `Grant` at all — promote their own org-wide row to admin. A workspace-scoped **owner** additionally holds `org.delete` over the whole organization

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0036 |
| Where | `internal/team/member.go:262` and `:282` (`Grant`), `:111` (`ChangeRole`), `:187` (`Remove`), `:362` (`manageable`), `internal/team/team.go:156` (`mayManage`), `:191` (`resolveRole`), `internal/invite/invite.go:227` (`Create`), `internal/team/organization.go:226` (`org.delete`) |
| Evidence | Reproduced end to end against the real services on a throwaway database. Controls first: acting in W1, Alice is **refused** `RenameWorkspace(W2)` and `DeleteWorkspace(W2)` by `writableWorkspace` — *"changing that workspace requires workspace.write in it"*. Three calls later, after `Grant(self, W2, admin)` succeeded, the same guard passes and she renames W2. Separately and needing no `Grant`: she holds org-wide `viewer` (rank 40) and workspace-scoped `admin` (rank 20); `GetUserRoleInWorkspace` takes the minimum, so `mayManage(20,40,10)` is true against **her own** org-wide row, which comes back `IsSelf: true` **and** `Manageable: true` — one dropdown on `/members` makes her an organization-wide admin. `refuseLastOwner` fires only on demotion, so promotion is unguarded; from there she can remove the real owner. The premise is a supported path: `resolveRole` refuses only `role.Rank < actor.RoleRank`, so `10 < 10` is false and an owner may grant **owner** scoped to one workspace, and `Roles` offers it. `internal/team/workspace.go` already does the right thing via `canInWorkspace`, with a comment naming this exact attacker — no member operation calls it. The UI does not limit it: `members.html:33-39` ranges over all of `.OrgWorkspaces` without filtering on `Manageable`. Every `Grant`/`ChangeRole`/`Remove` in `test/integration/team_test.go` uses `f.owner` as the actor; the one workspace-scoped identity the suite builds is only ever read |
| Severity | **Major.** Falsifies m28.md's *"An admin cannot demote themselves — self is not strictly below self"*, and contradicts `members.sql:69-71` (*"a workspace-scoped owner membership grants ownership of one workspace, not of the organization"*) and `team.go:236-238`. Reachable through the shipped UI in three dropdown picks, no forged request, no owner involvement after the initial grant. The UI describes the grant as *"It adds to whatever they already had"* |
| Reviewed | Yes — owner approved 2026-08-01 on LNK-M-0036's triage; **reopens LNK-M-0027**. It cannot be fixed at `Grant` alone — the self-promotion route uses no `Grant` at all. |
| Closed by | LNK-M-0027, 2026-08-02. Closed by D44: a write is authorized by the membership whose **scope covers its target**, not by the identity's union. `auth.MembershipAuthority` (`internal/auth/authority.go`) over a new `ListMembershipAuthority` query answers, per scope, whether the actor holds the permission there and at which rank; `In(nil)` is the organization-wide scope, which only an organization-wide membership reaches. `manageable` — shared by `ChangeRole` and `Remove` — resolves it against the target membership's own scope before any rank is compared, and `resolveRole`'s ceiling now reads that rank rather than `Identity.RoleRank`, which closes the second route this row's evidence did not reach: an organization-wide **admin** who also held a workspace-scoped **owner** row would otherwise have carried rank 10 against organization-wide targets. `Grant` resolves the authority in the workspace being granted into, which is the same question `canInWorkspace` already asked for `workspace.write`. `invite.Create` and `DeleteOrganization` require the organization-wide scope, because what they produce and destroy is organization-wide. `refuseLastOwner` became `guardOwnerSet`, called on promotion as well as demotion so every change to the owner set takes the same lock — its promotion refusal is deliberate depth rather than the operative guard, since after D44 minting an organization-wide owner structurally requires being one; the decisions entry says so plainly. `members.html`'s workspace select is filtered where the page loads, and `Members` computes `Manageable` per row against the same authority. Five integration tests drive a workspace-scoped identity as the **actor** of a write — the gap this row named as the reason the suite was green — and all five were shown red first by neutralizing the scope filter, which reproduced the escalation including the rows it wrote. This row's evidence is right on every point and is left as written; its line numbers have since moved. Out of its scope and left open: F31, which shares the root but falsifies LNK-M-0016's claim, and F63, raised while building this. |
| Status | closed |

## LNK-F-0030

**The invalidation subscriber never detects a Redis that holds the connection open and stops answering: it blocks in `ReceiveMessage` with no deadline, never reconnects, never flushes, and `establish`'…**

finding · 2026-08-01

cites: [LNK-M-0036](milestones.md#lnk-m-0036)

cites: [LNK-M-0018](milestones.md#lnk-m-0018)

cites: [LNK-D-0042](decisions.md#lnk-d-0042)

The invalidation subscriber never detects a Redis that holds the connection open and stops answering: it blocks in `ReceiveMessage` with no deadline, never reconnects, never flushes, and `establish`'s liveness ping reports healthy

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0036 |
| Where | `internal/redirect/invalidation.go:207` (`ps.ReceiveMessage(ctx)`) and `:238` (the `ps.Ping(ctx)` health check) |
| Evidence | Two go-redis facts verified at the installed v9.21.0 rather than taken on trust: `ReceiveMessage` is a bare loop over `Receive` → `ReceiveTimeout(ctx, 0)` → `deadline()` returning `noDeadline`, so `ReadTimeout` never applies; and `PubSub.Ping` is **write-only** — it writes the command and never reads a reply, so a nil return proves only that bytes entered the socket buffer. Reproduced on a purpose-built harness (not the finder's): real Redis behind a proxy discarding bytes both ways while holding sockets open, with a separate publisher. **Redis reported delivering the invalidation to 1 subscriber and it was silently lost**; `ReceiveMessage` stayed blocked 40s; `establish`'s ping returned nil in 0ms. Control with the socket *cut* — the only shape the existing tests cover — errored in 0.1s and recovered correctly. Keepalive measured off a real fd: `KEEPIDLE=300s INTVL=15s CNT=9` → death at **7m15s**, but only when probes go unanswered; an application-level stall (wedged Redis, proxy, sidecar) is ACKed by the peer kernel and the block is genuinely unbounded, proved by scaling keepalive to ~4s and still blocking at 30s. Note for whoever fixes it: go-redis's `Channel()` API would **not** help — its health check uses the same write-only `Ping` |
| Severity | **Major.** Falsifies m23.md's *"A dropped subscriber connection reconnects and degrades to TTL in the meantime — never to silence mistaken for freshness. Tested"* and `invalidation.go:238-240`'s claim that a successful ping means the subscription is *"genuinely live rather than merely not-yet-failed"*. Stale window is the remaining entry TTL, up to `REDIRECT_TTL` (24h default), because `mem.get` short-circuits before Redis is consulted; Redis itself stays correct, so it self-heals at expiry. Multi-replica only — the editing replica clears locally first. The test proxy already has a `stalled(true)` mode; it is pointed only at the writer |
| Reviewed | Yes — owner approved 2026-08-01 on LNK-M-0036's triage; **reopens LNK-M-0018**. Not via go-redis's `Channel()`, whose health check uses the same write-only `Ping`; the fix is a bounded read. |
| Closed by | LNK-M-0018, 2026-08-01. Closed by bounding the subscriber's read with a new `REDIS_SUBSCRIBER_READ_TIMEOUT` (30s) and treating an expired read as a question rather than an answer: the subscriber pings and then waits for the *reply*, which is the one thing a stalled connection cannot produce, and only then concludes that the subscription has stopped delivering. Unanswered, it logs, drops both in-process tiers rather than serving them as current, closes the connection go-redis deliberately keeps after a mere timeout, and resubscribes. This row's evidence is right on every point and is left as written, including its note that `Channel()` would not help — that was checked again at v9.21.0 before the fix was written. Two things it did not reach. The flush moved from the reconnect to the failure, because against a Redis that never returns "flush when we reconnect" is a flush that never happens; and the fix had to be shown *not* to answer the finding by emptying the cache on every quiet interval, which is what the new test's first half asserts. `TestAStalledSubscriberStopsTrustingWhatItCannotHear` (`test/integration/invalidation_test.go`) was run red against the shipped tree first, timing out on the stale entry it went on to drop. D42. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F30 |

A workspace-scoped admin reads the **entire organization's** audit log, including workspaces where they hold no membership at all

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0036 |
| Where | `internal/store/query/audit.sql:33` (`WHERE organization_id = @organization_id`) and `internal/audit/audit.go:313` (`org := actor.OrgID`) |
| Evidence | Verified against the live migrated database inside `BEGIN … ROLLBACK`: a user whose only membership is `role=admin, workspace_id=A` resolves `audit.read` and `members.write` in A and **0 permissions** in C, yet `ListAuditLogs` scoped to the organization returns C's rows — a planted `member.added` carrying `{"email":"carol@example.com"}` and a `destination.blocked` carrying `url_defanged`, each with `ip_prefix` and `actor_label`. The stronger form also holds: after the org-wide membership is removed she holds zero permissions in B and C, still resolves into A, and still reads their rows. The verifier corrected the severity argument — member emails are *already* org-wide readable by design, so what is new is `ip_prefix` bound to a named actor, the per-action timeline, and `url_defanged`, for workspaces they do not administer. `audit.sql:26-28` argues the org scope deliberately, but that reasoning is LNK-M-0016's, from when `audit.read` could only be held organization-wide; D31 enumerates the union's costs and does not name this one |
| Severity | **Moderate.** An unexamined composition of two intended decisions rather than an accepted trade-off. Read-only, leaves no trace (reads are not audited), and needs a direct JSON call since no UI page exists. Same root as F27 — the fix for one may not fix the other, since this is a read scope and F27 is a write scope |
| Reviewed | Approved as work 2026-08-04 — LNK-M-0052's triage, which took F15, F31 and F36 together and recorded that the shape was blocked on a design fork the owner had not been asked. That fork is D98. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-04 (`docs/build-notes/decisions.md`, *LNK-M-0052, building the principal D98 authorized*). This row's diagnosis is exactly right and the repair is the rule it names arriving one axis over: **D44** already says authority is per scope and only an organization-wide membership reaches the organization-wide scope, and until now that governed writes only. `auth.MembershipAuthority.Scopes()` answers which scopes a permission is held in; `audit.Service.List` loads it and `ListAuditLogs` gains `org_wide OR workspace_id = ANY(...)`. An organization-wide reader is **unaffected** — `audit.sql:26-28`'s argument is LNK-M-0016's and still correct — and a workspace-scoped one reads the workspaces its own scope covers. Rows with a NULL `workspace_id` are organization-level acts and a workspace-scoped reader does not see them, because `= ANY` is false against NULL, which is the same asymmetry `In(nil)` enforces for writes. `Can` stays the gate for *may you read at all*; the authority bounds *which rows*. The `workspace_ids` parameter is never nil — a nil `uuid[]` reaches Postgres as NULL and `= ANY(NULL)` is unknown, which would return nothing — even though `Can` makes the empty case unreachable. Fixed **on its own terms** rather than through the principal: F31 is an organization's log read by one of its own members, and the instance surface D98 adds is a different question, which is F36. Its sibling F27 was a write scope and closed separately, as this row predicted. `TestAWorkspaceScopedAdminReadsOnlyTheirOwnWorkspacesAuditRows` builds the row's own fixture — one workspace-scoped admin membership, no organization-wide one — and its sabotage forces `orgWide` true, which reproduces the finding verbatim. |

**Invitation and email-verification tokens are stored **in clear** in `mail_outbox.body`, so a read of the database yields redeemable credentials**

cites: [LNK-M-0026](milestones.md#lnk-m-0026)

cites: [LNK-M-0029](milestones.md#lnk-m-0029)

Invitation and email-verification tokens are stored **in clear** in `mail_outbox.body`, so a read of the database yields redeemable credentials

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0036 |
| Where | `internal/mail/mail.go:139` (`Body: body`, rendered at enqueue time), reached from `internal/invite/invite.go:749` and `internal/signup/signup.go:288` |
| Evidence | Reproduced against a real database: a token pulled out of `mail_outbox.body` **by SQL alone** hashed to `invitations.token_hash` and redeemed into an **admin** membership; the body still contains the token after send, and `PurgeFinishedMail` is age-only (30 days), never scrubbing. Four narrowings the finder missed. (a) It needs `SMTP_HOST` set **and** `SIGNUP_MODE != closed`; under the shipped default the leaked token is **refused** — verified. (b) The signup half is near-harmless: verification ends at the sign-in form and the plaintext password never survived the signup request, so the attacker force-completes a registration they cannot sign in as. (c) `docs/SECURITY.md:45` is an **over-read** — it sits in the Invitations row and describes how the invitation *record* stores its token, which is true. (d) The sentence that actually convicts is `docs/SECURITY.md:241`, which already discloses that the outbox stores each message rendered — so the design is accepted; what is false is its closing clause *"the first mail this ships, the audit-growth warning, contains no secret"*, written in LNK-M-0023 (`13df367`) and broken by LNK-M-0026's `invitation.txt` (`0a5b1fd`) and LNK-M-0029's `verification.txt` (`24b3c89`) without revisiting the paragraph |
| Severity | **Moderate.** Genuinely falsifies `01200_invitations.sql:34-35` — *"A database leak hands over no redeemable invites"* — and literally falsifies `01400_signup.sql:43-44`. Real window is 7 days per unredeemed invitation (`INVITE_TTL`), 24h for verification. On a mailer-configured instance a **read-only** database compromise becomes an authenticated foothold at up to admin. Scrubbing `body` on `MarkMailSent` would collapse it to minutes, at the cost of the operator-inspectability the outbox exists for — a trade worth recording as a decision rather than making silently |
| Reviewed | Approved as work 2026-08-04 — LNK-M-0052's triage, the moderate security cluster |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052** (`docs/build-notes/decisions.md`, *LNK-M-0052, three places a secret was sitting still*). Scrubbed at the terminal transition: `MarkMailSent` and `MarkMailFailed` set `body = ''` in the same statement that sets the status, and `03200` erases the bodies already in the table and adds `CHECK (status = 'pending' OR body = '')` so the scrub cannot be quietly removed. Every kind, not a sensitive-kind list — a list defaults new templates to unsafe, which is exactly how (d)'s sentence rotted. The two rejected options and what each cost are recorded in full: a send-time reference needs a plaintext home for a token that exists only as a hash, and shortened retention sets a window in days against a seven-day token. **Not fully closed as a class, and said so**: a *pending* row still carries its body, so an instance whose relay is down holds a live token for as long as the invitation is redeemable. `01200`, `01400`, `01100`, `docs/SECURITY.md`, `docs/configuration.md` and `.env.example` all now say that instead of the stronger claim. Asserted by `TestInvitationDeliveryWithAndWithoutAMailer/and_the_delivered_row_keeps_no_token` and `TestAnAbandonedMessageKeepsItsRecordAndNotItsContents`, both sabotage-verified |

A dispute stores the host that was **typed**, not the blocklist row that refused it, so the one-open-dispute-per-host bound is defeated by any subdomain — the queue shows the owner one host while **Allow** acts on another, and the query that documents the guarantee is defeated by its only caller

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0036 |
| Where | `internal/dispute/dispute.go:302` (`Host: verdict.Host`), against the unique index at `01600_destination_disputes.sql:77`. Flood limb: `internal/link/blocking.go:257-262`, `internal/dispute/dispute.go:344-368` (`disputable`), `PermFile = link.PermCreate` at `:85`, `internal/httpx/router.go:583`. Comment limb: `internal/store/query/disputes.sql:93-95` against `dispute.go:536` and `:551` |
| Evidence | Reproduced against a real database: 19 shortener hosts are seeded by default, the rule matches on **suffix**, and `ValidateDestination` performs no DNS lookup — so `a.bit.ly`, `b.bit.ly`, `c.bit.ly` each judge as `low_confidence.shortener_chain`, each open a distinct dispute, and each notifies **every instance owner**. One blocked row for `evil.example` produced two open disputes from `login.` and `mail.` children. The dashboard `POST /disputes` (`router.go:373`) carries **no rate limiter at all**. The verifier found a sharper consequence than the flood: `entryToLift` re-runs `HostCandidates(d.Host)`, so an owner clicking Allow on a dispute rendered `a[.]bit[.]ly` deletes **`bit.ly`** from the instance-wide blocklist, un-blocking it for every workspace — and `Dispute` carries no field naming the row that would be lifted. **Folded in from F95 (LNK-M-0051), 2026-08-04:** this row's flood already covers the missing limiter and the instance-wide fan-out, and F95 removes its *precondition*. `url_credentials` (`internal/link/blocking.go:257-262`) matches on `u.User != nil` with the host ignored, so a filer needs no blocked host at all — only distinct strings with an `a@` prefix — which widens the input space from hosts under a listed suffix to every string, and defeats `01600_destination_disputes.sql:67-75`'s own claim that *"a caller who wants a thousand rows in front of the owner needs a thousand distinct blocked hosts"*. Verification narrowed it twice: `tellReviewers` writes inbox rows only and sends no mail, and `router.go:693` confines the rate limiter to the API prefix so the browser route is unlimited. **Folded in from F125 (LNK-M-0051), 2026-08-04:** `internal/store/query/disputes.sql:93-95` states the opposite of this row's behaviour in the one place a reader would check it — a decision about `login.evil.example` *"cannot take 'evil.example' off the list by accident"* — while `dispute.go:536` and `:551` pass `link.HostCandidates(d.Host)` to `MatchBlockedDestination` and delete the longest match. The comment's first clause is accurate (the delete is a literal equality, no LIKE, no candidate walk in SQL); only the trailing claim is false. |
| Severity | **Moderate**, top of band. Falsifies `01600_destination_disputes.sql:26-30` in both clauses — *"it is the host the refusal actually matched rather than the one that was typed"* — and its stated bound at `:67-73`. Needs only `links.create`. The decision-integrity half (the string shown is not the string the button acts on) is worth more than the flood. Absorbs F95's amplification (the fan-out multiplier is `EveryOwner`, not the filer, so rate-limiting the route or capping the filer both leave it; and narrowing `url_credentials` changes what LNK-M-0030 refuses, which is a tier change rather than a queue fix) and F125's comment (**Cosmetic** on its own, and repaired *by* this row rather than beside it — storing the matched row on the dispute at filing time makes `disputes.sql:93-95` true as written; deleting the comment would be wrong, because the parent match is deliberate). |
| Reviewed | Approved as work 2026-08-04 — LNK-M-0052's triage, the moderate non-security set, which took F33, F95 and F114 together *"because the rows themselves say they should land together rather than beside each other"*. **F95 and F125 were merged into this row** by LNK-M-0052's queue hygiene, 2026-08-04: F95 said in as many words that it *"should land with F33 rather than beside it"*, and F125 has no independent fix. **F114 was deliberately not merged** — the existence oracle is a separate defect with a separate fix note and its own tenancy question, and it is approved separately. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052** (`docs/build-notes/decisions.md`, *LNK-M-0052, the queue showed one host and the button deleted another*). Both halves, and the two things it deliberately is not. `03300` adds `destination_disputes.blocked_host`, written at filing from `link.Verdict.ListedHost` — a new field set in `listedInDatabase` where the match happens and nowhere else, so it cannot name a row that did not refuse — and `entryToLift` now reads it and asks the new `GetBlockedDestination` for that exact host. `MatchBlockedDestination` has one caller again, which is the package that judges destinations. The queue and the API render it: `blocked_host_defanged`, beside the typed host on `/disputes`, with the Allow control's confirmation naming the entry rather than *that host*. **The sharper consequence the row named is what the repair is shaped around**: the walk answers with the longest entry, so re-deriving at decision time meant an entry added while the dispute waited retargeted a decision the owner believed they were making about what they were shown — `TestTheEntryLiftedIsTheOneRecordedAtFiling` is that scenario, and its sabotage reproduces this row's evidence verbatim. **Not a rewrite of `host`**, which stays the typed host and keeps the disclosure's other half; 01600's comment corrected in place to say which column is which. **Not a replacement index**: `03300`'s partial unique index on `blocked_host` stands beside 01600's on `host`, and skips rows with no entry (`blocked_host <> ''`) because every computed rule stores the same key and one open homograph dispute must not lock out every other destination. Existing disputes carry no entry and are refused rather than guessed at, in their own sentence. **F125 closes inside this** exactly as its note said: `disputes.sql:93-95` is true as written, with *accident* carrying it — `evil.example` still comes off, because it is what refused `login.evil.example`, and what changed is that the owner is told which of the two they are deciding. **F95's amplification does not**, and that is stated rather than implied: `url_credentials` still fires on userinfo for any host, still stores no entry, is still bounded only by the typed host, and each filing still notifies every owner over an unlimited browser route. Both repairs its note named remain out of reach here — narrowing the rule is a tier change, and the multiplier is `EveryOwner`, which is F15's question. The residue is **F137**, and 01600's index comment now claims only what the index can keep. **F15 is untouched in both directions**: the new bound is instance-wide because the list it argues with is, so answering F15 by scoping disputes per organization would need an organization column on both indexes, not one. **F114 is not closed** — its key moved from the typed host to the entry, which reduces the questions the oracle answers and removes none; it returns as an unanswered prompt. Eight sabotages, each red then counter-edited back, including the demo's open dispute reverted to a host equal to its entry, which the new `demoCoverage` row catches. |

**The full `FEED_URL` — which the tree elsewhere assumes carries an API key in its query string — is written to the application log at WARN on every transport-level feed failure**

cites: [LNK-M-0036](milestones.md#lnk-m-0036)

cites: [LNK-M-0052](milestones.md#lnk-m-0052)

The full `FEED_URL` — which the tree elsewhere assumes carries an API key in its query string — is written to the application log at WARN on every transport-level feed failure

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0036 |
| Where | `internal/link/blocking.go:444`, via the `*url.Error` wrapped at `internal/feed/feed.go:254` |
| Evidence | Reproduced through the real `feed.Client` and the real `observability.NewLogger`: `error="feed AcmeRep: Post \"https://feed.example.com/v1/check?apikey=SUPERSECRET123&mode=strict\": …"`. All four escape routes checked and closed: `slog.Any` renders errors via `Error()` (confirmed in `json_handler.go`); `redactAttrs` (`logging.go:65`) matches on the attribute **key**, which here is `"error"`; and `FEED_URL` is a plain `string`, not `config.Secret` (`config.go:318`). Fires on DNS failure, refused connection, TLS error and timeout — the common one at `FEED_TIMEOUT=2s`. One narrowing: `FEED_METHOD` defaults to **POST**, so the user's destination is only in the URL under `FEED_METHOD=GET`. The killer fact the finder missed is that the boot log already does it right — `cmd/linkctrl/main.go:461` logs `feedClient.Endpoint()`, deliberately query-stripped — and `internal/platform/postgres/postgres.go:62` refuses to wrap for exactly this reason: *"Do not wrap: the error may echo the DSN, which contains the password"* |
| Severity | **Moderate.** A live third-party credential reaching a lower-trust sink on an ordinary error path, precisely when logs get shipped and pasted into tickets. By the project's own DSN standard it is major-class; by absolute impact the secret belongs to a service the operator opted into and grants no access to this instance |
| Reviewed | Approved as work 2026-08-04 — LNK-M-0052's triage, the moderate security cluster |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052** (same entry). `feed.Client.transportError` replaces the URL inside a `*url.Error` with `Endpoint()` rather than dropping it, so the operator still learns which endpoint failed and the credential does not travel — applied at `c.http.Do` and at request construction, which reports an unparseable URL the same way. Replacing rather than filtering also removes the **user's destination** under `FEED_METHOD=GET`, where it is a query parameter on the request URL: the same mechanism, not a second fix. The `*url.Error` is not wrapped, only its cause is, so nothing can `errors.As` back to the URL. Asserted by `TestATransportFailureNamesTheEndpointAndNotTheCredential`, sabotage-verified — the control run reproduces this row's evidence exactly, destination included |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F34 |

finding · 2026-08-04

The feed disclosure strips a credential from the query string but not from the URL's userinfo, so `https://key:secret@feed.example/` is rendered verbatim to **every signed-in user**

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0036 |
| Where | `internal/feed/feed.go:185-193` (`Endpoint`), rendered at `internal/ui/templates/pages/feeds.html:57` and returned by `GET /api/v1/feeds` |
| Evidence | Reproduced: `Endpoint("https://apikey:SECRET@api.feed.example/v1/check")` returns the string unchanged, while the query-string form is stripped correctly. Config validation (`config.go:828-843`) parses the URL and checks only `u.Scheme == "https"`; `u.User` is never examined, so a userinfo URL validates clean. The counter — *userinfo is operator error, not a defect* — fails four ways: Go's client actually sends Basic auth from `req.URL.User`, so it **works** and the operator gets no warning; `Endpoint`'s own doc comment concedes the premise (*"a feed URL can carry an API key … the disclosure page is shown to every signed-in user"*), making this an incomplete redaction rather than an absent one; `FEED_AUTH_TOKEN` is typed `Secret`, `,unset` and in `FileSecretVars`, so a credential smuggled through `FEED_URL` bypasses the whole discipline; and the template prints the endpoint two lines above the sentence calling it *"the operator's own credential"*. `FeedsPage` is ungated by design (D40) and correctly so |
| Severity | **Moderate.** Converts an operator slip into full third-party-credential disclosure to any authenticated principal, including any stranger who registers under open signup. The clean fix is to **reject** userinfo in `FEED_URL` validation beside the existing https check, leaving `Endpoint`'s redaction as defence in depth |
| Reviewed | Approved as work 2026-08-04 — LNK-M-0052's triage, the moderate security cluster |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052** (same entry). Both halves. `Endpoint()` now parses and rebuilds from scheme, host and path — an allowlist, so a spelling nobody thought of is excluded by default rather than needing to be added to the strip list — and config validation **refuses** `FEED_URL` carrying userinfo at boot, pointing at `FEED_AUTH_HEADER`/`FEED_AUTH_TOKEN`, which is the discipline this bypassed. A breaking change for an instance that had one, stated in CHANGELOG.md. **The residue is named rather than closed**: a credential in a path segment is indistinguishable from a path, survives this, and is still printed on `/feeds`; the path is kept because dropping it would gut the disclosure, and `docs/configuration.md`, `.env.example` and `docs/SECURITY.md` each warn about it. Asserted by `TestDescribeNeverPrintsTheOperatorsCredential`'s six cases and two `TestValidateIndividualRules` rows, sabotage-verified |
| Status | closed |

finding · 2026-08-02

cites: [LNK-F-0020](#lnk-f-0020)

`TestNoPageDataStructShadowsTheShell` never inspects **embedded** fields, so the exact F20 defect can be reintroduced by an ordinary refactor while the guard reports green

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0036 |
| Where | `internal/httpx/web_shell_test.go:126` — `readStruct` routes every anonymous field into `s.embedded` and never into `fieldOrder`, which the clash loop at `:54` is the only thing that iterates |
| Evidence | Reproduced in a fresh scratch copy with three shadow shapes — a shared mixin naming `Path`, a local type named `Workspaces`, and an embedded `*auth.Identity`. **All three compile** (the attack's hypothesis that Go's ambiguity rules would reject them is false: `shell` *names* `Identity`, so an embedded one sits at depth 0 and wins), and the guard **passes**. Control with the named-field F20 shape fails correctly, so the test is not vacuous. Rendering the three through `text/template` reproduces F20's failure modes: two 500 on a plain field access, and the third renders an **empty workspace switcher silently**. No current page struct triggers it, but `struct{ shell; someMixin }` is the ordinary refactor that would — factoring `Notice`/`FieldErrors`/`Path` out of the dozen page structs that repeat them |
| Severity | **Moderate.** Falsifies m28.md's reopening, which asked for *"a test that fails if any page data struct in `internal/httpx` redeclares a field the shell already provides — the mechanism, not a comment"*: under Go's spec an embedded field **is** a field declaration. The test's own comment says *"Two limits, stated rather than hidden"*; this is an unstated third, which makes the comment worse than silence. Fix is one line in `readStruct` |
| Reviewed | No |
| Closed by | LNK-M-0027, 2026-08-02. Closed under phase-loop.md's *deferred overlap* rule rather than by owner approval — it falsifies LNK-M-0027's own first reopening, which asked for *a test that fails if any page data struct in `internal/httpx` redeclares a field the shell already provides*, and under Go's spec an embedded field **is** a field declaration. The exception is named in the commit message. `readStruct` now records every embedded field under the name Go gives it — the type identifier with any `*` and package qualifier dropped, so `*auth.Identity` is a declaration of `Identity` — and the clash check additionally walks the fields promoted from anything embedded that is *not* on the path to `shell`, which is this row's mixin shape: it does not shadow the shell's field, it makes the selector ambiguous, and a template resolving an ambiguous selector fails at render the way F20 did. Structs on the path to `shell` are skipped, because each is checked in its own right by the same loop. The test passed before the change, so it was shown red first against all three shapes recorded here — `sabotageOne` (mixin naming `Path`), `sabotageTwo` (embedded local `Workspaces`), `sabotageThree` (embedded `*auth.Identity`) — and the sabotage was removed by deleting the file that carried it. The *Two limits* comment this row called worse than silence now says one limit (methods) and names embedded fields explicitly. |

`CacheKeyVersion` was not bumped when LNK-M-0034 added bot-policy fields, so a snapshot written by a pre-LNK-M-0034 binary reads as "do not block" for up to `REDIRECT_TTL`

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0036 |
| Where | `internal/redirect/snapshot.go:44-50` and `internal/redirect/resolver.go:24` |
| Evidence | Reproduced at the Redis layer: with `{"block_bots":true}` in Postgres, dropping the in-process copy and overwriting the shared entry with the payload a pre-LNK-M-0034 binary would write (identical minus the `omitempty` `bb`/`db`) yielded **three 302s to a bot**, and the app never revalidates or rewrites the entry. Half the finding is dead, though: `SetBotBlocking` calls `InvalidateDomain` unconditionally, which sweeps `lc:a:v1:<domain>:*`, so entries written **before** blocking is switched on have a zero stale window. What survives needs an old binary writing entries **while blocking is already on** — reachable because `docs/releasing.md:102` runs migrations at boot before the listener opens, so a rolling restart has old and new containers serving concurrently, and `kindDomain` is new in `fa0a079`, so an old replica hits `apply`'s `default:` branch and neither clears its tier nor stops writing bot-less entries. `docs/releasing.md:120-124` calls in-series rollback *"safe"* and cross-series residue *"harmless"* |
| Severity | **Low.** Fail-open on an opt-in control whose failure mode is the pre-LNK-M-0034 status quo — no disclosure, no authz bypass — but silent, bounded only by a 24h TTL, on a sequence the release documentation calls safe. The comment's justification (*"nobody can have switched blocking on yet"*) is what is actually false |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 7, low. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05. **Closed by correcting the reasoning, with no version bump**, and the two halves are separate. The row is right that the comment's justification is false: *"nobody can have switched blocking on yet"* assumes the old build stops before the new one starts, and migrations run at boot before the listener opens, so a rolling restart has both serving at once. But the residue is empty by arithmetic — 0.1.0 is the only release that exists and it keys on `v1`, this build keys on `v3`, and LNK-M-0034, LNK-M-0039 and LNK-M-0041 all land inside the same unreleased minor — so no entry any released build wrote is one this build can read. Same shape as F132: the argument stays untried, the population is empty. What the comment now carries is the **rule for next time**, which is the part that would otherwise have licensed the same mistake: a new omitempty field may skip the bump only when its zero value means the same thing to a visitor as the true value would, never because nobody has had time to configure it. |

## LNK-F-0042

**`Dispute.Liftable` conflates "a blocklist row caused this" with "an allow can succeed", so the review queue draws an **Allow** button on exactly the disputes the code already knows will 409**

finding · 2026-08-05

cites: [LNK-M-0036](milestones.md#lnk-m-0036)

cites: [LNK-M-0030](milestones.md#lnk-m-0030)

cites: [LNK-M-0032](milestones.md#lnk-m-0032)

cites: [LNK-F-0021](#lnk-f-0021)

`Dispute.Liftable` conflates "a blocklist row caused this" with "an allow can succeed", so the review queue draws an **Allow** button on exactly the disputes the code already knows will 409

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0036 |
| Where | `internal/dispute/dispute.go:236` (`liftableRules` admits `operator_blocklist`), `:545` (`entryToLift` refuses `SourceEnv`), `:712`, and `internal/ui/templates/pages/disputes.html:82-89` |
| Evidence | Reproduced: `SeedBlocklist(["envblocked.example"])`, judge, file, Allow → `conflict: "envblocked.example" comes from LINKCTRL_DESTINATION_BLOCKLIST …`, dispute still `open`. A source census after a boot seed on a fully migrated database is `map[env:2 shortener:19]` — **no `review` row exists or can exist**, because the only runtime insert hardcodes `'env'` and the seed hardcodes `'shortener'`. The template renders the Allow form on `{{if .Liftable}}` and renders the *"nothing to remove"* warning only when `not .Liftable`, so an env-sourced dispute gets the button and not the warning. The 409 itself is deliberate, tested (`dispute_test.go:487`) and documented — it is the button that is wrong. LNK-M-0030's tier table is **not** falsified: a shortener row lifts cleanly, verified. Related and folded in: `01500:45` says `'review'` is *"what LNK-M-0032's owner review **will** write"* and `created_by` is written by no statement in the tree, which is the mechanical reason nobody noticed |
| Severity | **Minor to moderate.** Contradicts `dispute.go:140-145` — *"The page draws its buttons from this rather than making the owner discover it by clicking"* — for the most likely dispute an operator-configured instance will see, and `webError` turns the 409 into an error page rather than in-context guidance. Same family as F21: a control that looks like it does something and does not |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 2, minor to moderate. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05. `Liftable` now asks both questions: whether the *rule* is list-backed, and whether the **entry behind this refusal** is one a decision may delete. The queue's two queries carry the entry's source through a LEFT JOIN, and `canLiftEntry` is spelled once and consulted by the flag the page draws from — so the button and the refusal cannot disagree, which is what this was: `entryToLift` refused an `env`-sourced entry and `Liftable` never asked. A source census on a migrated database returns only `env` and `shortener`, so this was not an edge case but the most likely dispute on any operator-configured instance. Both paths that return a freshly written row resolve the source too — `File` with one lookup, `decide` from the row it already read **before** the decision, since an allow has just deleted the entry and reporting *not liftable* because the lift succeeded would be the opposite of informative. Shown red by restoring the rule-only flag. |
| Status | closed |

| Severity | **Low to moderate.** Nothing exploitable. All five sites that described erasure in the present tense are corrected — `00200_identity.sql`'s *"set by the GDPR erasure routine"* on a column with no writer, `00400_analytics.sql`'s scope sentence which was true of its own table and read as a claim about the others, `00600_phase2_dormant.sql`'s *"GDPR erasure overwrites the label"*, `internal/audit/audit.go`'s *"after the account is deleted"*, and `docs/SECURITY.md`'s copy of the same. The absence itself is now in the two lists a reader consults — Plan.md's *Not in Phase 2* and README's *Not built yet* — and has its own entry under SECURITY.md's *What is not defended*, each naming what **is** reclaimed (partitioned analytics, audit retention, invitation and notification cascades) so the gap is sized rather than gestured at. Both now **darken** rather than lighten: `#4338ca` (7.90:1) and `#be123c` (6.29:1), recorded beside the token definitions. Darkening is the direction the light theme already takes, and lightening is the instinct that produced the defect — on a dark background it makes the button more prominent against the surface and less legible for the text on it, and only one of those is a WCAG requirement. `#f43f5e` is rose-500, which m24.5.md's own *Risks* section predicted would drift. |

## LNK-F-0047

finding · 2026-08-05

cites: [LNK-M-0036](milestones.md#lnk-m-0036)

cites: [LNK-M-0052](milestones.md#lnk-m-0052)

For an account that belongs to nothing, the notification bell's **View all** link is a dead end — `/notifications` sits behind `RequireOrganization` and 303s straight back

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0036 |
| Where | `internal/ui/templates/partials/nav.html:224`, against `internal/httpx/router.go:344` + `:287` and `internal/httpx/web_team.go:469` |
| Evidence | Rendered the orphan page rather than reasoning about it: the only href not gated on anything is `/notifications`. `layout.html:33` invokes the bell unconditionally while the identity menu beside it gates Account and Feeds on `HasOrganization`. The finder's premise that organization deletion is soft is **false** (`organizations.sql:71-83` is a hard delete that cascades) — the conclusion survives for a better reason: `notifications.workspace_id` is nullable and all four producers leave it nil, so the workspaces cascade never reaches a notification row, and the count/preview queries are user-scoped. The orphan is also the *likeliest* holder: deleting an organization needs the owner role, and owners are the recipient class for audit-growth, invite-accepted and dispute-filed. `TestTheHeaderOffersNothingToAnAccountThatBelongsToNothing` cuts the nav *before* the bell, so despite its name it cannot see this |
| Severity | **Minor.** No authorization consequence — `RequireOrganization` is explicitly *"an affordance and not the authorization boundary"*. One dead control in a state whose design premise is that a nav made of redirects reads as broken, and the test written to enforce that premise stops one `div` short |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 6, minor — wrong behaviour nothing can provoke. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05. The bell is gated on `HasOrganization`, like the identity-menu entries beside it. Its **View all** was the only href in the header not gated on anything, and `/notifications` sits behind `RequireOrganization` and 303s straight back — offered to exactly the account most likely to hold unread notifications, since deleting an organization needs the owner role and owners are the recipient class for audit growth, invitations and disputes. The existing per-page header test now expects zero bells wherever the shell has no organization, which is the assertion `TestTheHeaderOffersNothingToAnAccountThatBelongsToNothing` could not make: it cuts the nav one `div` before the bell. |
| Status | closed |

## LNK-F-0048

**The root-redirect cache refills on the **application** pool with no timeout and no singleflight, from a mux to which no `RequestTimeout` is applied**

finding · 2026-08-05

cites: [LNK-M-0036](milestones.md#lnk-m-0036)

cites: [LNK-M-0018](milestones.md#lnk-m-0018)

cites: [LNK-M-0052](milestones.md#lnk-m-0052)

The root-redirect cache refills on the **application** pool with no timeout and no singleflight, from a mux to which no `RequestTimeout` is applied

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0036 |
| Where | `internal/httpx/rootredirect.go:57-71`, with `cmd/linkctrl/main.go:468`/`:506` and `internal/httpx/router.go:438`/`:522` |
| Evidence | All three absences verified. Bounded, which changes the emphasis: the path exists **only on split-host deployments** (`registerRoot` is called solely inside the `SplitHosts()` branch), the query is a unique-partial-index lookup on a table holding one row, and `WriteTimeout` (30s) does bound it. So the singleflight half is near-costless — a few duplicate index lookups per TTL, not a herd. The half that matters is the pool crossing: `main.go:278-280` says the redirect pool exists *"so a slow analytics query on the application pool cannot leave a redirect waiting to acquire a connection"*, and this is a redirect-tree path acquiring from `pools.App`. LNK-M-0018 makes the miss fleet-simultaneous, since `Subscriber.flush()` clears every replica's root cache on every re-establishment including the first |
| Severity | **Minor.** A stated architectural guarantee with a real hole, biting only on split-host under app-pool exhaustion, blast radius one URL rather than the alias traffic carrying the SLO |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 4, minor — redirect path and cache. The batch owes one k6 re-run, not six. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05. All three absences, and the pool crossing the row calls the half that matters is the one that took a new function. `link.LoadRootRedirectWith` takes a queries handle so the caller chooses the pool, and `main.go` now builds the loader on `pools.Redirect` — the read is two plain statements with no transaction and no service state, so the handle was the whole dependency and the crossing existed only because the sole loader available was a method on an application-pool service. The refill is serialized behind its own mutex, separate from the one guarding the fields so a load cannot block cache *hits*, with a re-check inside; and it carries `DefaultRootLoadTimeout`, because this handler is on the redirect mux and `RequestTimeout` lives in `appHandler`. `TestTheRootRedirectRefillsOnceAndUnderADeadline` was shown red by removing both: *8 concurrent requests produced 8 loads*, and *the refill ran with no deadline*. A second test asserts a lapsed TTL still refills, so serializing did not quietly become a one-shot. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F48 |

| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05. `WarnAuditGrowth` reads `ListInstanceGrantHolders` for `instance.admin` instead of every organization's owners. **The row's three candidate fixes all predate D98** — the instance principal did not exist to name when this was filed, and it is the recipient this package's own rule always implied: `audit_logs` is one table for the whole instance, and the only thing bounding it is `AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS`, an environment variable with no dashboard control, no API and no non-config consumer, so the person who can act is whoever administers the deployment. An instance whose principal grant has been revoked now hears nothing, which is correct rather than a gap: fanning back out to tenants would be the defect again. Two sabotages — the wrong permission fails the *principal hears it* half, restoring the fan-out fails the *nobody else does* half — because a test asserting only the first would pass against the original behaviour. `TestAuditGrowthWarningGoesToOwnersOnly` is now `...GoesToTheInstancePrincipalOnly` and carries a second tenant's owner, which is the party LNK-M-0029's open signup manufactures on every registration and the one the old recipient list could not tell apart. `TestAWorkspaceScopedOwnerHearsAboutTheirOwnWorkspaceAndNoOther` uses this warning as a *vehicle* for D102's no-workspace predicate rather than as its subject, so it grants the principal and still asserts what it is about. Three operator-facing claims corrected in `operations.md` and `configuration.md`. |

Analytics are unaffected — every recorded row carries `is_bot`, and `link_click_daily` non-bot clicks stayed 0 — but `links.click_count` is rendered raw at `links_table.html:29` and `dashboard.html:45` and is the `sort=clicks` key, so an archived link can accrue a visible count from crawler traffic and outrank active links. No milestone claim is falsified: m32.5.md:64 states *"A blocked attempt is counted, not audited"* unconditionally. The direction is safe — `click_count > 0` gates both `ReserveAlias` and `PurgeExpiredLinks`, so both alias-protection paths become more protective |
| Severity | **Minor.** An unstated consequence of a stated rule rather than a contradiction. Identical traffic is recorded or not depending on a setting about *responses*; the honest fix is a decision — record for every state or none — not a correction. F24's family, extended to links that previously counted nothing |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 6, minor — wrong behaviour nothing can provoke. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05, D101, owner-answered. Recorded **in every state** rather than in none: `OutcomeGone` now records, and so does `OutcomeNotFound` when a real link is behind it — a link that exists and was asked for a path it cannot forward — while an alias that does not exist still records nothing, because there is no link to attribute a click to. The row is right that this was a decision and not a correction: no milestone claim was falsified, since m32.5.md says *"a blocked attempt is counted, not audited"* without qualification, and that sentence is untouched. *Record for none* was rejected with a reason — it makes the redirect path decide what to record from the response it was about to send, which is coupling the current shape avoids, and leaves a blocked bot on a live link counted, so the rule gains an exception instead of losing one. `TestAnExpiredLinkRecordsItsTrafficWithOrWithoutBotBlocking` puts two expired links side by side, one blocking and one not, and asserts both record; shown red by removing the call. **What this deliberately does not fix** is the surprise the row opens with: archived links go on accruing visible counts from crawlers, because `links.click_count` is rendered raw beside a rollup that counts only humans — that is F24, approved separately. |

The refusal stays `ErrNotRedeemable`, so D27's uniform answer is untouched and the lockout is not observable through redemption; a refusal does not spend the invitation. Both halves sabotaged separately — short-circuiting the lock check fails four assertions, forcing the threshold to zero fails the counter one — because a test claiming two things needs to fail for each of them. |

## LNK-F-0059

**Two narrow privacy truncation gaps: `/48` preserves the entire client IPv4 for 6to4 addresses, and the in-memory salt cache retains salts past the database deletion described as the de-identification…**

finding · 2026-08-05

cites: [LNK-M-0036](milestones.md#lnk-m-0036)

cites: [LNK-M-0052](milestones.md#lnk-m-0052)

Two narrow privacy truncation gaps: `/48` preserves the entire client IPv4 for 6to4 addresses, and the in-memory salt cache retains salts past the database deletion described as the de-identification step

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0036 |
| Where | `internal/auth/session.go:167-186`; `internal/analytics/salt.go:86-96` and `:138-153` |
| Evidence | Arithmetic reproduced: `2002:cb00:712a::1` → `2002:cb00:712a::/48`, whose bytes 2–5 are `203.0.113.42`. Every other v4-in-v6 scheme was tested and is safe — Teredo, NAT64 and ISATAP all embed in the low bits that `/48` discards, and `::ffff:` is folded explicitly with a comment naming the bug class. 6to4 is a single blind spot against a population RFC 7526 deprecated in 2015. The salt half was corrected in the **worse** direction: `Purge` evicts to `today−2` in the same call that deleted `today−2`'s row, so the leader is affected too and it reproduces on the single-replica default; and the eviction inside `For` runs only on a cache miss, so a replica that stops receiving clicks never trims. But the category is over-read: `README.md:126` and `salt.go:135` are claims about what a **database** holds — an erasure request, a backup, a dump — and a heap copy in a live process is none of those |
| Severity | **Trivial**, both. Filed together because both are one-line corrections on the privacy boundary that cost nothing to take, and because the salt one is the kind of off-by-one that makes a proud sentence not quite true. Neither is at risk from any attacker who does not already have more |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 8, cosmetic and trivial. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05. Both one-line corrections on the privacy boundary, and both checked rather than assumed. **6to4** folds to its embedded IPv4 before masking: `2002::/16` carries the client's address in bytes 2-5, inside the `/48` an IPv6 address is kept at, so `2002:cb00:712a::1` masked to `2002:cb00:712a::/48` — `203.0.113.42` in full. Every other v4-in-v6 scheme was tested and needs nothing: Teredo, NAT64 and ISATAP all embed in the low bits a `/48` discards, and each is now a test case, because a fold applied too widely would turn a real IPv6 client into somebody else's IPv4 address. **The salt cache's predicate is now the SQL's**, not an approximation: a salt for day D carries `purge_at = D + 2` and the statement deletes `purge_at < now()`, so D is gone the moment D+2 begins — while the cache evicted `d.Before(today-2)`, which keeps exactly that day. The process held the one salt the de-identification step had just deleted. Eviction also runs on a cache **hit** now, and Purge trims unconditionally: the other evictor runs under leadership, so on a follower a hit was the only eviction there was. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F59 |

## LNK-F-0064

**`ServeMux`'s own path-cleaning redirect is the one response on the redirect tree that carries none of the tree's headers — no `nosniff`, no `X-Robots-Tag`, no `Cache-Control` — and it serves an HTML …**

finding · 2026-08-05

cites: [LNK-M-0037](milestones.md#lnk-m-0037)

cites: [LNK-M-0052](milestones.md#lnk-m-0052)

`ServeMux`'s own path-cleaning redirect is the one response on the redirect tree that carries none of the tree's headers — no `nosniff`, no `X-Robots-Tag`, no `Cache-Control` — and it serves an HTML body

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0037 |
| Where | `net/http`, `ServeMux.findHandler`; the rule it sits outside is stated at `internal/httpx/redirect.go`, `errorPage` — *"the redirect tree is outside the security-header chain, so every response it writes sets nosniff itself"* |
| Evidence | Reproduced on the built image: `GET /ld1//deep` answers `307 Temporary Redirect`, `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8`, `Location: /ld1/deep`, 45 bytes of HTML, and **none** of the three headers every other response on that tree sets. Same for `/ld1/../ld2` → `/ld2`. `ServeMux` cleans the escaped path before dispatching and answers the redirect itself, so no handler in this repository is involved and nothing the project writes can add headers to it. **Pre-existing rather than caused by LNK-M-0037** — `cleanPath` applies to every request whatever patterns are registered, so `/foo/../bar` behaved this way before the deep-link route existed. What LNK-M-0037 changes is how many paths reach it and end somewhere real: before, a cleaned two-segment path redirected and then 404ed. Verified **not** a 301, which would have broken the absolute *redirects are 302, never 301* rule: it is 307. The body is Go-escaped, so the reflected path is not an injection vector |
| Severity | **Minor.** No alias or destination is disclosed that the request did not already contain, and the missing header with any bite — `nosniff` on a `text/html` body — protects against sniffing content that is already HTML and already escaped. The cost is that the tree's stated invariant is not actually true of every response it produces, and the honest fix is either to wrap the mux so the headers are set on the way out or to amend the claim |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 4, minor — redirect path and cache. The batch owes one k6 re-run, not six. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05. `alwaysNosniff` wraps every mux that can serve an alias — the split-host link mux, the custom-hostname mux, and the single-host mux — so `X-Content-Type-Options` is on the one response no handler in this repository writes: `ServeMux`'s own path-cleaning 307, which carries a `text/html` body. **Only nosniff, and that is a choice with a reason.** It is the missing header with any bite on an HTML body, and it is already set by every handler here and by the application tree's middleware, so applying it everywhere changes no response this project writes. `X-Robots-Tag` and `Cache-Control: no-store` are *error-page* policy rather than tree policy — `Location` deliberately sets a different `Cache-Control` and no robots header, because a short link is meant to be shared — so setting those in the wrapper would have changed successful redirects in order to fix a 307. The comment in `redirect.go` claiming the invariant now says what it covers. Shown red by removing the wrapper's one line. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F64 |

## LNK-F-0067

**The per-link rule ceiling and the one-kind-per-split rule are both **read outside the transaction that writes**, so two concurrent creates can pass a check neither would pass alone**

finding · 2026-08-04

cites: [LNK-M-0041](milestones.md#lnk-m-0041)

cites: [LNK-M-0039](milestones.md#lnk-m-0039)

cites: [LNK-M-0052](milestones.md#lnk-m-0052)

cites: [LNK-F-0108](#lnk-f-0108)

cites: [LNK-F-0127](#lnk-f-0127)

The per-link rule ceiling and the one-kind-per-split rule are both **read outside the transaction that writes**, so two concurrent creates can pass a check neither would pass alone

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0041 |
| Where | `internal/link/routing.go:144` — `CountRoutingRules` is called before `s.pool.Begin` in `CreateRule` (LNK-M-0039); `internal/link/split.go` — `CreateVariant` reads `CountRoutingRules` and `loadSplit` the same way, before its own `Begin` |
| Evidence | Noticed while writing `CreateVariant`, which replicates LNK-M-0039's pattern deliberately so that the two writers behave identically. The window is real: two `POST /links/{id}/rules` at 20 rules each see 19, both insert, and the link ends with 21 — past the ceiling that exists because the whole list travels inside the cached snapshot and is walked on every uncached resolve. The split version is worse in kind rather than in size: two concurrent `POST /links/{id}/split`, one `weighted` and one `sequential`, both read a link with no arms, `ValidateSplitKind` passes for both, and the link ends with a **mixed split** — the exact state the validation exists to make impossible. The redirect path survives it (`Snapshot.Split` takes the first arm's kind and ignores the other), but the state should not be reachable. No `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`, no advisory lock and no unique constraint stands between them |
| Severity | **Minor.** Needs two writes to the same link inside a few milliseconds, which is a person double-submitting a form or a script, not ordinary use; and the worst outcome is a slightly over-long rule list or a split whose second kind is silently ignored rather than anything a visitor can observe as wrong. The fix is to move both reads inside the transaction — a `FOR UPDATE` on the link row would serialise every writer for that link — and it belongs to both milestones rather than to one, which is why it is a row rather than an in-spec fix here |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 6, minor — wrong behaviour nothing can provoke. Deliberately **not merged** with F108 or F127 by LNK-M-0052's queue hygiene, 2026-08-04. One class — a read-check-write with nothing serializing it — at three sites, but three files, three invariants, three fixes and three tiers: this row needs `FOR UPDATE` on the link row, F108 needs a transaction and a cycle predicate on the folder tree, F127 needs a row lock on an organization count and loses nothing when it races. Only F127 is approved as work. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05. `LockLink` takes `FOR UPDATE` on the link row inside the transaction that writes, and every guard the write depends on is decided after it: the rule ceiling in `CreateRule`, and the ceiling plus the one-kind and one-fallback rules in `CreateVariant` via a new `loadSplitWith` that reads through the transaction's handle. The link rather than the rules, because Postgres takes `FOR KEY SHARE` on a parent when a referencing row is inserted — so a locked link cannot acquire a rule or an arm, including the first one, where a lock over the rules would have had no rows to take. The outer checks stay, and are now the *message* rather than the rule: they let a caller learn about a full link beside a bad destination in one answer. Each ceiling message is one function, so the two call sites cannot drift. **Two test designs passed against the defect before one held** — racing goroutines (the window is tens of microseconds; six racers produced one winner with the fix removed) and merely holding the link row (the insert's own `FOR KEY SHARE` blocks either way). What discriminates is moving the count *under* a create already parked on the lock; removing only the re-read then writes the twenty-first rule and fails three assertions. **Coverage is honest about its edge**: the deterministic test drives `CreateRule`, and `CreateVariant` shares the mechanism rather than having a race test of its own. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F67 |

| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0044 |

The same registration already reaches `destination_disputes`' sibling gap (F15), so the two want one answer rather than two |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 3, minor — a principal can act on it, in scope by the 2026-08-04 standing rule. **Blocked on D38**, the missing instance-level principal that also blocked F15 and F31 on the first triage. And `domainForWrite`'s *this is the instance default* refusal moved **above** the permission check: it is a fact about the row rather than the actor, nobody may rename or delete it including the principal, and until now every owner passed the permission check and reached it anyway, so the two orders were indistinguishable. The migration confers the scope on **whoever already holds the principal** rather than re-deriving the earliest account, so a principal moved with `lctl instance principal move` stays moved. `TestTheInstanceRootIsThePrincipalsAndNotAnOrganizationOwners` replaces the old *needs domains.write* test, whose premise D100 falsified — instance grants survive a demotion, so demoting the fixture owner no longer removes the capability — and it asserts a full organization **owner** is refused, which is the finding stated as a test. `demoCoverage`'s idempotency assertion is **time-dependent**: today's clicks are generated at minute granularity and dropped when they land after the current instant, so two seeder runs seconds apart on either side of a minute boundary produce different click counts and the test fails

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0044 |
| Where | `cmd/lctl/demo_data.go:361` and `:387` — `if at.After(now) { continue }`, against `at` built from `rng.IntN(60) * time.Minute` at `:358` and `:384`; asserted against by `cmd/lctl/demo_coverage_test.go:534` |
| Evidence | Hit once while running the full `make test-integration` for LNK-M-0044: *"Click history (LNK-M-0005) counted 34532 on the first run and 34540 after the switch"* — eight rows, the number of today's clicks whose random minute fell inside the minute the wall clock crossed between the first and third runs, which the logged runtimes put about ten seconds apart. Not reproducible on demand and it did not recur in four consecutive re-runs; the mechanism is nonetheless visible in the two lines above rather than inferred from the symptom, and it is independent of anything LNK-M-0044 changed — the seeder's click generation is untouched by this milestone. What LNK-M-0044 adds is two more service calls to each run, which lengthens a run by tens of milliseconds and therefore makes straddling a minute boundary marginally likelier |
| Severity | **Minor, and a flaky gate rather than a broken demo.** The demo it produces is correct either way; what fails is the assertion that two runs match, and it fails at random. The cost is that a red `make test-integration` has to be re-run to find out whether it meant anything, which is the property that makes a flake expensive. The fix is to truncate `now` — or to freeze it once per run and pass it to every generator — so the boundary is not crossed mid-comparison, rather than to relax the assertion. It belongs to LNK-M-0038, whose claim is that this test is the thing stopping the demo rotting |
| Reviewed | No. Deliberately **not merged** with F74 by LNK-M-0052's queue hygiene, 2026-08-04, for the reason F74 gives itself: its 252-click delta is two orders of magnitude past what the mechanism recorded here can produce, so folding it in would make this row's stated cause look confirmed. Fix this first — freezing `now` once per run is right either way — then check whether F74 closed with it. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052, 2026-08-04.** The mechanism this row records is real and was never the whole cause. `if at.After(now) { continue }` did drop a different handful of today's clicks between two runs — but the `continue` sat **inside** the sequence of PRNG draws for that click, so a discarded click consumed three fewer draws than a kept one and every link and every day generated after it came off a shifted stream. One click crossing the line therefore re-rolled the rest of the dataset, which is where F74's unequal, unbounded, sometimes-negative deltas came from and why the failing assertion varied. Both halves are fixed in `cmd/lctl/demo_data.go`: every draw for a click is now taken before the discard, so a discard costs one row and nothing else; and the cutoff is `now.Truncate(time.Hour)` rather than the instant, so every run inside one hour generates the identical history. `demoClickRows` was split out of `demoClicks` so the property could be asserted on the generator — `cmd/lctl/demo_clicks_test.go`, two tests, each sabotage-verified against its own half. **Not F68**: `demoActor` (D61) pins the workspace before the reset runs, and `click_events` is truncated wholesale rather than by workspace, so nothing the counts measured was ever workspace-scoped. Reasoning, the alternatives refused and the residual accepted are D99 |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F71 |

## LNK-F-0073

**The verified-hostname cache has **no periodic reload**, so a replica that misses a pub/sub message serves a stale set until it restarts or hears another one**

finding · 2026-08-04

cites: [LNK-M-0045](milestones.md#lnk-m-0045)

cites: [LNK-F-0030](#lnk-f-0030)

cites: [LNK-M-0052](milestones.md#lnk-m-0052)

cites: [LNK-M-0018](milestones.md#lnk-m-0018)

cites: [LNK-F-0052](#lnk-f-0052)

The verified-hostname cache has **no periodic reload**, so a replica that misses a pub/sub message serves a stale set until it restarts or hears another one

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0045 |
| Where | `internal/redirect/hosts.go` — `Reload` is called at boot, on `kindHost`, and by the subscriber's `flush` on every (re-)establishment; nothing is on a timer. The alias tier does not need one because every entry carries `REDIRECT_TTL`; this set has no TTL by construction, which is what makes it exact |
| Evidence | Reproduced by reading. The gap is narrower than it looks: `Subscriber.establish` reloads on the first connection and on every reconnection, and `Subscriber.Run` bounds silence with `REDIS_SUBSCRIBER_READ_TIMEOUT` and probes rather than trusting it (F30's fix), so a replica that stops hearing gets a reload when it notices. What has no backstop is a **published message that is simply lost** while the subscription stays healthy — Redis pub/sub is at-most-once — and on an instance with no Redis at all, where a second replica would never reload |
| Severity | **Moderate** on any multi-replica deployment, restated 2026-08-04 (LNK-M-0052) from *"moderate … with Redis unavailable, minor otherwise"*, which named only one of the two limbs its own evidence establishes. Both limbs are moderate and neither needs Redis to be down: a published message simply **lost** while the subscription stays healthy — pub/sub is at-most-once, and `Subscriber.establish`'s reload only catches silence it notices — and an instance with no Redis at all, where the only reload sites are boot (`cmd/linkctrl/main.go:654`) and `HostCache.Refresh` (`internal/redirect/hosts.go:164-177`), which nothing but the subscriber calls — so a second replica never reloads at all. **Minor** on a single replica, where boot and on-demand reloads cover it. It fails in the direction of continuing to serve a hostname that has been unverified, which is exactly the staleness LNK-M-0045 exists to bound. A ticker calling `Reload` at `DOMAIN_VERIFY_INTERVAL` would close both for a query against a table of tens of rows. Out of spec here because m40.md asks for invalidation *wired into LNK-M-0018's pub/sub*, which is what shipped |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 1, moderate and above. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05. A `host-reload` job re-reads each replica's verified-hostname set on `DOMAIN_VERIFY_INTERVAL`. **It takes no leadership, and that is the fix rather than an oversight** — the set is in-process, so a reload the leader performs does nothing for the other replicas; it is the only job on that clock without leadership and the comment says why. Both limbs close together: a message lost on a healthy subscription is never noticed because `establish` only catches silence the replica *notices*, and an instance with no Redis has no subscriber at all. `Reload` rather than `Refresh`, because a timer has no burst to collapse and inline means a slow query delays the next tick instead of overlapping it; a failure is logged and the replica keeps the set it has. **`cmd/linkctrl` had no tests at all**, which is part of why this shipped — the claim is about a job running without leadership, and `test/integration` cannot import package main. `jobs_test.go` is the first, and `make test-integration` and the Taskfile mirror now cover the package. Sabotaged by removing the reload. Four operator-facing claims corrected: `operations.md` gains the job row (and its `mail` row stops asserting F52's false half), `configuration.md` says the interval drives both halves and what `0` now costs, and `SECURITY.md`'s *on every replica* names the two mechanisms carrying it instead of the weaker one alone. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F73 |

Five recorded deltas now read 252, 152, 4, 67, 8 and 127, they are unequal, one was negative, and the measured base rate from a clean worktree at HEAD is roughly one failure in three or four runs. **That rate is now a release problem rather than only a finding**: `make release-check` needs a green integration run, and a gate that fails a quarter of the time blocks a tag at random and trains a reader to re-run rather than look. F71's recorded mechanism — a minute boundary — cannot produce unequal deltas of this size, so whatever the second cause is remains unidentified. **Sixth observation, LNK-M-0052 group 8's gate, 2026-08-04:** delta **21**, and this time *only* the owner-switched assertion fired, the other two passing in the same run. Recorded deltas are now 252, 152, 4, 67, 8, 127 and 21 — every one different, one negative, and the failing assertion varies between runs. Seven sightings across an afternoon in which six independent commits were gated. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052, 2026-08-04, by the same edit as F71** — and this row's refusal to merge is what found the cause. The magnitudes could not come from a minute boundary because the boundary was only the *trigger*; the amplifier was the PRNG stream moving under a discarded click, which re-rolls every link and day generated afterwards. That produces exactly what was recorded: deltas of any size, either sign, and a failing assertion that varies — the third limb fires alone most often because it sits furthest from the first run in wall-clock time. Measured after the fix at **0 failures in 60 consecutive runs** — `-run TestDemoSeederShowsEveryFeatureItClaimsTo`, `GOFLAGS=-count=1`, `-race`, each on a fresh database, 2026-08-04. Against the pre-fix rate of roughly one in three or four this row recorded, that outcome has probability under 1e-9, and it puts a 95% upper bound of 4.9% on the rate that survives. What remains is bounded and named in D99: two runs on either side of an hour boundary still differ, by that hour's clicks and by nothing else |

## LNK-F-0075

finding · 2026-08-05

cites: [LNK-M-0049](milestones.md#lnk-m-0049)

cites: [LNK-F-0103](#lnk-f-0103)

cites: [LNK-M-0069](milestones.md#lnk-m-0069)

Revoking an API key is scoped to the key's id and its **owner**, with no organization check, while listing keys is scoped to the owner *and* the organization — so the two disagree about which keys an actor acting in one organization can reach

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0049 |
| Where | `internal/store/query/apikeys.sql`, `RevokeAPIKey` (`WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2`) against `ListAPIKeysForUser` (`WHERE user_id = $1 AND organization_id = $2`); the caller is `internal/auth/apikey.go` `Revoke`, which passes only `actor.UserID` |
| Evidence | Read from the two statements, not reproduced. A user belonging to two organizations sees only the current organization's keys in the list, but a `DELETE /api/v1/api-keys/{id}` naming a key issued in the other one answers `204` and revokes it. Both keys are that user's own, so nothing crosses a tenancy boundary and no key is destroyed that its owner could not have destroyed by switching organization first. What it does give is a weak existence oracle — `204` versus `404` distinguishes *my key, elsewhere* from *not mine* — against ids the caller would have to guess. Not touched by LNK-M-0049: rotation adds no revoke path, and the milestone's org-wide keys are still revoked by their own owner |
| Severity | **Low.** An inconsistency between two statements of the same scoping rule, with a negligible oracle attached. The fix is one `AND organization_id = $3`, and the argument against it is that it would make a key unrevokable from the organization somebody is signed into, which is worse |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 7, low. **Re-homed 2026-08-05, owner-directed, and still open.** The owner's answer to this row is a change of model rather than a filter: a key minted by an *account*, reaching the organizations that account belongs to, GitHub-style. Validated as dissolving this row — revoke and list would both be owner-scoped, so they agree by construction instead of by a filter that makes a key unrevokable from the organization somebody is signed into, which this row's own severity calls worse than the defect. **Not built in LNK-M-0052**: it reverses F103's bound, LNK-M-0049's `organization_id` parameter on `ResolveWorkspaceForUser`, D43's role cap and D87's rotation rule, so it is a tenancy model changing rather than a defect being fixed, and a phase close is not where that happens. Scheduled as a *Not in Phase 2* row in Plan.md, which carries the work it implies. This row stays **open** until that lands: scheduled elsewhere is not resolved. **Scheduled 2026-08-06 as LNK-M-0069**, Phase 3 — which dissolves this row rather than filtering it, because revoking and listing both become owner-scoped. Still open until LNK-M-0069 lands. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0069**, 2026-08-08 — **dissolved rather than filtered**, which is what the owner's 2026-08-05 direction bought. `ListAPIKeysForUser` lost `AND organization_id = $2` and now asks the same question `RevokeAPIKey` always asked: whose key is this. The two cannot disagree because there is one predicate, and an account-wide key has no organization to be filtered by at all. The `AND organization_id = $3` this row's own severity cell proposed and argued against was never written. `TestRevokingAndListingReachTheSameKeys` asserts the agreement on the list rather than on the oracle — the oracle was the symptom — and it was shown red by reinstating the organization predicate in `List`, which reported *a key the owner can revoke from here is absent from the list they see from here*. The cost is stated rather than hidden: somebody in two organizations now sees every key they own on one page instead of the current organization's, which is what a personal access token list looks like everywhere else. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F75 |

A domain verification can be made to verify a hostname the caller does not control — including the instance's **own** app or link host

| Where | `internal/link/verification.go:166` reads the row, `:175` resolves DNS (up to `DOMAIN_VERIFY_DNS_TIMEOUT`, 5s), `:201` writes `MarkDomainVerified(ctx, row.ID)`; `internal/store/query/domains.sql:162-170` is `WHERE id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL`.
