| Evidence | Read-check-write with an attacker-pausable network call in the middle, no transaction and no `FOR UPDATE` (`domainForWrite` is a bare `GetDomainByID`). `RenameDomain` is concurrently reachable at `PATCH /api/v1/domains/{domainID}` and clears `verified_at`; the late write then fills exactly that NULL through `COALESCE(verified_at, now())`. Nothing re-reads or re-compares the hostname, and `MarkDomainVerified`'s `RETURNING` row is consumed only to stamp the audit record at `:206-208` — **so the audit trail corroborates the hijack instead of catching it**. Adversarial verification established the impact is wider than a customer hostname: D69 and `hostname.go:39-96` refuse no self-host name, and `customHostRouter` sits in front of both router branches (`router.go:826`), so renaming the in-flight row to the instance's **app host** hides the dashboard and API behind the custom mux (ops + root + aliases only), and renaming it to the **link host** repoints every alias lookup at the attacker's `domain_id` via `redirect.go:177-179`. DNS and certificates for those names already exist |
| Severity | **Critical.** Falsifies m40.md's *"Only after `verified_at` is set does the host router resolve aliases on that hostname"* and `domains.sql:71-76`'s rename rationale. Reachable by any principal holding `domains.write` in any workspace — every organization owner and admin, and one registration on `LINKCTRL_SIGNUP_MODE=open`. The attacker owns the nameserver, so they choose the window length. Fix note: a transaction around read and write does **not** close it, because the rename commits in the gap between two separate transactions, and `FOR UPDATE` across the lookup holds a row lock for 5s inside a 500-row job. The shape that closes it is a conditional write (`WHERE id = $1 AND hostname = $2 AND verification_token = $3`) with a zero-rows-affected branch, applied at both sites |
| Reviewed | No |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0045, reopened.** `MarkDomainVerified` is predicated on the hostname and the token the check was made against, with an explicit zero-rows branch, at both call sites; the audit record is stamped from the checked hostname. D92 records why a transaction and `FOR UPDATE` were both refused. `TestARenameCannotStealAVerificationInFlight` and `TestTheJobCannotVerifyANameItDidNotCheck` rename into the instance's own link and app hosts mid-lookup, and both fail on a build without the predicate. |

## LNK-F-0077

**A host spelled with Unicode label separators or fullwidth characters walks past every destination tier, and is stored and served**

finding · 2026-09-13

cites: [LNK-M-0051](milestones.md#lnk-m-0051)

cites: [LNK-F-0026](#lnk-f-0026)

cites: [LNK-M-0030](milestones.md#lnk-m-0030)

cites: [LNK-D-0046](decisions.md#lnk-d-0046)

cites: [LNK-D-0093](decisions.md#lnk-d-0093)

A host spelled with Unicode label separators or fullwidth characters walks past every destination tier, and is stored and served

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Dated | on import: the row carries no date |
| Found in | LNK-M-0051 |
| Where | `internal/link/destination.go:147` is the whole of host canonicalisation (`strings.TrimRight(strings.ToLower(u.Hostname()), ".")`); `looksNumeric` at `:219` uses `strings.LastIndexByte(host, '.')`; `internal/link/punycode.go:37` returns early unless a label starts `xn--` |
| Evidence | **Reproduced live against the current build.** `POST /api/v1/links` accepted and stored `http://169。254。169。254/latest/meta-data/`, `http://１６９.２５４.１６９.２５４/`, `http://ｌｏｃａｌｈｏｓｔ/`, `http://metadata。google。internal/computeMetadata/v1/` and `http://127。0。0。1/admin`, each percent-escaped into storage, while the control `http://169.254.169.254/` was refused 422. No `destination.blocked` row is written for the accepted ones. There is no IDNA/UTS-46 step anywhere and `golang.org/x/net` is deliberately absent from go.mod (decisions.md ~5847). A browser's WHATWG host parser percent-decodes the host, then runs UTS-46 ToASCII, which maps U+3002/U+FF0E/U+FF61 to `.` and the fullwidth ranges to ASCII. **The finder's belief that Go's client is immune was refuted by measurement**: `net/http`'s `canonicalAddr` calls the standard library's vendored `golang.org/x/net/idna`, and a dial probe showed the stored form connecting to `169.254.169.254:80` |
| Severity | **High**, the tier F26 was given, over a wider spelling space. Not critical: nothing reads the response back, and the webhook dialer's `guardDial` judges the *resolved address*, so the private-address line holds for the one server-initiated fetch. But `guardDial` judges addresses only, so the Postgres blocklist, the shortener list and the homograph tier — all name-based — are bypassed, and this server can be made to POST signed workspace payloads to a host the operator blocked. Falsifies `docs/SECURITY.md:40` (*"a name cannot be spelled past a check that would otherwise refuse it"*) and m30.md's central claim, so it **reopens LNK-M-0030** rather than F26, whose `TrimRight` fix is correct for what it names. Fix note: canonicalise, do not reject — refusing non-ASCII kills `müller.de`, which a recorded decision protects — and a hand-rolled map of the three separators misses the fullwidth spellings, which carry no separator at all. Only full UTS-46 catches both, the ToASCII form must be what is **stored**, and it needs `golang.org/x/net/idna` in go.mod, which the punycode decision refused. **That dependency is a decision for the owner, not a correction** |
| Reviewed | No |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0030, reopened a second time.** `canonicalHost` in `internal/link/destination.go` puts a non-ASCII host through UTS-46 ToASCII before any tier looks, at the single fold D46 already established, with the trailing-dot trim moved *after* the mapping so a separator that is not yet a dot still becomes one. The stored value is the ToASCII form. The profile is WHATWG's `domain to ASCII` and deliberately not `idna.Lookup`, which refuses `my_host.example`, `under_score.example.com` and `r3---sn-apo3qvuoxuxbt-j5pe.googlevideo.com`; an all-ASCII host skips the mapping as `net/http`'s own `idnaASCII` does; a host UTS-46 cannot map is refused with the untiered `invalid` code. `LINKCTRL_DESTINATION_BLOCKLIST` and `blocked_hosts.txt` fold through the same function, or the fix would have re-broken the sentence it was closing. D93. `TestAUnicodeSpellingDoesNotDefeatAnyTier` pairs each of the five spellings with its ASCII control and pins the profile; `TestAUnicodeHostIsRefusedAndRecorded` proves the audit row that was missing; both fail on a build without the fold. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F77 |

D94 records why. |

| Evidence | No goroutine and no errgroup exist anywhere in `internal/webhook` — the drain is inline on the shared scheduler goroutine, and Go tickers hold a cap-1 channel, so every other job's tick is silently dropped for the duration. Registration refuses only *private* addresses, so a webhook aimed at a blackholed public address passes |
| Severity | **High.** Tenant-triggerable degradation of subsystems with nothing to do with webhooks: invitation and verification mail sit in the outbox, automation stops firing on its advertised clock, rollups go stale. Needs only `webhooks.write` from a signed-in member — never an API key, since the scope is non-delegable — and on open signup, anybody. Fix note: delivering concurrently inside `Drain` breaks D77, because `withLeadership` releases the advisory lock when its function returns and goroutines outliving it would deliver unlocked; and giving webhooks their own ticker fixes nothing, because the stall is the shared goroutine rather than the shared clock |
| Reviewed | No |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0047, reopened.** `Drain` dials the claimed batch together and waits for it — `DeliveryConcurrency = DrainBatch` — so one drain costs one `WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT` rather than `DrainBatch` of them, and the two hundred seconds this row measures are ten. The concurrency is **inside** `Drain` with a `sync.WaitGroup` waited on before it returns, which is what makes this row's own fix note inapplicable rather than survived: no goroutine outlives the function `withLeadership` releases the advisory lock on, so D77 holds unchanged. This row's second fix note is right and goes further than it says — a webhook goroutine of its own fixes nothing *even with its own ticker*, because `pg_try_advisory_lock` is session-scoped and every other job would then skip for the same duration it used to stall for. D95. `TestOneDrainSpendsOneAttemptRatherThanTwenty` asserts the overlap rather than the clock — the receiver holds every request until `DrainBatch` are in flight together — and was run against the shipped tree first, where it reported a peak of one and 8.08s for twenty rows. F90 and F91 were out of scope and stay open: F90 is untouched in both directions, and F91 is no longer reachable at any permitted `WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT` without being fixed. **Superseded in one detail, 2026-08-04 (LNK-M-0052):** F91 no longer stays open — LNK-M-0052's queue hygiene re-derived it against this fix and closed it, since its whole mechanism was the twenty sequential dials this commit removed. F90 is unchanged and still open. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F82 |

## LNK-F-0087

**A sequential split on a password-gated link advances the rotation twice per visit, so at any even arm count half the arms are served to nobody**

finding · 2026-08-04

cites: [LNK-M-0051](milestones.md#lnk-m-0051)

cites: [LNK-D-0057](decisions.md#lnk-d-0057)

cites: [LNK-M-0040](milestones.md#lnk-m-0040)

cites: [LNK-M-0052](milestones.md#lnk-m-0052)

A sequential split on a password-gated link advances the rotation twice per visit, so at any even arm count half the arms are served to nobody

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0051 |
| Where | `internal/httpx/redirect.go:327` runs `h.split` before `passGates` at `:360`; `internal/httpx/redirect_gates.go:153-156` answers any non-POST with the challenge; `internal/httpx/redirect_split.go:136` calls `Rotate` unconditionally |
| Evidence | The challenge GET reaches `:327` and consumes a position, then is answered with the form; the verifying POST is not refused (`redirect.go:274-275` exempts `HasPassword`), reaches `:327` again and consumes a second. The arm served is therefore always index `(2k-1) mod N` — **for N=2 that is `arms[1]` on every visit, forever, and `arms[0]` is never served to anyone**. D57 states the opposite at `decisions.md:9408`, repeated verbatim at `Plan.md:810` and `redirect_split.go:117`: *"the distribution is unaffected — whether a gate passes is independent of which arm came up."* That is true of a refusal and false here, because the password gate is the one gate that manufactures a guaranteed second request. `test/integration/split_test.go:215-236` pairs sequential with a one-time gate and uses three arms, an odd count that would mask it |
| Severity | **Moderate.** A shipped A/B feature silently reports zero traffic to half its arms whenever the link is also password-gated, and `click_events.destination_id` faithfully records the arm that was served, so the analytics confirm the skew rather than expose it. Fix note: moving `h.split` after `passGates` is the obvious move and breaks LNK-M-0040's load-bearing ordering (`decisions.md:9224-9231`) — the budget gate would then run before the destination exists, so an unforwardable deep link on a one-time link would spend its single click on a request about to 404. The fix belongs in the challenge branch |
| Reviewed | Approved as work 2026-08-04 — LNK-M-0052's triage, the moderate non-security set. Fixed under **LNK-M-0052's own number**: m45.md's Findings bullet is this work, so no milestone is reopened. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052** (`docs/build-notes/decisions.md`, *LNK-M-0052, four ways the redirect path was not the path it described*), and in the challenge branch exactly as the fix note required. `challengePending` — one comparison over the snapshot and the request method — is asked **before** `h.split`, so a request that is going to be answered with the password page chooses no arm and writes no rotation; the POST that answers it chooses the arm that is actually served. `h.split` did **not** move after `passGates`: the gates run after the destination is known so an unforwardable deep link is a 404 before the budget gate can spend a one-time link's only click, and reordering would have bought this at that price. The reasoning is now written down rather than assumed — the password challenge is not a refusal but the first half of a visit arriving in two parts, which is what makes it the one gate D57's *the distribution is unaffected* does not cover. That sentence is corrected in `Plan.md` at both sites and in `redirect_split.go`; decisions.md is append-only, so the new entry corrects `:9425` rather than editing it. A **wrong** password still spends a position, which is D57's case and stays true. Driven by `TestASequentialSplitBehindAPasswordAdvancesOncePerVisit` — **two** arms, the count that makes the failure total, and the rotation asserted between the challenge and the POST rather than only at the end — sabotage-verified. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F87 |

finding · 2026-08-04

cites: [LNK-M-0051](milestones.md#lnk-m-0051)

cites: [LNK-M-0045](milestones.md#lnk-m-0045)

cites: [LNK-F-0072](#lnk-f-0072)

cites: [LNK-M-0052](milestones.md#lnk-m-0052)

On a single-host deployment, a `Host` spelling that does not fold serves a customer's verified hostname the dashboard, the API and the default domain's aliases — and on a split-host deployment the same spelling of a configured hostname gets the ops-only 404

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0051 |
| Where | `internal/config/config.go:643-657` (`CanonicalHost`) folds case and strips only `:80`/`:443`, never a trailing dot; `internal/redirect/hosts.go:117` keys the verified-host cache through it and `:106` records that it does so deliberately; `internal/httpx/redirect_hosts.go:62` reaches that cache with the raw `r.Host`; `internal/httpx/router.go:867-871` builds the combined mux that is the fall-through arm on a single host; `internal/httpx/router.go:912-925` is the split-host `switch` |
| Evidence | `Host: go.customer.example.` or `go.customer.example:8080` misses the host cache, falls through, and is served by `registerOps + registerApp + registerRedirect` — and `redirect.go:176-179` then resolves against `h.DomainID`, the instance default, so another workspace's aliases answer on the customer's name. This contradicts `router.go:833-836` and `redirect_hosts.go:52-54` (*"a customer's hostname must not serve the management UI, and a session cookie must never be offered a second origin"*) and `docs/deployment.md:239-243`. Reachable over HTTPS: SNI carries no trailing dot per RFC 6066, so the certificate handshake completes and Go passes `r.Host` through unnormalized. The whole LNK-M-0045 suite pins `SplitHosts: true`, the one configuration where the fall-through is the ops mux. **Folded in from F72 (LNK-M-0045)**, which found the same gap from the other side: `CanonicalHost("lnk.links.test.")` returns itself, matching neither `appHost` nor `linkHost` in `hostRouter.ServeHTTP`, so on split hosts the request lands on the ops mux. The mismatch is entirely request-side — `domain.ValidateHostname` drops a trailing dot at `internal/domain/hostname.go:66` and the unique index is on `lower(hostname)`, so a stored name can never carry one — and commit `6f95079` (*"Fold the dot before any tier reads the host"*) folded it for **destinations** and not for the `Host` header. Pre-existing since the split-host router; LNK-M-0045 inherited it rather than introducing it |
| Severity | **Moderate.** F72 filed the same normalization gap at Minor on the strength of a conclusion this row refutes — *"it fails closed (a 404, never a wrong host's links)"* — which holds only for split-host; on single-host the failure is open, and serving the default domain's aliases is exactly "a wrong host's links". F72 also named only the trailing dot, not the port spelling. Fix note: `TrimSuffix` closes half — the non-default-port limb still misses — and stripping the port unconditionally breaks any deployment where the app and link hosts differ only by port, which is what `SplitHosts()` compares. One `CanonicalHost` edit reaches the split-host router, the single-host mux and the verified-host cache together, which is why the two rows were never separable |
| Reviewed | Approved as work 2026-08-04 — LNK-M-0052's triage, the moderate non-security set. **F72 (LNK-M-0045) was merged into this row** by LNK-M-0052's queue hygiene, 2026-08-04: one function, one gap, and F72's stated conclusion was false, so it could not have been triaged on its own terms |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052** (same entry), and the two limbs are closed by two functions because they were always two questions. `config.CanonicalHost` now folds the DNS root dot, in both the ported and unported branches — a lone `TrimSuffix` on the whole string misses `host.:8080`, which the test pins — and it still **keeps** a non-default port, because `SplitHosts()` compares two configured origins through it and stripping the port would collapse a deployment serving the dashboard and short links on one name and two ports into a single-host one. The verified-hostname cache asks the new `config.HostOnly`, which is `CanonicalHost` with any port dropped as well: `domains.hostname` is stored bare, validated bare, and served on whichever port the listener uses, so there is no port to compare against. `HostCache.Reload` keys through the same function, so the two sides cannot drift — which is the failure one level up. `TestHostOnlyIsWiderThanCanonicalHost` pins the direction: the narrow spelling is the one that fails silently. **F72's severity argument is refuted in the test rather than in prose**: `TestAHostSpellingThatDoesNotFoldStillReachesItsOwnHostname` runs on a **single-host** fixture built for it, and the sabotage answered `https://example.com/the-instances` on the customer's hostname and served `/links` — the open failure, not a 404. `TestAConfiguredHostnameFoldsItsTrailingDot` is F72's own case on split hosts. The collision widening could create is named in `hosts.go` and in decisions.md: it still needs a DNS TXT record under the operator's own name, so the precondition is unchanged and only the set of `Host` spellings is. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F88 |

| Evidence | One link write in a workspace holding the permitted twenty subscriptions produces twenty rows, so two link writes a minute from one workspace saturate instance-wide capacity. `EnqueueWebhookDeliveries` applies no cap on pending rows and `WEBHOOK_RETENTION_DAYS` prunes only *finished* ones, so a backlog is unbounded in size and duration; every row a tenant queues has an earlier `next_attempt_at` than everything queued after it. The headline capacity is low enough to be a design fault rather than only an abuse case: one customer creating links through the API at 40/min with a single subscription reaches the ceiling with no attacker involved. Compounds F82. Fix note: `DISTINCT ON (workspace_id)` or a round-robin term reintroduces the tenant-ordered delivery the file refuses **and** cannot sit under `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`; a per-workspace pending cap silently drops events, which Plan.md already says nothing recovers |
| Reviewed | **Reviewed 2026-08-05 and deliberately carried**, LNK-M-0052's third triage, Tier 1. Not approved as work and not closed: the row stays open and the defect is published as a *Known limitations* row in Plan.md. The reason is **not** cost. This row has no repair — its own fix note disposes of both obvious mechanisms, since `DISTINCT ON (workspace_id)` reintroduces the tenant-ordered delivery the query file refuses *and* cannot sit under `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, while a per-workspace pending cap silently drops events Plan.md already says nothing recovers. What is left is choosing a fairness model for a queue, which is a design decision, and a phase close is the worst point in this project's calendar to take one. |

| Evidence | Combined with F95's observation that `url_credentials` blocks any host, the probe works for arbitrary targets with only `links.create`, needing no `destinations.review`. Narrowed by verification: **the oracle destroys itself** — a negative probe *creates* the open dispute it was testing for, notifies every owner, and leaves a queue row carrying the filer's identity, so each host answers truthfully exactly once and never quietly. **Re-derived 2026-08-04 (LNK-M-0052), after F33's repair landed:** the oracle survives and its *key* moved. `03300` adds a second partial unique index on `destination_disputes.blocked_host`, so a filing now also conflicts when an open dispute exists about the **blocklist entry** that refuses the probed host — `login.evil.example` and `mail.evil.example` are one answer where they used to be two. The conflict is still reported to the filer as a distinct outcome, and its wording changed from *that destination* to *that refusal* — which is more accurate about the new bound and no less an answer |

Fix note: collapsing the conflict into the success answer breaks the honest case, where a second filer needs to be told their appeal is already queued; adding a tenancy column to the index removes the bound `01600:67-73` claims and the instance-wide semantics the service argues for, so it is a tenancy decision rather than a de-duplication tweak. **Re-derived 2026-08-04 (LNK-M-0052) a second time, against the mitigation the owner asked to have evaluated.** One fact in this cell moved and the verdict did not: *F15 already grants every owner the full queue* is stale, because `03400_instance_principal.sql:108-109` deletes `destinations.review` from the owner role — but `notify.EveryOwner` was left untouched deliberately, so `internal/dispute/dispute.go:691` still walks every organization and `:703-710` puts the defanged host and the reason code in every owner's inbox on every accepted filing. The mechanism changed and the narrowing survives. What decides every proposed mitigation is that **the two answers do not cost the same**. A *yes* is a failed INSERT at `dispute.go:368-379` — no row, no notification, repeatable, and unmetered, because `internal/httpx/router.go:628` mounts `POST /disputes` behind `signedIn` alone while the limiter at `:770` covers only `APIPrefix`. A *no* writes an attributable row, notifies every owner, and flips the answer to yes for everyone afterwards. So the free, silent, unbounded half is *yes*, and the *no* half is the one this row already calls self-limiting. **A per-filer cap on open disputes was evaluated and is not a mitigation for this row**: it can only ever bound the *no* answers, and its two orderings each fail structurally rather than by tuning N — checked before the INSERT it closes the oracle only for a filer who has chosen to spend the cap on N loud attributable writes, and it breaks the honest second-filer case this cell protects by answering *too many open appeals* to somebody whose appeal genuinely is queued; checked after, the conflict wins and the oracle is untouched. What a cap does bound is disputes-per-account, which is F137's flood rather than this row's disclosure — and F137 is unapproved, and its own fix note already rejects *capping the filer* because the multiplier is `EveryOwner`. Rate-limiting the browser route fails the same test: it meters the answers without removing one, and it is likewise F137's. **The only change that makes this row's claim false is removing the distinct outcome**, and with both rule-outs above standing that means a co-appellant model — one decision row, many appellants, every filing answered identically because it genuinely is queued for all of them. Sized and rejected as worse than the finding: `internal/httpx/api_disputes.go:53-58` returns the whole `Dispute` to the filer, so the obvious implementation hands a prober the first filer's address out of `filed_by`, a **wider** disclosure than the existence bit being closed; avoiding that needs the appellant row to carry its own id, created_at and label so `File` can synthesize an indistinguishable reply, plus `tellFiler` fanning out to N appellants, which newly builds a filer-controlled fan-out on the decide path — the shape F137 complains about. That is a migration, three queries, a restructured `File` and `tellFiler`, a queue change and an API semantic change, at phase close, against a Low existence-only leak |
| Reviewed | Approved as work 2026-08-04 — LNK-M-0052's triage, with F33 and F95. Deliberately **not merged** into F33 by LNK-M-0052's queue hygiene, 2026-08-04, although F95 was: this is a disclosure defect rather than a queue-integrity one, its fix note opens a tenancy question F33's repair does not, and the honest second-filer case it protects has no counterpart there. The `url_credentials` observation it leans on now lives in F33's evidence, folded in with F95. Reviewed 2026-08-04 on LNK-M-0052's triage: **approved as work**, then examined against the tree once F33 had landed and **deliberately not built**. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052, approved and declined** — the third disposition, and the Closed section's intro already allows for a row that leaves without being fixed. The oracle's two answers do not cost the same: *yes* is a failed insert, free, silent and unmetered on the browser route, while *no* writes an attributable row and notifies every organization owner. Every mitigation proposed for this row bounds the second. A per-filer cap checked before the insert closes the oracle only for a filer who chose to spend it, and refuses a second filer whose appeal genuinely is queued; checked after, the conflict wins and nothing changes — what it really bounds is disputes per account, which is F137's flood, unapproved and already rejecting this repair on its own row. The one change that removes the distinct outcome is a co-appellant model whose obvious implementation returns the first filer's address to whoever probed. Recorded in decisions.md and in commit `90c51ec` so the argument survives rather than the conclusion alone. |
| Status | closed |

The **address** limb stays spent deliberately: a correct password is still traffic from that address. The measurement had to be taken on the alias bucket directly, because a fixture has one address and the per-address limb refuses first — which is itself the reason the defect is invisible from a single client. The limb this does **not** close is D54's accepted cost, now written against the decision rather than left to be discovered: a stranger can hold the bucket empty with wrong guesses at roughly one request every three seconds. |

## LNK-F-0116

**With `forward_path` on, the deep-link remainder is visitor-controlled, unbounded to 1 MiB, and walked or copied several times per request**

finding · 2026-08-04

cites: [LNK-M-0051](milestones.md#lnk-m-0051)

cites: [LNK-F-0064](#lnk-f-0064)

cites: [LNK-M-0052](milestones.md#lnk-m-0052)

With `forward_path` on, the deep-link remainder is visitor-controlled, unbounded to 1 MiB, and walked or copied several times per request

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0051 |
| Where | `internal/httpx/redirect.go:721-761`; `internal/platform/httpserver/server.go:43-56` sets `Addr`, `Handler`, `ReadHeaderTimeout`, `WriteTimeout` and `ErrorLog` and never `MaxHeaderBytes` |
| Evidence | No length check exists between the router and the joiner. `joinable` walks every `/`-separated segment calling `url.PathUnescape`, then the concatenation, the unescape of the join and `u.String()` each copy the whole remainder — roughly five passes over up to a megabyte, on a request that touches no database. A cache hit is never charged to the 404-probe limiter, and `docs/slo.md:913-917` records that as deliberate |
| Severity | Minor, corrected down from the tier it was filed at: it is CPU and allocation amplification rather than disclosure or corruption, it needs `forward_path` switched on per link, and 1 MiB is a real ceiling rather than none. Fix note: capping total length alone misses it, because `joinable`'s per-segment unescape is driven by segment **count** — a 40 KiB path of 20,000 empty segments is 20,000 allocations. Bound both, and refuse through the existing not-forwardable 404 rather than inventing a 414 on a tree whose header invariants F64 already shows are fragile |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 3, minor — a principal can act on it, in scope by the 2026-08-04 standing rule. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05. `MaxForwardedPath` (4096) and `MaxForwardedSegments` (64), checked in `joinable`. **Both, because either alone misses it** — the row's own fix note, and it is right: length alone leaves the per-segment cost, which is driven by segment *count*, so a 40 KiB path of twenty thousand empty segments is twenty thousand `PathUnescape` calls under any sane length cap. Refused through the existing not-forwardable 404 rather than a 414, as the row asked, because a new status on this tree would tell a prober something the 404 does not — and the tree's header invariants were fragile enough that F64 was open against them at the time. Generous on purpose: an amplification bound, not a validation rule. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F116 |

Narrowing to the organization-wide rank is right for invitations and **wrong here**: an invitation admits somebody to the whole organization, one ceiling governs it; a role assignment is per membership, and the weakest authority would hide admin from the workspace-scoped admin who may genuinely grant it. No single list is exact for many targets, so the comment now says the service is where exactness lives. D43's cap stays applied, because it is absolute rather than per-target. Absorbs F62. |

## LNK-F-0123

**The shared limiter's circuit breaker has no half-open state, so every concurrent request retries when the cooldown lapses**

finding · 2026-08-04

cites: [LNK-M-0051](milestones.md#lnk-m-0051)

cites: [LNK-M-0052](milestones.md#lnk-m-0052)

The shared limiter's circuit breaker has no half-open state, so every concurrent request retries when the cooldown lapses

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0051 |
| Where | `internal/ratelimit/shared.go:250-257` — `allow()` reads under the mutex, sets nothing, and marks no probe in flight; `openUntil` is re-armed only in `recordFailure` at `:267`, after the failed call returns |
| Evidence | The comment at `:228-233` promises *"an outage costs the timeout a few times and then nothing until the cooldown lets **one** request through to check"*, and `:61-62` repeats it. Severity corrected down by verification: the cost is `REDIS_READ_TIMEOUT` (50ms by default) once every five-second cooldown, a one per cent duty cycle rather than a stall, and it only becomes the herd the finding describes if an operator raises that timeout |
| Severity | Cosmetic to minor at defaults, moderate at a retuned read timeout. The comment is what the next person would trust when deciding whether the breaker needs work. Fix note: a compare-and-swap half-open must re-arm `openUntil` when the probe is **dispatched**, not on its result, or the probe's own timeout window is an open door; and a failed probe must re-open immediately rather than waiting for the failure threshold again. **Tier restated 2026-08-04 (LNK-M-0052) and held.** The range already reflects the widening: verification is what corrected it down, and the tier is stated as a function of the one setting that moves it, `REDIS_READ_TIMEOUT`. Cosmetic at the shipped 50ms, where the cost is a one per cent duty cycle; moderate wherever an operator has raised it, which is a documented thing to do. |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-05**, LNK-M-0052's third triage — Tier 8, cosmetic and trivial. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, 2026-08-05. A real half-open, built the way the row's fix note required: `allow()` **re-arms `openUntil` when the probe is dispatched**, not when it answers, so exactly one caller per cooldown reaches Redis and the rest are refused without paying the timeout. Deferring the re-arm to the result would leave the probe's own timeout window open to the same herd, which is the trap the note names. A failed probe needs no special case — the breaker is already armed, so it stays shut for another cooldown without having to reach the failure threshold again — and a successful one clears it in `succeed()`. Shown red by restoring the read-without-write: twenty of twenty requests admitted. The tier the row carried was Cosmetic at the shipped 50ms and moderate at a retuned `REDIS_READ_TIMEOUT`, which is a documented thing to do; the comment that promised this behaviour is now true at both. |
| Status | closed |

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0047 |
| Where | `internal/mail/mail.go:164-166` sends a claimed batch sequentially; `DrainBatch = 20` at `:62`; `SMTP_TIMEOUT` defaults to `10s` (`internal/config/config.go:339`) and becomes the dial deadline at `internal/mail/smtp.go:136-142`; `cmd/linkctrl/jobs.go:202-203` runs `runMail` **before** `runWebhooks` in the one `case <-outbox.C` |
| Evidence | Found while closing F82, which is the identical shape: the comment at `mail.go:58-61` makes the same claim F82 falsified — a backlog *"drains over several runs instead of holding the job for minutes"* — and twenty messages at the default 10s is 200 seconds spent inline on the select that reads every job ticker, whose channels hold one tick. Closing F82 removed half of that harm class and left this half: the webhook drain no longer stalls the scheduler, and the mail drain that runs immediately before it still can. Reproducing it needs a relay that blackholes rather than refuses, which is what a firewalled SMTP host looks like |
| Severity | **Moderate.** Not tenant-triggerable, and that is the whole of the difference from F82: the relay is one host an operator named in configuration, so this needs the operator's own SMTP to fail in the one way that is slow rather than the several that are fast. The consequence when it does is F82's exactly — automation stops firing on its clock, domain re-verification does not run, rollups go stale, and the outbox that is stalling is also the thing invitations are waiting in. The fix is the one D95 records, applied to a second `Drain`; whether the two packages should share it rather than spell it twice is the part worth deciding rather than assuming |
| Reviewed | Approved as work 2026-08-04 — LNK-M-0052's triage, the moderate non-security set. Fixed under **LNK-M-0052's own number**: m45.md's Findings bullet is this work, so no milestone is reopened. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052** (same entry). D95's fix applied to the second `Drain`: `SendConcurrency = DrainBatch`, a bounded channel, a mutex over the error slice, and a `sync.WaitGroup` waited on before `Drain` returns. **The leadership constraint was checked rather than assumed**, which is what the row's open question turned on: `runMail` calls `withLeadership` exactly as `runWebhooks` does and `ClaimDueMail` is `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` exactly as the webhook claim is, so D95's reasoning transfers whole — the advisory lock sits on a pooled connection released when the function returns, and `pg_try_advisory_lock` is session-scoped, so no goroutine may outlive the call and none does. **The one thing D95 does not cover is named rather than inherited**: a webhook batch spreads over as many receivers as it has rows, this one opens up to twenty sessions to the single relay the operator configured. A relay capping concurrency lower refuses the extra ones and those messages retry with backoff, so nothing is lost, but an outbox held continuously above that cap for `MaxAttempts` abandons the overflow — accepted deliberately and written into `internal/mail/mail.go`, `docs/SECURITY.md`, `docs/configuration.md` and CHANGELOG.md. **Spelled twice rather than shared**, which is the part the row asked to be decided: the two bounds are different decisions that agree on twenty for different reasons, and this milestone has already recorded why an abstraction built to make unrelated call sites look alike is one more thing to get wrong. Driven by `TestOneMailDrainSpendsOneSendRatherThanTwenty`, sabotage-verified. **F90 is untouched in both directions** — same batch size, same ordering, still no per-tenant term. |

So the option is what the tree hand-builds twice: `internal/ratelimit/shared.go:164-210` abandons the call to a goroutine and enforces the deadline with a timer, and D26's `REDIS_INVALIDATE_BUDGET` bounds the retry loop that turned the same property into 9.07s (F2). `redis.go:39-49` already says the resolver's per-lookup deadline is not what holds it, so the fact is recorded — what is not recorded anywhere is that a one-line option would make every context bound its own call |
| Severity | Minor, and latent rather than active: every path that matters is bounded by something else, and both bounds are documented. The cost is that a deadline passed to a Redis call means nothing in this tree and nothing at the call site says so, which is a trap for whichever call site next relies on one. Not fixed on sight because turning it on changes the client the redirect path uses, so it owes LNK-M-0025's measurements again — and because it would then bound calls that today deliberately carry `context.Background()` (`shared.go:159-163`, so a client cannot dodge a limiter by hanging up) |
| Reviewed | Approved as work 2026-08-04 — LNK-M-0052's second triage. Filed by the comment sweep that re-measured F8's mechanism rather than inheriting it. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, `internal/platform/redis/redis.go` — `opt.ContextTimeoutEnabled = true`, and nothing else changes. Every call site was walked before it was set. It can only **shorten** a call: `pool.Conn.deadline` takes the minimum of `now+ReadTimeout` and the context's deadline, so `REDIS_READ_TIMEOUT` is still the ceiling and the two sites that ask for more — the analytics pipeline's 5s, the readiness probe's 750ms — were already 50ms on the wire. Almost every other site asks for exactly the ceiling, because `Options.RedisTimeout` *is* `REDIS_READ_TIMEOUT`. The two that carry no deadline at all still carry none: `fromRedis`'s corrective `Del` and `sweepRedis`'s walk both go through `context.WithoutCancel`, which drops the deadline with the cancellation. So the one behaviour that changes is a caller with **less** than the ceiling left, which on the redirect path is the request context. This row's own note about `shared.go:159-163` is answered: that context is still `Background`, so a client still cannot dodge the limiter by hanging up. **Neither hand-built defence is removed**, and that was measured: `Shared.take` cost 50.46ms without the option and 50.28ms with it because the external timer was already binding, while `takeSHA.Run` inside it went from 400.85ms to 50.32ms — so what the option buys there is the abandoned goroutine releasing its connection eight times sooner, not a defence to delete. D26's budget bounds a three-attempt loop the option bounds one attempt of. `TestAContextDeadlineBoundsARedisCall` and `TestReadTimeoutStillCapsAGenerousDeadline` guard both directions, each sabotage-verified against the field it names. Six comments, two test comments, `redisProxy.clientAsDeployed`, `docs/configuration.md` and D26's Plan.md row are corrected — the reason moved, the decision did not. The redirect path's k6 measurement was re-run; see `docs/slo.md`. |

| Where | `internal/auth/instance.go` — `InstanceGrantable` holds `destinations.review` and `destinations.decide` and deliberately not `instance.admin`; `internal/instance/instance.go` `RevokeReviewer` loops over that same set, so no surface confers or withdraws the principal; `internal/auth/service.go` confers it only under `IsFirstUser`, and `NeedsSetup` is false forever once one account exists |
| Evidence | Named while building D98 rather than found by testing, and bounded before it was written: **nothing in this product deletes or soft-deletes a `users` row** — no `DELETE FROM users` and no write to `users.deleted_at` anywhere in `internal/store/query/`, checked 2026-08-04 — so a conferred principal cannot be lost through the product. What is reachable is an operator losing access to the account itself: a forgotten password with no mailer configured, a departed colleague, or an instance whose earliest surviving account was never theirs, which migration 03400 confers on. `docs/operations.md` documents the `INSERT INTO instance_grants` that fixes it |

It is recorded because the *obvious* repair is the one D98 forbids — an operation that confers `instance.admin` would let a principal mint another principal, and the delegation bound exists precisely to stop the set of delegators growing. Any in-product recovery path is a variation on that, so this needs a decision rather than a fix. A CLI command, `lctl` acting on the same filesystem-access trust `/setup` claims, is the shape most likely to be right |
| Reviewed | Approved as work 2026-08-05 — the owner's review of the rows LNK-M-0052's own fix work produced, **and the owner chose the shape: an `lctl` command**, which is what this row's severity cell nominates. Fixed under **LNK-M-0052's own number**. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0052**, `internal/instance` and a new `cmd/lctl/instance.go`. `lctl instance principal show` names who administers the box; `lctl instance principal move --to <email>` hands it over. **It moves and cannot add**: the transaction confers all four `InstancePrincipalScopes` on the target, withdraws all four from every other holder, and re-reads the holders of `instance.admin` before committing — anything other than exactly the named account refuses and changes nothing. That check is D98's delegation bound asserted rather than claimed, and it is why the recovery does not undermine the thing it recovers. `Service.MovePrincipal` takes **no actor and makes no permission check**, because the authority is filesystem access to the box — the claim `internal/auth`'s `Register` already rests the whole setup flow on — and asking for a `--user` to act as would be asking the operator which identity to pretend to be. The absence of a check is safe only while nothing routes there, so `TestThePrincipalMoveIsReachableFromTheShellAndNowhereElse` scans the tree and fails the build on the symbol appearing outside `internal/instance` and `cmd/lctl`. It is guarded like `lctl seed` and `lctl demo` — refused under `APP_ENV=production` without `--force` — and audited instance-wide with the actor recorded as `system`, since nobody signed in to do it. **No migration**: the four queries it needs already existed. Reviewers already appointed keep the queue. Three integration tests and two CLI tests, every one sabotaged red and restored by counter-edit. |

| Where | No route: `grep` for `forgot`, `reset`, `recover` across `internal/httpx/router.go` returns nothing. No template: `internal/ui/templates/mail/` holds four — `invitation`, `verification`, `dispute-decided`, `audit-growth`. The only password write is `POST /account/password` (`internal/httpx/router.go:482`), behind `signedIn` |
| Evidence | Found while validating the owner's question on F140 — *is account recovery possible as long as a mailer is set up*. The answer is no, and the mailer is irrelevant: the mechanism does not exist to be enabled. Three things make it worse than an absent feature. **Plan.md does not list it** in *Not in Phase 2* or anywhere else, so it is not a deferred decision, it is a gap nobody recorded. **The product has every part needed to build it** — a token-hash pattern used twice (invitations, signup verification), an outbox, a mailer, and argon2 rehashing on `POST /account/password` — so its absence reads as an oversight rather than a choice. And it **compounds F140**: D98's instance principal is one account, that account's only credential is a password, and losing it now strands the instance with `psql` as the sole route back, which is precisely what F140 is about |
| Severity | **Moderate to major.** No data loss and no disclosure, and an operator with database access can always rewrite a hash — so it is an availability and product-completeness defect rather than a security one. It is the highest tier of that class: on an instance with real users, the first forgotten password is a support request the product cannot answer, and there is no workaround short of the operator editing the database on somebody's behalf, which is also the only route to re-appointing a lost instance principal |
| Reviewed | No, and deliberately still no. Reviewed 2026-08-05: the owner chose to **record the absence and schedule nothing**, so this row is now documented in the two places a reader looks — Plan.md's *Not in Phase 2* and README's *Not built yet* — and each says the concrete thing rather than the abstract one: a forgotten password cannot be recovered by the person who forgot it, a mailer does not change that because no mechanism exists to use one, and the operator's route is editing the database. Both name `lctl instance principal move` as covering the instance principal and nothing else. **The row stays Open**: it is documented, not resolved, and the first limb of this cell's own argument — that Plan.md does not list it — is the only one that has stopped being true. **Scheduled 2026-08-06 as LNK-M-0065**, Phase 3, and a hard prerequisite of LNK-M-0068's second factor. Still open until LNK-M-0065 lands. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0065**, 2026-08-07 — the milestone this row was scheduled as, and the whole of it. `password_resets` in migration `03900`, modelled on `pending_registrations`: a `token_hash bytea` unique index, an expiry, a `consumed_at`, and a partial index so the purge is an index range. **Two routes on each surface** — `GET/POST /forgot` and `GET/POST /reset/{token}` on the dashboard, `POST /api/v1/auth/forgot` and `POST /api/v1/auth/reset` on the API — in the public block under the same `guard(...)` as `POST /login`, so recovery and credential stuffing share one budget and the milestone adds no limiter of its own. The token is minted by `auth.NewOpaqueToken` and stored only as `auth.HashOpaqueToken`; a test greps the row for the plaintext it just issued. The new hash goes through `auth.WritePassword`, **extracted so there is one password-writing function rather than two call sites that agree** — `ChangePassword` calls it too. **Four refusals, one answer, each with its own test**: spent, lapsed, a status that is not `active`, and a null `password_hash` are all `404` and never `410`. **Enumeration**: the response is byte-identical whatever the address, `recovery.Requested` carries the normalized address and nothing else so there is no timestamp to keep identical (the residue F13's test found), and a dummy argon2 verification is spent before the lookup on every branch. An address that cannot be recovered gets a mail saying so, mirroring `account-exists` — one template for *no account* and *not recoverable*, per D144. **Blast radius**: every session revoked with none kept, every sibling token consumed, API keys deliberately untouched (D9, D87), audited as `password.reset` with the account as actor, an IP prefix and no organization. The purge joins the hourly `housekeeping` pass at `purgeBatch`, with no new job family. **One limb of the finding survives on purpose and is now a *Known limitations* row rather than this one**: the row said *whether or not a mailer is configured*, and a mailer is exactly what changes it — with `SMTP_HOST` unset there is still no recovery, and D143 is the decision that it **refuses out loud** rather than degrading, which is the one place this product breaks the mail-free pattern D1 established. That is a documented default, not the undocumented absence this row was filed about. D143–D145 carry the reasoning; Plan.md's *Not in Phase 2* row is amended rather than removed, so the Phase 2 deferral keeps its reason. |

## LNK-F-0160

**The demo instance can never show the country breakdown or the choropleth**

finding · 2026-08-06

cites: [LNK-D-0174](decisions.md#lnk-d-0174)

cites: [LNK-M-0075](milestones.md#lnk-m-0075)

cites: [LNK-D-0114](decisions.md#lnk-d-0114)

cites: [LNK-F-0195](#lnk-f-0195)

**The demo instance can never show the country breakdown or the choropleth**, while two `demoCoverage()` rows exist specifically to guarantee that it can. Both surfaces are suppressed on a GeoIP-**configuration** check rather than on data presence, so an instance holding country history shows *"Geographic data is unavailable"* over data that is present

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | Phase 3 planning |
| Where | `internal/ui/choropleth.go:45` and `:78` (`GeoUnavailable`, and *"the map is not rendered at all in that state"*), `internal/httpx/web_links.go:443-450` (the ranked list is *"given nothing to rank when the instance cannot resolve a country"*); the coverage rows are `cmd/lctl/demo_coverage_test.go:405-419` |
| Evidence | `.env.demo` sets no GeoIP path — verified 2026-08-06, the file has no such line. The demo database nevertheless holds **8,123** `link_dimension_daily` rows at `dimension = 'country'` and **34,683** `click_events` carrying a country, counted the same day against `linkctrl-demo-postgres-1`. The two coverage rows each require ≥12 distinct countries and state their purpose as *"the choropleth as a map rather than as one shaded country"* and *"that the seeded codes are ones the 110m map has shapes for"* — so the test built to prevent an empty map passes while the map is unreachable, which is the failure mode a coverage test is supposed to be immune to. Found by blind task 6 of the Phase 3 redesign walkthrough (2026-08-06): the task was *find which country most of last week's clicks came from*, and it could not be completed on the instance built for evaluating this product |
| Severity | **Moderate.** No data loss and no security consequence — the rows are intact, the rollup is correct and the analytics API is unaffected. It is the demo failing at its one job while the mechanism built to catch that failure reports success. The suppression is also not demo-specific: any instance that configured GeoIP, accumulated country history and later removed the database file would see the same sentence over real data |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-09**, D174 — **carried to LNK-M-0075**. The column was stale rather than open: D114 approved all seven at planning — *"a defect does not need a milestone: it is a row in deferred-findings.md and it is fixed at LNK-M-0075 alongside the rest"* — and this row never recorded it. D174 resolves that conflict in D114's favour rather than approving afresh, so the approval dates from 2026-08-07. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-09. Suppression now follows the **data** and not the configuration: `fillLinkAnalytics` drives the empty state, the choropleth and the ranked list from `data.GeoAvailable` **or** `hasResolvedCountries(...)`, which excludes `""` and `"unknown"` exactly as `countryValues` does and keys on clicks-or-visitors rather than the metric on screen. Configuration still counts, so *database configured, no clicks yet* keeps its ordinary **No data yet** rather than a claim about the instance — the sentence is reached only when both are false. **Both are evaluated per link and per window, not per instance**, which is narrower than this row's own fix and the claims first written around it: `stats` is one link over the 7, 30 or 90 days on screen, so a database-less instance holding country history still shows the sentence on a link with no country inside the selected window. Corrected across the class 2026-08-10 in the same milestone — **twenty-nine** statements of this rule in the tree, **twenty-two** rewritten to state the bound and **seven** already exact — and the residual behaviour is F195 rather than a widening taken silently. `link_rule_form.html` is deliberately **unchanged** and pinned by `TestOnlyTheRuleFormAsksWhetherGeoIPIsConfigured`: whether a geo *routing rule* can ever match is genuinely a question about the database, not about history. **The dashboard needed nothing**, checked rather than assumed — it renders no map and no country breakdown, and `web_links.go` holds the only `ui.Choropleth` call in the tree. Shown red by reverting to the configuration check, which reported the choropleth undrawn for an instance holding country history. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F160 |

## LNK-F-0161

**The domains page can state, in one response, that a hostname is verified and that it is not**

finding · 2026-08-07

cites: [LNK-D-0070](decisions.md#lnk-d-0070)

cites: [LNK-D-0174](decisions.md#lnk-d-0174)

cites: [LNK-M-0075](milestones.md#lnk-m-0075)

cites: [LNK-D-0114](decisions.md#lnk-d-0114)

**The domains page can state, in one response, that a hostname is verified and that it is not.** Pressing *Check DNS* on a domain inside D70's grace window renders the flash *"&lt;host&gt; is not verified: …"* directly above a row whose badge reads *"Verified — links are served here"*

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | Phase 3 planning |
| Where | Flash: `internal/link/verification.go:199-205`, surfaced by `internal/httpx/web_domains.go:230-245` into `internal/ui/templates/pages/domains.html:17`. Badge: `internal/link/domains.go:204` (`Verified: r.VerifiedAt != nil`) → `web_domains.go:96` → `domains.html:58-62` |
| Evidence | The failure write is `MarkDomainVerificationFailed` (`internal/store/query/domains.sql:255-291`), which **deliberately leaves `verified_at` untouched** — D70, so a serving domain goes on serving through the grace window. That part is correct and is not what this row reports. The defect is that the manual re-check returns a `ValidationErrors` string asserting *not verified* while the badge it renders beside re-reads `verified_at` and asserts the opposite. The grace-window pair the owner first noticed (*Verified* beside *"links … stop being served at &lt;time&gt;"*) is **not** a contradiction: during grace the hostname genuinely is served, and `StopsAt` is guarded on `VerifiedAt != nil` at `verification.go:113` so the two can only appear together. **Second limb, ≤1 hour wide:** between grace expiry and the next hourly pass, `StopsAt` is in the past and `domains.html:96-98` has no past/future branch, so the page reads *"stop being served at &lt;a past time&gt;"* beside *"links are served here"*. Minimal reproduction, live on the demo at the time of writing: `/domains` → *Check DNS* on `go.linkctrl.example`. Found by blind task 4 of the Phase 3 redesign walkthrough |
| Severity | **Low to moderate.** Nothing serves wrongly — `verified_at` alone gates the redirect path (`internal/store/query/domains.sql:150-154`, *"There is no second predicate anywhere that could disagree with this one"*) and it is correct throughout. The cost is that the one page an operator consults to find out whether their hostname works contradicts itself, on the exact action taken to resolve the doubt |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-09**, D174 — **carried to LNK-M-0075**. The column was stale rather than open: D114 approved all seven at planning — *"a defect does not need a milestone: it is a row in deferred-findings.md and it is fixed at LNK-M-0075 alongside the rest"* — and this row never recorded it. D174 resolves that conflict in D114's favour rather than approving afresh, so the approval dates from 2026-08-07. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-09, **both limbs**. The flash: `MarkDomainVerificationFailed`'s returned row is now kept and the refusal branches on its `VerifiedAt`, so a serving hostname inside D70's grace window is told it *failed its DNS check* and that its links are still served until a stated time, while a never-verified one keeps the original sentence verbatim. The clause is built in **database time** — both timestamps come out of the same write, so no app clock is consulted. The past deadline: `StopsAtPassed` is computed by a pure `domainStopsAt` with `now` injected, and the template branches on it. The grace-window pair that is **not** a contradiction is byte-identical and asserted to still render. Shown red twice, once per limb, including the finding's own reproduction. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F161 |

## LNK-F-0162

**The demo is guaranteed to lose its only verified custom hostname 24 hours after every reseed, and the coverage row that exists to prevent that will fail rather than catch it**

finding · 2026-08-06

cites: [LNK-M-0045](milestones.md#lnk-m-0045)

cites: [LNK-F-0160](#lnk-f-0160)

cites: [LNK-D-0174](decisions.md#lnk-d-0174)

cites: [LNK-M-0075](milestones.md#lnk-m-0075)

cites: [LNK-D-0114](decisions.md#lnk-d-0114)

**The demo is guaranteed to lose its only verified custom hostname 24 hours after every reseed, and the coverage row that exists to prevent that will fail rather than catch it.** `demoCoverage()` asserts exactly one verified custom domain, bounded above and below; the domain it counts can never re-verify against a real resolver

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | Phase 3 planning |
| Where | `cmd/lctl/demo_coverage_test.go:478-485` (`Min: 1, Max: 1`); seeder `cmd/lctl/demo_phase2.go:1434-1498` with the in-process stub resolver at `:198`, `:203-223`; the job that unverifies is `internal/link/verification.go:352-483` via `UnverifyDomain` (`internal/store/query/domains.sql:292-308`) |
| Evidence | `lctl demo` verifies `go.linkctrl.example` through `VerifyDomain` against `demoChallengeResolver`, a map that lives inside the seeder process and dies with it. The long-running server wires the real resolver (`cmd/linkctrl/main.go:615` → `internal/dnsx/dnsx.go:39-47`), and `go.linkctrl.example` is an RFC 2606 `.example` name that cannot resolve for anybody. The hourly `domains` job (`cmd/linkctrl/jobs.go:295-301`) has therefore failed the check every hour since seeding — 13 consecutive passes visible in the demo app log — and at `verification_failing_since + DOMAIN_VERIFY_GRACE` it calls `UnverifyDomain` and the count becomes **0**. Read from the demo database 2026-08-07 01:04 UTC: `go.linkctrl.example` has `verified_at` set, `verification_failing_since = 2026-08-06 11:31:08+00`, grace 24h unset therefore default, so it unverifies at **2026-08-07 11:31:08+00**. The assertion's own comment says the ceiling *"is the whole assertion"* — one hostname verified, one not — and after that moment the demo shows neither state. **The coverage row cannot catch this, and the reason is structural rather than a bug in the row:** `newDemoDB` (`cmd/lctl/demo_coverage_test.go:1133-1147`) creates a throwaway database per run, seeds into it and asserts in the same instant, so it never reads the live demo and no hourly job ever runs against what it measured. The assertion is true at seed time and stays true forever in the only database it looks at. `make test-integration` and CI are therefore **unaffected** — this breaks nothing that is checked, which is the whole difficulty |
| Severity | **Moderate.** The demo silently stops demonstrating the feature LNK-M-0045 built, an hour at a time, and the mechanism built to guarantee otherwise is incapable of observing it: it measures a database that is destroyed before the state can arise. Nothing fails, nothing goes red, and the only signal is somebody opening the page. Related to F160: both are `demoCoverage()` rows asserting a state the running demo cannot sustain, and this one adds the reason — **the coverage test measures the seed, not the instance** |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-09**, D174 — **carried to LNK-M-0075**. The column was stale rather than open: D114 approved all seven at planning — *"a defect does not need a milestone: it is a row in deferred-findings.md and it is fixed at LNK-M-0075 alongside the rest"* — and this row never recorded it. D174 resolves that conflict in D114's favour rather than approving afresh, so the approval dates from 2026-08-07. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-09 — **by a setting, not by code**. `scripts/instance.sh` writes `LINKCTRL_DOMAIN_VERIFY_INTERVAL=0` into a freshly generated `.env.demo`, which disables the pass and the host reload and leaves verification on-demand only, exactly as the variable is documented to mean. The two alternatives are recorded at the statement and both are worse: an unbounded grace leaves the domains page reading *verification failing since …* for the life of the instance, which is the product telling the truth and the demo showing a broken feature; a hostname a real resolver can satisfy needs a TXT record in a zone somebody owns, which no seeder can publish. `TestTheDemoInstanceDoesNotReverifyWhatTheSeederStubbed` asserts the pair — the seeder verifies only RFC 2606 `.example` names, **and** the generator sets the interval to 0 — and reads the generator rather than `.env.demo`, which is untracked. **The running demo needs the line added by hand**: `instance.sh init` refuses to touch an env file that exists, and a worker may not touch the demo instance. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F162 |

## LNK-F-0163

**Granting somebody a role weaker than one they already hold reports success and changes nothing**

finding · 2026-08-07

cites: [LNK-D-0031](decisions.md#lnk-d-0031)

cites: [LNK-D-0174](decisions.md#lnk-d-0174)

cites: [LNK-M-0075](milestones.md#lnk-m-0075)

cites: [LNK-D-0114](decisions.md#lnk-d-0114)

**Granting somebody a role weaker than one they already hold reports success and changes nothing.** The members page's confirmation says *"Access granted. It adds to whatever they already had"* when the added role's permissions are a subset of the target's existing reach, so nothing was added

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | Phase 3 planning |
| Where | `internal/httpx/web_team.go:130-131` (the flash), `internal/team/member.go:301-374` (`Grant`, which has no comparison against the target's existing rank), warning copy at `internal/ui/templates/pages/members.html:20-25` |
| Evidence | Verified against the demo: adding `morgan@example.com` as **editor** on the *Default* workspace while they hold org-wide **admin** inserts a `memberships` row (`internal/store/query/auth.sql:103-106`), emits `audit.ActionMemberAdded`, and adds a second row to the members list — while `GetUserPermissions` (`auth.sql:247-260`) returns a `DISTINCT` union and editor's 8 permissions are a strict subset of admin's 19, counted against the live `roles` and `role_permissions` tables. `MembershipAuthority.In` keeps the minimum rank (`internal/auth/authority.go:88-108`), so the effective role stays admin. **The coexistence is intended and is not the finding** — the `COALESCE` unique index at `00200_identity.sql:144-146` is written to permit it and D31 explicitly rejected refusing it, because the same path carries the useful *org editor plus workspace admin* case. The finding is that the success message asserts an effect that did not occur, and the warning at `members.html:25` is generic rather than conditioned on the selected target and role. Found by blind task 2 of the Phase 3 redesign walkthrough |
| Severity | **Low.** No privilege is granted that was not already held — the direction of the no-op is toward *less*, never more. The costs are an audit entry recording a grant that changed nothing, a duplicate row a reader must reconcile, and a confirmation that is false as written |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-09**, D174 — **carried to LNK-M-0075**. The column was stale rather than open: D114 approved all seven at planning — *"a defect does not need a milestone: it is a row in deferred-findings.md and it is fixed at LNK-M-0075 alongside the rest"* — and this row never recorded it. D174 resolves that conflict in D114's favour rather than approving afresh, so the approval dates from 2026-08-07. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-09, and the grant is **not** refused — D31 stands. Two fixes, both to what is said. `MemberGrant` keeps the returned member, asks whether an organization-wide role of rank ≤ the granted one already exists, and redirects to a notice that says the grant changed nothing; on a lookup error it falls back to the weaker claim rather than the false one. The warning is now a `#grant-note` conditioned on the selected target, workspace and role, with three outcomes — refused, changes-nothing, widens — refreshed by `hx-get`/`hx-select` on all three selects and **correct server-rendered without script**. Subsumption is by rank, and the assumption that the four built-ins nest is written into the doc comment with `00700_seed.sql` named as the only `INSERT INTO roles` in the tree. The API needed nothing: `GrantWorkspaceAccess` returns 201 with the membership and asserts no effect. Shown red at the equal-rank boundary and on the unconditional redirect. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F163 |

**Every bar chart in this product labels its axis ceiling as the peak**

finding · 2026-07-23

cites: [LNK-M-0075](milestones.md#lnk-m-0075)

cites: [LNK-D-0114](decisions.md#lnk-d-0114)

**Every bar chart in this product labels its axis ceiling as the peak.** The dashboard reads *"peak 5,000/day"* on a series whose true maximum is 2,351 — a 113% overstatement, and the only number the chart carries

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | Phase 3 planning |
| Where | `internal/ui/funcs.go:93` assigns `c.MaxY = top`, where `top = niceCeil(maxV)` (`:71`, `:257-273`) rather than `maxV`; rendered as the peak at `internal/ui/templates/partials/series_chart.html:18`. Both the dashboard (`pages/dashboard.html:28`) and the link page (`pages/link_detail.html:40`) call the same `barChart` and inherit it |
| Evidence | `niceCeil` rounds up to 1, 2 or 5 × 10ᵏ so an axis is readable — correct, and not the defect. The defect is that the rounded ceiling is then presented as an observation. Measured against the demo 2026-08-07: `workspace_click_daily` for the default workspace has a 30-day human maximum of **2,351** on 2026-07-23; `niceCeil(2351) = 5000`; the footer renders *peak 5,000/day*. The overstatement is unbounded within a decade — a true peak of 2,001 renders as 5,000, 149% high. **Two adjacent observations, recorded here rather than as their own rows because they share the file and the fix:** `Tick.Label` is populated at `funcs.go:94-97` and never rendered — `series_chart.html:7-9` emits only `<line>` elements — so the 16 units `PlotH = h - 16` reserves for labels (10% of the box) are spent on nothing; and the same rounding is what makes the plot look empty, since fill is `maxV / niceCeil(maxV)` ∈ (40%, 100%] and the demo sits at 46.5%. Found by blind task 1 of the Phase 3 redesign walkthrough, from the note *"clicks per day should be scaled so the highest reading fills the chart"* |
| Severity | **Moderate.** A displayed number that is wrong, on the product's front page, with nothing beside it to contradict it. Nobody reading *peak 5,000/day* has any way to discover the peak was 2,351. The scaling complaint that found it is a design choice and is not claimed as a defect here |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-09**, D174 — **carried to LNK-M-0075**. The column was stale rather than open: D114 approved all seven at planning — *"a defect does not need a milestone: it is a row in deferred-findings.md and it is fixed at LNK-M-0075 alongside the rest"* — and this row never recorded it. D174 resolves that conflict in D114's favour rather than approving afresh, so the approval dates from 2026-08-07. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-09. `Chart.Peak` is the largest reading; `MaxY` keeps the `niceCeil` ceiling and its doc now says it is not a reading. **The scaling algorithm is untouched** — the row is explicit that the complaint which found it is a design choice, not a defect. Both adjacent observations went with it: the computed `Tick.Label`s are now drawn, in an outer viewport with no viewBox nested around a `preserveAspectRatio="none"` plot so the digits are not stretched (at `max-w-6xl` the box is 1.49× its units wide), each on a `fill-sunken` chip because `subtle` on `fill-accent-hover` measures **1.82:1** light and 3.15:1 dark against 6.84:1 and 12.0:1 on the chip; and a third tick labelled `0` finally spends the 16 units `PlotH = h - 16` had always reserved. Only utilities already in the built `app.css`, both themes, no CSS rebuild, CSP unchanged. `TestBarChartGeometry` gained a note that it **cannot** tell ceiling from peak — its series makes the two coincide, which is how this survived to be found. |

D174 resolves that conflict in D114's favour rather than approving afresh, so the approval dates from 2026-08-07. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-09. The four gated links and `spring` are now backdated by the same `UPDATE links SET created_at` the catalogue path uses and given weighted history through the extracted `demoCopyClicks`, so their ages interleave with the catalogue's rather than all landing at seed time. The gap-shaped assertion the row asked for is coverage row **LNK-M-0004**: of the five newest non-deleted links in the workspace a sign-in lands in — the dashboard's exact ordering — at least one must have `click_count > 0`. Shown red by restoring the pre-fix seeder exactly. |

## LNK-F-0168

**`make demo-update` fails permanently once the second workspace's links have landed in the wrong workspace, and the reset cannot recover it**

finding · 2026-08-02

cites: [LNK-M-0056](milestones.md#lnk-m-0056)

cites: [LNK-M-0053](milestones.md#lnk-m-0053)

cites: [LNK-F-0169](#lnk-f-0169)

**`make demo-update` fails permanently once the second workspace's links have landed in the wrong workspace, and the reset cannot recover it.** The demo instance is stuck: two consecutive runs failed at the same statement, and no re-run can clear it, because the rows that block the seed are in a workspace the reset does not reach

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0056 |
| Where | `cmd/lctl/demo_phase2.go:1796-1798` (the reset deletes the second workspace by `demoWorkspace2Slug`, so it reaches only links *inside* it) and `:529-552` (`seedSecondWorkspace` creates `demoWorkspace2Catalogue()`'s five aliases through an actor switched into that workspace) |
| Evidence | Reproduced twice, 2026-08-07, against the demo instance at `b01f512`: `lctl: create Campaigns links: create "spring-webinar": conflict: alias "spring-webinar" is already in use on default`. The demo database holds `spring-webinar`, `roadshow`, `partner-portal` and `cw-survey` — four of `demoWorkspace2Catalogue()`'s five — in the **Default** workspace (`019fc2d4-69a4-7d8a-8093-52799bcd5a59`, 26 links) while the freshly created **Campaigns** workspace holds **zero**. Aliases are unique per *domain*, not per workspace, and both workspaces are on the default domain, so the Default copies block the Campaigns creation and the reset — scoped to the `campaigns` slug — never sees them. A second, independent instance of the same shape is visible beside it: a **`Marketing` workspace (slug `marketing`, created 2026-08-02)** is still in the demo's organization with zero links, because the reset matches slug `campaigns` and a rename of `demoWorkspace2Name`/`demoWorkspace2Slug` orphans whatever the previous name created. **Not caused by LNK-M-0056**, and that was checked rather than assumed: `git diff 099b561 HEAD` touches `internal/httpx/web_links.go` and three test files and nothing under `cmd/lctl/`, `internal/link` or `internal/team`. What LNK-M-0056 did was be the next milestone to run the gate |
| Severity | **Major, and it blocks the loop rather than the product.** Nothing an operator runs is affected — this is the demo seeder — but `make demo-update` is phase-loop.md step 3.7 and a milestone cannot land while it fails, so every subsequent milestone stops at the same place. The demo instance is also now one milestone behind and showing LNK-M-0053's build. Two things are wrong and they are separable: the reset cannot clean up after a workspace rename (the `Marketing` relic), and links that should be in the second workspace are in the first, which nothing asserts |
| Reviewed | **No — raised 2026-08-07, unreviewed.** It stopped the LNK-M-0056 landing at 3.7, so it is reported with the run rather than left for the next drain |
| Closed by | **Fixed 2026-08-07**, in its own commit rather than inside a milestone, on owner approval given when it stopped LNK-M-0056 at step 3.7. Two edits. `demoReset` now collects `demoWorkspace2Catalogue()`'s aliases as well as the main catalogue's (`cmd/lctl/demo_data.go`), so the organization-scoped delete reaches those five wherever they sit rather than relying on the workspace delete to cascade them. And the workspace delete became `slug <> 'default'` rather than `slug = demoWorkspace2Slug` (`cmd/lctl/demo_phase2.go`), so a rename of the second workspace stops orphaning what the old name made — which is what left `Marketing` standing since 2026-08-02. Verified against the broken instance itself rather than a fresh one: the jammed demo database recovered with no manual SQL, and two consecutive seeds produced the same demo. The `Marketing` relic is gone. **This row's second half did not close with it** and is F169: the links are still created in the wrong workspace, and the reset now recovers from a state that should not arise. |

## LNK-F-0169

**The demo's second workspace has never held a single link, so the one thing it exists to demonstrate — that the list, the tags and the analytics change when you switch — is not demonstrated**

finding · 2026-08-07

cites: [LNK-M-0056](milestones.md#lnk-m-0056)

cites: [LNK-F-0165](#lnk-f-0165)

cites: [LNK-F-0166](#lnk-f-0166)

cites: [LNK-D-0022](decisions.md#lnk-d-0022)

cites: [LNK-M-0022](milestones.md#lnk-m-0022)

**The demo's second workspace has never held a single link, so the one thing it exists to demonstrate — that the list, the tags and the analytics change when you switch — is not demonstrated.** `seedSecondWorkspace` cannot move the owner into the workspace it just created, and every link it makes lands in the first one instead. Nothing fails, and no `demoCoverage()` row asks

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0056 |
| Where | `cmd/lctl/demo_phase2.go:569-580` (`actAs` writes `last_workspace_id` through `SetLastWorkspaceForUser`) against `internal/store/query/auth.sql:111-121` (`ResolveWorkspaceForUser`'s precedence: **2. the workspace the user pinned as their default**, *then* 3. the workspace they used last) |
| Evidence | Reproduced 2026-08-07 across two consecutive clean seeds at `dd049ce`+fix: the **Campaigns** workspace holds **0** links and **Default** holds **31**, where `demoWorkspace2Catalogue()` defines five that belong in Campaigns. The mechanism is one row: `select default_workspace_id, last_workspace_id from users where email='dev@killerofpie.com'` returns **both** pointing at Default. `actAs` sets rung 3 and the demo owner has rung 2 pinned, so rung 2 wins and the identity `actAs` returns is still in Default — `link.Service.Create` then reads `actor.WorkspaceID` (`internal/link/service.go:328`) and files the link there. The seeder reports success either way, because nothing compares where a link was asked for with where it went. `demoWorkspace2Catalogue()`'s own comment says its job is to *"make workspace scoping observable"*; it is not observable, and has not been |
| Severity | **Moderate.** No product defect — this is the demo seeder, and `ResolveWorkspaceForUser`'s precedence is correct and deliberate. The cost is that the demo instance misrepresents the product to whoever is evaluating it: the switcher moves between two workspaces, one of which is empty, which reads as a broken feature rather than an unseeded one. It is also the upstream half of F168 — those five aliases sitting in the wrong workspace are what jammed `make demo-update` — so the reset now recovers from a state that should not arise. **Nothing catches it**: the inherited *a new feature somebody can see* rule points at `demoCoverage()`, and no row there constrains which workspace anything is in |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-09**, D174 — **carried to LNK-M-0075**. Raised 2026-08-07 while fixing F168, out of that fix's spec, and it blocked nothing: `make demo-update` succeeds either way. Approved with the rest of the demo cluster — F160, F162, F165, F166 — because the demo is the first thing an evaluator opens. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-09. `actAs` clears the pinned default (rung 2) through the product's own `SetDefaultWorkspaceForUser` before writing last-used (rung 3), then **re-resolves and checks** that the identity landed where it was asked to, erroring if not — so the seeder can no longer report success while filing links somewhere else. Clearing rather than re-pinning is deliberate and recorded: re-pinning would leave the pin on the second workspace for the length of the seeding, and a run dying in that window leaves an account `demoActor` then refuses to seed as. NULL is D22's default. Coverage row **LNK-M-0022** bounds the Campaigns workspace both sides at the catalogue's length. Shown red in two stages — removing the check reproduced the abort, removing the clear as well reproduced F169 exactly at 0 links of 5. |
| Status | closed |
