## LNK-F-0171

**Uploading a logo can make a code's PNG download stop working**

finding · 2026-08-07

cites: [LNK-M-0062](milestones.md#lnk-m-0062)

cites: [LNK-M-0059](milestones.md#lnk-m-0059)

cites: [LNK-D-0182](decisions.md#lnk-d-0182)

cites: [LNK-D-0179](decisions.md#lnk-d-0179)

cites: [LNK-D-0174](decisions.md#lnk-d-0174)

cites: [LNK-M-0075](milestones.md#lnk-m-0075)

**Uploading a logo can make a code's PNG download stop working.** A logo forces error correction to level H, which grows the symbol; the stored margin and scale are carried forward unchanged, so a code already near the 2000px raster bound is pushed past it and `GET …/qr.png` starts answering `422` for a code that downloaded a moment earlier

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0062 |
| Where | `internal/link/qr.go`, `SetQRCodeLogo` — it rewrites the style's level and nothing else; the refusal is `RenderQRPNGBySlug`'s `qr.ErrTooLarge` arm, and the growth is `qr.OutputSize` over a larger `Code.Size` |
| Evidence | Measured 2026-08-07 in `internal/qr`: an 89-byte payload (`https://links.example/` + a 60-character alias + `?src=qr`) encodes to **37 modules at level L** and **53 at H**. `qr.FitSize(37, 2000)` returned margin 13, scale 31 — then a legitimate style the size control would produce — drawing **1953px**. *(Amended 2026-08-12 at LNK-M-0059's reopening and again 2026-08-13 at its second, which reversed the first: D182 makes the requested size exact, so `FitSize(37, 2000)` returns scale 44 with a 186-pixel quiet zone — 4.2 modules — and draws **2000px**, the number asked for. D179's intermediate answer was margin 4, scale 44 and 1980px. Either way the size control cannot produce margin 13 at any request. That shape is now reachable only over the API or from a row written before this date, which is what the test that reproduces this finding hand-builds. The finding's own arithmetic is untouched — 89 bytes, 37 modules at L, 53 at H — because it is a property of the payload and the level, not of the fit.)* Uploading a logo raises the level, and the same margin and scale on the 53-module symbol draw **2449px**, past `qr.MaxSize`. The SVG is unaffected (no raster bound) and the dashboard's inline drawing is unaffected; what breaks is the PNG download and the PNG the panel links to. The existing refusal is correct and its message already says what to do — *set a smaller size and download it again* — so the reader is not stranded, but nothing warned them and the size they set is no longer the size they get |
| Severity | **Minor.** Recoverable in one action, with a message that names it, and reachable only from a style already within about 20% of the raster ceiling. It is a row rather than nothing because the cause is invisible from the surface: the reader uploaded an image and a download stopped working. The fix is a decision rather than a patch — re-fit the size at H on upload (which restyles a code that may be printed) or refuse the upload for a code that would outgrow the bound (which refuses a picture the SVG can still draw) — which is why it is not taken here |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-09**, D174, **and the design question the row raised is answered with it** — **carried to LNK-M-0075**. The owner chose **re-fit the size at H on upload**, silently, over refusing the upload: the payload is unchanged so a code already printed still scans, and refusing would say no to a picture the SVG draws correctly. Raised 2026-08-07, out of LNK-M-0062's spec: no bullet in m50.6.md is made false by it. The occlusion cap, the level forcing, the two-output parity and the contract all hold; the picture is drawn correctly at every size the raster path accepts. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-09, taking D174's answer exactly: **re-fit at level H on upload, silently.** `refitForLogo` encodes at both levels, takes the pre-upload output size as the target — clamped into `[MinSize, MaxSize]`, because a pre-LNK-M-0059 style can describe a picture outside the range — and applies `qr.FitSize`'s margin and scale. Any failure returns `ForLogo()` alone, so a fit that cannot be made never costs a logo already written. **No user-facing copy was added**, which is the part the owner took less than the recommendation on. The row's own arithmetic was reproduced and then closed: 37 modules at L, 53 at H, 1953px before, 2449px after, and **1953px exactly** with the re-fit. *(Amended 2026-08-12 at LNK-M-0059's reopening and again 2026-08-13 at its second, without changing what LNK-M-0075 did: `refitForLogo` still targets the pre-upload size, and since D182 a fit lands on that number exactly — `FitSize(53, 1953)` returns scale 32 with a 128-pixel quiet zone — so the same case comes back to **1953px**, where it started. D179's intermediate snap to a 61-module span put it one pixel off, at 1952px. The 1953px and 2449px halves are unchanged; both are `OutputSize` over a hand-built style, which no fit is consulted for.)* One shipped assertion had to be amended rather than kept — `TestTheDefaultCodeCarriesALogoToo` asserted an upload changes the level *and nothing else about the picture*, which D174 makes false on purpose. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F171 |

## LNK-F-0173

**A configured but unreachable SMTP relay blocks the whole server from starting, for the full SMTP timeout, at every boot**

finding · 2026-08-08

cites: [LNK-M-0066](milestones.md#lnk-m-0066)

cites: [LNK-M-0053](milestones.md#lnk-m-0053)

cites: [LNK-M-0065](milestones.md#lnk-m-0065)

cites: [LNK-M-0023](milestones.md#lnk-m-0023)

cites: [LNK-M-0071](milestones.md#lnk-m-0071)

cites: [LNK-M-0072](milestones.md#lnk-m-0072)

cites: [LNK-M-0075](milestones.md#lnk-m-0075)

cites: [LNK-D-0166](decisions.md#lnk-d-0166)

**A configured but unreachable SMTP relay blocks the whole server from starting, for the full SMTP timeout, at every boot.** The reachability probe runs before the HTTP listener does, so nothing — including the redirect path — is served until the relay answers or the dial times out

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0066 |
| Where | `cmd/linkctrl/main.go:395`, `sender.Verify(ctx)` called synchronously in `run`; the listener does not start until `internal/platform/httpserver/server.go:76` is reached, later in the same function; the timeout is `LINKCTRL_SMTP_TIMEOUT` (`internal/config/config.go`, `docs/configuration.md:600`, default `10s`) |
| Evidence | **Measured on the test instance, 2026-08-08**, with `LINKCTRL_SMTP_HOST=192.0.2.1` (RFC 5737, routes nowhere): `starting` at 06:52:01.216, relay error at 06:52:11.262, `http server listening` at 06:52:11.266 — **10.05s of dead server**, equal to the timeout. At `LINKCTRL_SMTP_TIMEOUT=300s` the container never became healthy at all and `docker compose up --wait` gave up with *"container linkctrl-test-app-1 is unhealthy"*. The code's own comment at `main.go:386-394` is what this contradicts: *"A warning and not a fatal error, for the same reason Redis is: the relay being down is not a reason for a link shortener to stop serving redirects."* It is not fatal and it does stop serving. Redis is not comparable — its dial timeout is `1s` (`config.go:123`) against SMTP's `10s`. Not an LNK-M-0053–LNK-M-0065 defect: this is LNK-M-0023's mailer, found because LNK-M-0065 is what makes a mailer worth configuring |
| Severity | **Moderate.** Nobody has met it because `SMTP_HOST` unset is the default and an unset host skips the probe entirely — LNK-M-0065 is the milestone that gives operators a reason to set one. It lands on LNK-M-0071/LNK-M-0072: a rolling deploy's new container is unavailable for the timeout at every start, and a healthcheck with a shorter start period fails it. The fix is to run the probe after the listener, or in a goroutine |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-08**, LNK-M-0066's triage. **Scheduled into LNK-M-0071**, not LNK-M-0075 — it is a failover defect and LNK-M-0071 is the failover contract, and leaving it for the phase's last milestone would have LNK-M-0072 measure a rolling deploy against a replica that is dead for ten seconds at every start |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0071**, the failover milestone it was scheduled into. The probe now runs in a goroutine of its own (**D166**): *after* the listener was the other option in m56.md and is not available at the cost it implies, because `srv.Run` blocks and is the last statement of `run`. Nothing between the probe and `ListenAndServe` ever read its result — the outbox retries regardless — so the ten seconds of dead server bought the order of two log lines and nothing else. Guarded by `TestTheSMTPProbeDoesNotGateTheListener` in `cmd/linkctrl`, which parses `main.go` and fails if the `Verify` call is not lexically inside a `go` statement; its blind spot is written into the test. The contradicted comment at `main.go:386-396` is true again, and `docs/configuration.md`'s `SMTP_TIMEOUT` row now says the probe is off the startup path |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F173 |

The dashboard pictures render correctly and the per-code scan counts are there, so `demoCoverage()`'s LNK-M-0060 row passes — this is F160's shape exactly: **the coverage test measures the seed, not the instance**, and cannot see that the link the seeded codes point at is dead. Nothing in LNK-M-0060's or LNK-M-0062's demo bullet is falsified as written; what fails is the inherited rule they serve — *a feature only reachable by building the state yourself is one nobody evaluating this product will find* |
| Severity | **Moderate**, and entirely to the demo's job. No correctness or security consequence. Three milestones of QR work — sized codes, several per link, a logo in the middle — are demonstrated by pictures of codes that refuse every scan, on the instance built for evaluating this product |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-08**, LNK-M-0066's triage — worked immediately, because the demo is the instance the owner evaluates from and it is currently showing three milestones of QR work through codes that refuse every scan |
| Closed by | **2026-08-08, in its own commit under LNK-M-0066's triage.** `demoQRStyled` moves from `summer-sale` — which exists in the catalogue to demonstrate expiry — to `launch`, the demo's most-visited link, on the default host with no expiry, no click budget and no gate. **The guard that could not see this is what the commit is really for**: a `demoCoverage()` row, *No QR code points at a link that refuses*, counts codes whose link is expired, exhausted, gated or deleted and requires none. ## LNK-F-0177

**Erasure scrubs the actor snapshot and not an address carried in an audit record's `metadata`**

finding · 2026-08-09

cites: [LNK-M-0067](milestones.md#lnk-m-0067)

cites: [LNK-D-0174](decisions.md#lnk-d-0174)

cites: [LNK-M-0075](milestones.md#lnk-m-0075)

cites: [LNK-F-0181](#lnk-f-0181)

cites: [LNK-D-0148](decisions.md#lnk-d-0148)

**Erasure scrubs the actor snapshot and not an address carried in an audit record's `metadata`.** An erased account's address survives in the detail of records where the account is the *subject* of somebody else's action — and in one case in the detail of its own record

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0067 |
| Where | `internal/store/query/accounts.sql`, `EraseDeletedAccounts` — the three label columns and nothing else. The writers: `internal/invite/invite.go:437` (`invitation.created`) and `:860` (`invitation.redeemed`), `internal/team/member.go:197`, `:258`, `:386` (`member.added`, `member.removed`, `member.role_changed`), `internal/instance/instance.go:502` |
| Evidence | Six sites, counted rather than recalled, every one of them writing the key `"email"`. Reproduced by the demo seeder: the departed account joins by redeeming an invitation, and after `seedDeletedAccount` has deleted and erased it, its `invitation.redeemed` record reads `actor_label = 'deleted account'` with `metadata->>'email'` still holding the address. The administrator's `invitation.created` record holds it too, and that one has a *live* actor — so the row that carries an erased person's address is somebody else's audit entry. Not reachable without `audit.read`, which is not delegable to an API key, and the records are governed by `AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS` |
| Severity | **Moderate.** No exposure beyond an existing permission and no loss, but it is a limit on a claim the product now makes about itself, which is the kind of gap a compliance reader is entitled to have stated rather than to discover. It is stated: `docs/SECURITY.md`'s *What is not defended* names it, and Plan.md's discharged row points here |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-09**, D174 — **carried to LNK-M-0075**, and **bundled with F181**: both are an erased address surviving somewhere the erasure pass does not reach, and that pass is opened for F181 anyway. Raised at LNK-M-0067, out of its spec and deliberately not decided inside it — m52.md identifies the residue as the actor snapshot, with a file:line, and D148 settles only what the tombstone is. Both halves the owner weighed stand unchanged: the address sits inside a record of what somebody *else* did, so removing it edits their audit entry, and the only mechanism that reaches it — matching `metadata->>'email'` against the erased address — is a sequential scan of a partitioned table that is the largest thing in this schema after analytics. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-09, **bundled with F181** as D174 directed — one erasure pass, opened once. `EraseDeletedAccounts` now scrubs the `"email"` key inside `audit_logs.metadata`, case-folded on both sides because `invitation.created` stores what the administrator typed. **Seven writers, not the six this row counted**: the row's `instance.go:502` is stale and `instance.go` writes two. Written by the **same** `UPDATE` as `actor_label` rather than a second one, and that is not tidiness — Postgres applies one of two data-modifying CTEs that write the same row and silently drops the other, which the existing tombstone test caught immediately, and an `invitation.redeemed` record is both the erased actor's and carries their address. The new `batch` CTE aggregates rather than joining `pending`, for the same hazard across a batch of more than one. **`HAVING count(*) > 0` is load-bearing** and was proved with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)`: with it an idle pass shows `never executed` on all seven partitions; without it every partition is scanned hourly on an instance where nobody has ever deleted an account. Shown red in both directions, including the over-reach one. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F177 |

## LNK-F-0180

**Two leaders of the domains family record one custom-domain verification twice**

finding · 2026-08-09

cites: [LNK-M-0072](milestones.md#lnk-m-0072)

cites: [LNK-D-0174](decisions.md#lnk-d-0174)

cites: [LNK-M-0075](milestones.md#lnk-m-0075)

cites: [LNK-F-0185](#lnk-f-0185)

**Two leaders of the domains family record one custom-domain verification twice.** The pass decides whether to write a `domain.verified` audit record from `full.VerifiedAt`, which it read *before* its own write, rather than from what the write returned — so two passes that both read the row unverified both record the event, and the idempotent `UPDATE` underneath them hides nothing because it was never the thing being duplicated

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0072 |
| Where | `internal/link/verification.go:400-406` — the `if full.VerifiedAt == nil` branch and the `recordDomainEvent` inside it, against the `full` read at `:371`. `MarkDomainVerified` itself is safe (`internal/store/query/domains.sql:230-231`, *"sets verified_at only when it is not already set"*), which is why the duplicate is a record and not a state |
| Evidence | **Reproduced, five runs of five.** Two concurrent `ReverifyDomains` passes on one pool against a freshly registered hostname whose challenge resolves produced **2 `domain.verified` audit records** for one verification, every time; the probe was written against `newDomains` in `test/integration/custom_domains_test.go`, run, and deleted. The *failing* path did not duplicate in the same probe — 1 `domain_failing` notification of 1 — because the second pass usually re-reads `verification_failing_since` after the first has COALESCEd it, so that half is a narrower race and is not claimed here. `UnverifyDomain` is genuinely closed: its `verified_at IS NOT NULL` predicate makes the second leader's write affect zero rows and the audit record is never reached. **The one other read-then-write guard in the eight families was probed and did not reproduce**: `notify.Service.WarnAuditGrowth` (`internal/notify/notify.go:797-805`) reads `NotifiedSince` and then inserts, which is the same shape, but two concurrent calls produced **1 notification, five runs of five** — the two statements have nothing slow between them, so the second caller sees the first's row. It is recorded here rather than filed, because a race nobody has shown is a report and not a finding; if it is ever shown, it is this row's shape at a second site and needs a different fix, since `Notify` is an unconditional insert with nothing to branch on |
| Severity | **Minor.** Nothing is lost, nothing is served wrongly, and no state diverges — the duplicate is one extra row in an audit log, on a hostname that was correctly verified. What it costs is that the audit trail stops being a count of events: somebody reconciling *how many times was this hostname verified* gets two for one. It is also the **only** one of the eight job families whose second-layer defence is a read rather than a write, which is worth more than the row's own severity — the pattern is what to watch for, and the domains pass is the most exposed to the window because it is the longest (a batch of DNS lookups, bounded at ten minutes) |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-09**, D174 — **carried to LNK-M-0075**. Raised at LNK-M-0072 while enumerating what each of the eight families does under two leaders, which is that milestone's own bullet — and m57.md says in as many words that the unsafe one *"is a finding rather than something this milestone quietly fixes"*, so it was filed rather than repaired. The fix was stated in the row so the review was about scheduling rather than design: branch on `verified.VerifiedAt` (what `MarkDomainVerified` returned) instead of on `full.VerifiedAt` (what was read a DNS round trip earlier). |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-09, by the fix this row stated: the pass branches on what `MarkDomainVerified` returned rather than on what it read a DNS round trip earlier. `newlyVerified` exploits what the write already guarantees — `verified_at = COALESCE(verified_at, now())` beside `updated_at = now()` in one statement means the two are equal exactly when this call filled the NULL — so no SQL changed and no column was added. The residual is documented rather than claimed away: two transactions sharing a microsecond `now()` remain possible, because `now()` is taken before the second writer blocks on the row lock. The integration test makes the interleaving **deterministic** through the file's existing `stubZone.interrupt` rather than probabilistic, and reproduced the finding's 2-of-1 exactly when reverted. **The manual *Verify* button has the same defect twelve lines away and is F185**, filed rather than folded in, because this row scopes itself to the job family. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F180 |

The scrub that does not reach it: `internal/store/query/accounts.sql:149-231` (`EraseDeletedAccounts` — three label columns and the account row, and nothing else). **There is no purge**: `invitations.sql` declares `RevokeLapsedInvitation` and no delete, and no job removes the row |
| Evidence | Reproduced end to end on the test instance 2026-08-09, through the product rather than by SQL: an account invited into an organization, redeemed, then deleted through `POST /account/delete` and erased by the hourly pass. Afterwards `users.email` is `''`, `anonymized_at` is set, both of its audit entries read `deleted account` — and `select email from invitations` returns `review-editor@killerofpie.com`, which `GET /invites` then renders under *Address* beside the role and *accepted*. `mail_outbox.recipient` holds it too, bounded by `PurgeFinishedMail`; the invitation is bounded by nothing. **The reach is what makes this a row rather than a note**: F177's residue needs `audit.read`, which is not delegable, and ages out under `AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS`; this one needs only whatever role sees invitations, and no setting expires it |
| Severity | **Moderate.** No exposure outside the organization and no loss — the invitation is that organization's own record, which is the argument for keeping it. The cost is that `docs/SECURITY.md:86-99` enumerates the erasure residue and names one item, the audit `metadata`, so a compliance reader is told the shape of what survives and is told it is bounded by a permission and a retention window. This one is neither, and the sentence it falsifies is the claim in the same table that *the residue identifies nobody from inside this instance*. Fix note: purging or scrubbing redeemed invitations is a design question about whose record it is, and the cheaper half — saying so in *What is not defended* — is not |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-09**, LNK-M-0074's triage — **carried to LNK-M-0075**, and the owner chose the scrub over documenting it. Out of LNK-M-0067's spec when raised: its bullets enumerate the two tables carrying an actor snapshot with no foreign key to `users`, and this is neither of them |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-09 — the owner chose the scrub over documenting it, and it is bundled with F177 in one pass. `invitations.email` is blanked on the invitations the erased account **redeemed**, joined by `redeemed_by` rather than by the address. An **outstanding** invitation addressed to the same text is deliberately left alone and the test proves that direction too: it is an offer to an address rather than a record of a person, the address became reusable the moment the account was deleted, and blanking it would break the redemption comparison for whoever takes it next. Empty string rather than the tombstone, for the reason `users.email` is one — redemption compares against this column, and a placeholder that reads like a label is a value that comparison would then have to rule out. `invitations_outstanding_email_key` cannot collide on the blanks: it excludes redeemed rows, which is every row this reaches. |

## LNK-F-0182

**Both forms that hand out authority default to the most privileged role the actor can assign**

finding · 2026-08-09

cites: [LNK-M-0074](milestones.md#lnk-m-0074)

cites: [LNK-D-0043](decisions.md#lnk-d-0043)

cites: [LNK-M-0075](milestones.md#lnk-m-0075)

cites: [LNK-M-0053](milestones.md#lnk-m-0053)

cites: [LNK-M-0058](milestones.md#lnk-m-0058)

cites: [LNK-D-0173](decisions.md#lnk-d-0173)

**Both forms that hand out authority default to the most privileged role the actor can assign.** The invitation form and the members *give somebody access* form each render their roles in rank order and mark none of them `selected`, so a browser selects the first — `owner` for an owner, `admin` for an admin. Filling in an address and pressing the button, without touching the select, sends an **owner** invitation

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0074 |
| Where | Invite: `internal/ui/templates/pages/invites.html:41-45` (`{{if eq $.Form.Role .Slug}} selected{{end}}`, against `internal/httpx/web_invitations.go:40-60`, which never sets `Form.Role` on `GET`). Grant: `internal/ui/templates/pages/members.html:48-52`, which has no `selected` limb at all. The contrast is forty lines away: `members.html:88-95`, the *change* form, marks the member's current role |
| Evidence | Found by doing it accidentally, 2026-08-09: a walkthrough that filled in an address and submitted produced *"You have been invited as owner"* on the redemption page. Confirmed by reading the control rather than the markup — Playwright reports `#role` and `#grant_role` both returning `owner` as their value on a freshly loaded page, with options `[Owner, Admin, Editor, Viewer]`. The service is not what is wrong: `Invites.Roles` and the D43 cap both bound the list to the actor's own rank, which is why the default is the actor's *maximum* rather than the instance's |
| Severity | **Low to moderate**, and it is a default rather than a hole. Nothing is escalated — the actor could have chosen owner deliberately, and an admin cannot offer owner at all. The cost is that the least deliberate path through the form is the most powerful one, on the two surfaces that create authority, while the third form on the same page gets it right. An owner invitation cannot be narrowed afterwards without removing and re-adding the person |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-09**, LNK-M-0074's triage — **carried to LNK-M-0075**, and the owner chose the lowest role as the default on **both** creation forms over requiring a deliberate choice. Out of every reviewed milestone's spec when raised: LNK-M-0053–LNK-M-0058 redesigned the shell, the links list and the link page, and neither form is on them |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-09, taking D173's answer exactly — **the lowest role is the default on both creation forms**, not an empty first choice. `weakestRole` picks the highest *rank* rather than the last list entry, so a reordered list cannot change the default; it is set on every load of both pages including `GET`, and a posted role is only restored when non-empty, which is what used to reproduce the defect on an error re-render. `invites.html` was already correct — its `selected` limb existed and the handler never fed it. The tests scope to each `<select>` by id, because a member row whose role is editor emits identical option markup and a whole-body match would pass on the wrong control. Shown red by flipping the rank comparison, by removing each `selected` limb in turn, and by blanking `Form.Role` in both loaders. |
| Status | closed |

## LNK-F-0183

**Cutting an organization out of an account-wide key's reach stops it acting there and not reading about it**

finding · 2026-08-09

cites: [LNK-M-0074](milestones.md#lnk-m-0074)

cites: [LNK-F-0103](#lnk-f-0103)

cites: [LNK-M-0075](milestones.md#lnk-m-0075)

cites: [LNK-M-0069](milestones.md#lnk-m-0069)

**Cutting an organization out of an account-wide key's reach stops it acting there and not reading about it.** `GET /api/v1/workspaces` goes on listing the barred organization's name, slug and workspace ids to the revoked key, because the bound it applies is *pinned or not* rather than *reachable or not*

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0074 |
| Where | `internal/auth/workspace.go:131` — `if actor.IsAPIKey() && actor.APIKeyOrgID != nil && r.OrganizationID != *actor.APIKeyOrgID`, and `APIKeyOrgID` is nil for exactly the keys a reach revocation applies to. The revocation itself is honoured everywhere else: `internal/store/query/apikeys.sql:65-110` excludes barred organizations when resolving one, and `:43-63`'s coarse membership check excludes them too |
| Evidence | Driven through the product 2026-08-09, no SQL: an account-wide key minted for an account belonging to two organizations; an **administrator of the second** revoked its reach with `DELETE /api/v1/api-keys/{id}`, which wrote the `api_key_org_revocations` row and answered 204. Afterwards the key's writes land in the *other* organization, which is the revocation working — and `GET /api/v1/workspaces` still returns both, the barred one included. The function's own comment argues an account-wide key is unbounded because *"the tenants it would be reading about are the tenants it works in"*, which is the premise a revocation removes |
| Severity | **Minor.** What leaks is an organization's name and its workspace ids, to a credential whose legitimate holder is a member of that organization anyway and can see all of it in a browser. It is a row because the case the revocation exists for is the credential that is **not** in legitimate hands, and that is precisely the case where the administrator has been told the key is cut out and half of it is not. Same shape as F103, which is the finding this bound came from. Fix note: one more clause on the same line, reading the revocations for the acting key — but it is a query per listing unless it rides the resolution that already happened |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-09**, LNK-M-0074's triage — **carried to LNK-M-0075**: the read half is closed rather than stated as a bound. Out of LNK-M-0069's spec when raised: it requires the reach revoke be *distinguishable from a full revoke*, which it is, and says nothing about what a revoked key may still read |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-09 — the read half is closed rather than stated as a bound. `ResolveOrganizationForAPIKey` aggregates the revocations once into a `barred` CTE and returns them alongside the chosen organization, so the bound costs **zero extra queries**: it rides the resolution that was already happening, which is the route the row's fix note said was the difference between a bound and a bound somebody later drops. `Identity.APIKeyBarredOrgIDs` carries them; the unexported `keyReaches` reads pinned-and-account-wide together in one predicate, so the two reaches cannot drift apart. Shown red both ways — `return true` reported the barred organization's name, slug and workspace ids still being disclosed, and `return false` caught the over-correction of telling an unrevoked key about neither. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F183 |

## LNK-F-0184

**`/account/mfa` scrolls sideways on a phone**

finding · 2026-08-09

cites: [LNK-M-0074](milestones.md#lnk-m-0074)

cites: [LNK-M-0053](milestones.md#lnk-m-0053)

cites: [LNK-M-0068](milestones.md#lnk-m-0068)

cites: [LNK-M-0075](milestones.md#lnk-m-0075)

**`/account/mfa` scrolls sideways on a phone**, by 174px at a 360px viewport — the one page in the dashboard that does. The offender is the enrolment QR: `internal/qr` writes fixed `width`/`height` onto the `<svg>`, and the `w-40` wrapper around it sizes the box without constraining the child

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0074 |
| Where | `internal/ui/templates/pages/mfa.html:90` — `<div class="w-40 shrink-0 rounded-md border border-line-strong p-1">{{.QR}}</div>`. The scan that does not see it is `internal/ui/overflow_test.go:18-30`, which checks `<table>` and `<pre>` and states a fixed-width SVG as one of the three things it deliberately does not claim |
| Evidence | Measured 2026-08-09 in Chromium at 360×780, signed in, over eighteen dashboard routes: seventeen report `document.documentElement.scrollWidth - window.innerWidth` of **0** and `/account/mfa` reports **174**. The outermost offending element is a single `<svg>`, 488px wide, right edge at 534 against a 360px viewport; `/account` on the same sweep is 0. It is enrolment-state dependent — the QR is only drawn while the second factor is off, which is the state somebody setting one up is in, and m53.md:56 names enrolling *"from the same device"* as a case it designed for |
| Severity | **Low.** Nothing is unreachable: the page scrolls, the secret is printed in text beside the QR for exactly this reader, and every control still works. It is worth a row because it is the first thing to break the redesign's headline property since LNK-M-0053 shipped it, and because the amendment that narrowed LNK-M-0053's bullet at its reopening named *"a fixed-width SVG"* as what the scan would not catch — two milestones before LNK-M-0068 added one. Fix note: `max-w-full h-auto` on the emitted SVG, or a `max-w-full` wrapper, either of which the scan still cannot assert |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-09**, LNK-M-0074's triage — **carried to LNK-M-0075**, and the owner asked for **both halves**: constrain the SVG *and* make the test able to see it, which the recommended option had left out. Out of spec both ways when raised: LNK-M-0053's bullet as amended claims the shell and the two scanned tags, and explicitly disclaims this element; LNK-M-0068 makes no claim about the page's width |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-09, and the owner asked for **both halves**. The SVG: `qr.FluidClass` (`max-w-full h-auto`) on the emitted root for the inline renders, both utilities already in the shipped `app.css` so no stylesheet rebuild is involved — an inline `style` was not available, the dashboard CSP being `style-src 'self'` with no `unsafe-inline`. **The `.svg` download is byte-identical**, because a class list resolves only against the dashboard's stylesheet and that document leaves the product. `mfa.html` needed no change: `max-w-full` on the child resolves against the `w-40 … p-1` box, where a `max-w-full` **wrapper** would not have constrained a fixed-width child at all. The test: `overflow_test.go` now also checks `<svg>` with a stated pixel width past the 360px viewport, accepting either a scrolling ancestor or `max-w-full` on the element — a QR code inside a scroll box is one you must drag into view before you can photograph it — and the header's *what it does not enforce* list no longer names a fixed-width SVG. **The fixture is why the scan was blind**: `mfa`'s `QR` stub said `width="8"`, and it now carries what `qr.Render` actually emits. Re-measured in Chromium at 360×780 against the real page over a real stylesheet: **142 → 0**, the 32px difference from the row's 174 being the fixture's 456px symbol against the real account's 488px. |
| Status | closed |

**The manual *Verify* button has F180's defect at the second of the two sites, twelve lines from the one LNK-M-0075 fixed.** `VerifyDomain` decides whether to write the `domain.verified` audit record from the row it read *before* the DNS lookup, rather than from what `MarkDomainVerified` returned — so two concurrent verifies of one hostname both record the event

| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0075 |
| Where | `internal/link/verification.go:240` — `if row.VerifiedAt == nil`, against the `domainForWrite` read above it. The helper that fixes it already exists in the same file: `newlyVerified` (`:295`), written at LNK-M-0075 for the job-family site at `:482` |
| Evidence | Read from the two paths, not driven. The mechanism is F180's exactly: `MarkDomainVerified` is idempotent (`internal/store/query/domains.sql:230-231`, *"sets verified_at only when it is not already set"*), so the `UPDATE` is safe and the duplicate is the audit record rather than the state. The window is a DNS round trip wide, which is the same thing that makes F180's reproducible — F180's own probe needed `stubZone.interrupt` to interleave deterministically, and this path is reachable by an ordinary double-click on the button or by two administrators pressing it at once. **Not reproduced against this site**, which is why the evidence says *read* rather than *measured*: F180's integration probe drives `ReverifyDomains`, and driving two concurrent `POST /domains/{id}/verify` requests is a different harness. Found 2026-08-09 by the agent that fixed F180, while checking whether the fix's shape appeared anywhere else in the file |
| Severity | **Minor**, and identical to F180's: one extra row in an audit log, on a hostname that was correctly verified. Nothing is lost, nothing serves wrongly, no state diverges. What it costs beyond F180 is that the two sites now **read inconsistently** — one branches on the write's return and one on a stale read — so the next person to touch this file learns the wrong pattern from whichever they open. Fix note is one line, and the helper is already imported: `newlyVerified(verified)` in place of `row.VerifiedAt == nil` |

The owner's ground was class rather than severity: it is the same defect as something LNK-M-0075 is already fixing, and a milestone that repairs one instance and files its twin is how a tracker fills with rows reading *see the one above*. Raised at LNK-M-0075, out of spec when filed: the milestone's approved row was F180, which named one of the two sites. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-10, by the one line the row stated: `newlyVerified(verified)` in place of `row.VerifiedAt == nil`, so the manual button branches on what `MarkDomainVerified` returned rather than on a row read a DNS round trip earlier. No SQL changed and no column was added — the discriminator is the one F180 established, that `verified_at = COALESCE(verified_at, now())` beside `updated_at = now()` in one statement makes the two equal exactly when this call filled the NULL, and its one-microsecond residual is the same and is documented on the helper. **The two sites now read alike**, which was the cost this row named beyond F180's, and `newlyVerified`'s own comment names both callers so neither can be tightened without the other being read. `TestTwoPressesOfVerifyRecordOneVerificationOnce` drives the second press inside the first one's lookup through the file's existing `stubZone.interrupt`, so the interleaving happens on every run rather than on most of them; it reproduced 2 records for one verification when the fix was reverted. |

**`TestDemoSeederShowsEveryFeatureItClaimsTo`'s LNK-M-0067 row reported zero erased actors in a run where the seeder reported erasing one, and has not done it since.** A coverage row asserting *an erased actor in the audit trail* failed on all three seeds inside one process, and on a second test in the same binary, while the seeder logged its success every time

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0075 |
| Where | Assertion: `cmd/lctl/demo_coverage_test.go:1113-1120` (LNK-M-0067's row and its query). Producer: `seedDeletedAccount`, which logs `deleted account: jordan@example.com, erased (1)`. The tombstone write is `internal/store/query/accounts.sql:247-274` |

Which leaves the two candidates the observation cannot distinguish: a visibility or ordering problem between the erasure write and the assertion's read inside one throwaway database, or a genuine intermittent failure of the write. **Neither has been shown**, which is why the evidence says *observed* and not *reproduced* |

A row that fails once in eight and passes the rest is worse than one that fails always, because the next person to meet it will re-run it. Same class as F11, the flaky invalidation test, and worth the same treatment: characterise it before deciding it is the test's fault |

| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-10, **characterised rather than repaired, because the cause was fixed before the row was written and the row could not know it.** The observation was not intermittent and was not the test's fault: while F177's fix was being built, `audit_logs`'s two scrubs were briefly **two data-modifying CTEs**, and Postgres applies one of two CTEs writing the same row and drops the other — which is the hazard F187 names on `destination_disputes` and which F177's own evidence records being corrected on `audit_logs`. The single row the LNK-M-0067 coverage query counts is the departed account's `invitation.redeemed`, and it satisfies **both** predicates: the actor is the erased account and its metadata carries that account's address. The metadata write won and the label write was dropped, so `actor_label` stayed `jordan@example.com` and the count was 0 — on every seed, deterministically, while the seeder's `erased (1)` came from a different UPDATE in the same statement. **Reproduced 2026-08-10 by splitting the CTEs again**: `M52 — An erased actor in the audit trail: 0 rows, want at least 1` on all three seeds of `TestDemoSeederShowsEveryFeatureItClaimsTo` and on `TestTheSecondWorkspaceFillsWhenTheOwnerHasPinnedADefault` beside it, which is the observation entire; the merged shape was then restored byte-for-byte, the generated code diffed to prove it, and the full suite re-run. **Eight consecutive green runs of the two tests were taken before the experiment** and are what established that brute force would not find it — they are this milestone's, and separate from the seven invocations the row already recorded. Neither candidate in the evidence was right — there was no visibility problem and no intermittent write. **No code changed**, because the merge had already landed and the regression is already caught: on the split shape `TestErasureTombstonesTheActorAndKeepsTheEntriesCorrelated` fails at `account_test.go:461` and `:466`, verified in the same experiment. What the row bought is the note now on `scrubbed_audit` saying the single statement is a correctness requirement and naming what forgetting it cost. |

**A self-filed, self-decided dispute keeps one of its two labels through erasure**, and so does a pair of accounts erased in the same batch where one decided the other's dispute. Postgres applies one of two data-modifying CTEs that write the same row and silently drops the other

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0075 |
| Where | `internal/store/query/accounts.sql`, `EraseDeletedAccounts` — `scrubbed_filed` and `scrubbed_decided` are two separate `UPDATE`s against `destination_disputes`. The pattern that works is twelve lines above them: the audit scrub writes `actor_label` and `metadata` in **one** `UPDATE` with a `CASE` each, precisely because a row can be both |
| Evidence | Proved 2026-08-09 while building F177's fix, which hit the same hazard on `audit_logs` and was corrected there: erasing an account that had filed a dispute and decided it leaves `created_by_label="both@example.com" decided_by_label="deleted account"`. The existing `TestErasureScrubsBothDisputeLabels` cannot see it — it erases its two accounts on **separate passes**, so the two CTEs never contend for one row. This is a defect of LNK-M-0067, not of the LNK-M-0075 work that found it: the two-CTE shape has been there since the erasure pass was written |
| Severity | **Moderate.** It falsifies a claim LNK-M-0067 makes about itself and the one this product now makes to a compliance reader — that erasure reaches every actor snapshot with no foreign key to `users`. An address survives in one of two columns of a record about the person who asked to be erased. Bounded the way the rest of that residue is: `destination_disputes` is reachable through the review queue rather than through `audit.read`, and nothing expires it. Fix note: the merge already applied to the audit pair — one `UPDATE`, two `CASE`s, joined against the `batch` CTE that exists now |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-09**, D175 — **and it reopens LNK-M-0067** rather than being carried to LNK-M-0075. The row's own evidence is why: *this is a defect of LNK-M-0067, not of the LNK-M-0075 work that found it — the two-CTE shape has been there since the erasure pass was written*, and workflow.md says a defect that makes a shipped milestone's claim false reopens that milestone, because a successor leaves a `done` row asserting something untrue. The cost was stated before the choice and is accepted: LNK-M-0075's work is already built, so the two cannot share a commit — LNK-M-0075 lands first, then LNK-M-0067's row goes back to `in progress (reopened)` and the correction is written into m52.md under LNK-M-0067's own number. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0067, 2026-08-10, by the reopening this row asked for.** The two CTEs are one `UPDATE` with a `CASE` per column, joined against the `batch` CTE rather than `pending` — arrays are a single row, so a dispute is matched once however many of the batch's accounts name it, which is the half of the hazard that joining `pending` twice would have kept. `TestErasureScrubsBothDisputeLabelsWhenOneBatchTakesBothAccounts` is the regression: three accounts deleted and erased in **one** pass, over a dispute filed by one and decided by another, a dispute filed and decided by a third, and a third dispute whose decider is still here — the last because a single statement setting both columns unconditionally would satisfy the first two assertions while destroying a live person's record. **Sabotage-verified against the split shape** on 2026-08-10: restored, both contended rows read `created_by_label` as the live address and `decided_by_label` as the tombstone — the `decided` write won and the `created` write was dropped, deterministically — while the uncontended row passed and `TestErasureScrubsBothDisputeLabels` passed beside it, which is exactly why this survived from the pass being written until LNK-M-0075 read the two statements side by side. The merged shape was then restored byte-for-byte and the generated code checksummed to prove it. **It reached no release**: three documents stated the exception as live at 0.3.0 — `README.md`, `docs/SECURITY.md` in **three** places, and `Plan.md` in two — **six sites, counted against `git diff` rather than recalled** — and each now states the requirement instead. SECURITY.md's three are the *account deletion and subject erasure* row, the *six things, not two* paragraph, and its whole entry in *What is not defended*, which is removed. This cell said *two* and *five* until the reviewer counted the hunks, inside the milestone whose own defect was a statement nobody counted. |

cites: [LNK-D-0176](decisions.md#lnk-d-0176)

**An erased account's address survives in the notification sent to whoever invited them.** Deleting an account removes that account's own notifications; this row belongs to somebody else, and nothing reaches it

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0075 |
| Where | `internal/invite/invite.go:973` writes `"email": out.Email` into `notifications.data` for the **inviter**. The scrub that does not reach it is `internal/store/query/accounts.sql`, `EraseDeletedAccounts`, which after LNK-M-0075 covers `audit_logs.metadata` and `invitations.email` and no third table |
| Evidence | Read from the writer and the scrub, not driven. Same shape as F177 at a table F177 did not name: an address written into a jsonb detail column as the *subject* of somebody else's record, with no foreign key to `users` to find it by. Found 2026-08-09 while counting F177's writers against the tree — the count went six to seven inside `audit_logs`, and this is the eighth site, in a different table, which is why it is its own row rather than a correction to that one |
| Severity | **Low to moderate.** Reachable by one person — the inviter — in their own notification list, rather than by a role. No retention window removes it: notifications are scoped to a reader and are not swept by age. It is worth a row because the product's erasure claim is now specific enough to be checked, and this is the kind of site that makes a specific claim wrong. Fix note: either one more scrub in the same statement, keyed on `data->>'email'`, or a decision that a notification is the reader's record and not the subject's — which is the argument that kept **outstanding** invitations out of LNK-M-0075's scrub |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-09**, D175 — **carried to LNK-M-0075**, over a recommendation that carried it. The owner's ground was class rather than severity: it is the same defect as something LNK-M-0075 is already fixing, and a milestone that repairs one instance and files its twin is how a tracker fills with rows reading *see the one above*. Raised at LNK-M-0075, out of spec when filed: F181's approved scope was the address on `/invites`, and a notification belonging to somebody else is a different reader. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-10, by one more scrub in the same statement — `scrubbed_notifications`, its own CTE because it is its own table and nothing else in the pass writes `notifications`. The row's *or* was declined: a notification is a record **about** a person delivered to somebody else, which is exactly what `audit_logs.metadata` is, so it gets the same answer rather than the outstanding-invitation one. **It reaches the title as well as the detail, and that is wider than the row's fix note.** `invite.go:973` writes the address into `data->>'email'` *and* into `"<address> accepted your invitation"`, and `/notifications` renders the title — so a scrub reaching only the jsonb key would have left this row's own headline claim true. The title is rewritten with `replace(n.title, n.data->>'email', …)` rather than against the batch, so the statement knows nothing about how the sentence is worded; both CASEs read the pre-update row, so the address is still there to be replaced. Judged and recorded as D176 rather than taken silently. **Not hypothetical on the demo**: the running instance's `notifications` table held *jordan@example.com accepted your invitation* — jordan being the demo's own deleted-and-erased account — read out of `linkctrl-demo-postgres-1` on 2026-08-10, and `make demo-update` after this commit replaces it with the tombstone. `TestErasureReachesTheAddressInAnArrayAndInSomebodyElsesNotification` drives the real redemption so the row is the one the product writes; sabotage-verified twice — dropping the CTE leaves the address in the detail, and leaving `title` alone leaves *member@example.com accepted your invitation* standing on the page. |
| Status | closed |

## LNK-F-0189

**`instance.principal_moved` carries a second address-bearing key that the erasure scrub does not reach**

finding · 2026-08-09

cites: [LNK-M-0075](milestones.md#lnk-m-0075)

cites: [LNK-F-0186](#lnk-f-0186)

cites: [LNK-M-0067](milestones.md#lnk-m-0067)

**`instance.principal_moved` carries a second address-bearing key that the erasure scrub does not reach.** A prior instance principal who later deletes their account keeps their address in an array beside the key that *is* scrubbed

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0075 |
| Where | `internal/instance/instance.go:642` writes `"from": [addresses]` alongside `"email"`. The scrub handles `metadata->>'email'` (`internal/store/query/accounts.sql`, LNK-M-0075's F177 work), which is the shape F177 specifies and the only shape it specifies |
| Evidence | Read from the writer while re-counting F177's seven sites, 2026-08-09. The scrub's predicate is a scalar comparison on one key; the array is a different shape and was left deliberately rather than by oversight — complicating the predicate to reach it would have widened a fix the owner approved against a stated site list. The address is the *previous* principal's, so the record is about them and about the administrator who moved the role |
| Severity | **Low.** One action, on an instance-level event that happens rarely, reachable only through `audit.read.instance`, and expiring at `AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS` like the rest of the audit residue — so it is the *most* bounded of the erasure residues rather than the least. It is a row because LNK-M-0075 made the erasure claim specific and a specific claim with a known exception should carry the exception in writing. Fix note: a jsonb array rewrite in the same statement, or accept and state it |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-09**, D175 — **carried to LNK-M-0075**, over a recommendation that carried it. The owner's ground was class rather than severity: it is the same defect as something LNK-M-0075 is already fixing, and a milestone that repairs one instance and files its twin is how a tracker fills with rows reading *see the one above*. Raised at LNK-M-0075, out of spec when filed: F177's six metadata writers were counted before this seventh was found. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-10, by the jsonb array rewrite the row offered, in the same UPDATE as the scalar key rather than a second one — the note on `batch` forbids a second, and F186 is what forgetting that cost. The two metadata keys merge through `\|\|` over a `jsonb_object_agg` of only the arms that matched, so each key names its own predicate once and a third would be one more arm; `jsonb_object_agg` over no matching arm is NULL and `metadata \|\| '{}'` is the row unchanged. Elements are rewritten rather than dropped, ordered by `WITH ORDINALITY`, because how many principals the role moved away from is part of what the record says; a `from` that is not an array is guarded to `'[]'` rather than erroring, so a record written by hand cannot fail a batch. The test moves the principal **out to the departing account and back**, so the surviving record's scalar `"email"` names the account that stays and its actor is nobody — which means only this scrub can clean it, and a green run cannot be F177's work or LNK-M-0067's label scrub doing the job. Sabotage-verified by removing the arm: the address stays in the array and the tombstone never appears in it. |
| Status | closed |

**The QR size control fits against the level stored on the row, not the level the renderer will actually draw at**

finding · 2026-08-09

cites: [LNK-F-0171](#lnk-f-0171)

cites: [LNK-D-0175](decisions.md#lnk-d-0175)

**The QR size control fits against the level stored on the row, not the level the renderer will actually draw at**, so a row whose stored level is below H while a logo forces H stores a margin and scale that draw some other number of pixels than the reader typed

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0075 |
| Where | `internal/link/qr.go:661` — `SetQRSizeBySlug` calls `qr.Encode(QRContent(…), current.Level)` where `current` comes from `storedQRStyle` and is **not** passed through `ForLogo()`. The defence that exists twelve functions away is `qrCodeFrom` (`internal/link/qr.go:435`), which does apply it on read, for exactly this reason |
| Evidence | Read from the two call sites, not driven. `qrCodeFrom` applying `ForLogo()` on read is itself the evidence that a row can disagree with the renderer — it was written to defend against a row holding a level below H while a logo is present, which happens for a row written before LNK-M-0062, one written by hand, or a style write that raced an upload. The size control has the same exposure and no such defence. Found 2026-08-09 while building F171's re-fit, which had to reason about exactly this pair of levels |
| Severity | **Low, and not reachable through the product's own writes today**: both `SetQRCodeLogo` and `SetQRStyleBySlug` write H into the row whenever a logo is present, so the disagreement `qrCodeFrom` defends against cannot currently be produced from a form or an endpoint. It is a row because the defence exists at one of two sites that need it, which means somebody already judged the state reachable, and because a size that silently is not the size you asked for is the class of defect F171 just was |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-09**, D175 — **carried to LNK-M-0075**, over a recommendation that carried it. The owner's ground was class rather than severity: it is the same defect as something LNK-M-0075 is already fixing, and a milestone that repairs one instance and files its twin is how a tracker fills with rows reading *see the one above*. Raised at LNK-M-0075, out of spec when filed: F171's approved fix is the level forced on upload, and this is the size control reading a stored level rather than the drawn one. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-10, by applying `ForLogo()` to the stored style before the fit, which is the defence `qrCodeFrom` has had on read since LNK-M-0062 and the reason it has it. `SetQRSizeBySlug` now reads the row through `storedQRCode` rather than `storedQRStyle`, because the level it needs to force is a fact about the row (`HasLogo`) that the style alone does not carry; the two other callers of `storedQRStyle` copy a stored blob into a new code and are deliberately left alone. **Not reachable through the product's own writes**, as the row said — so the test writes the disagreeing row by hand, which is the only way to reach a state `qrCodeFrom` was written to defend against. Sabotage-verified at the numbers: with the fit taken against the row's `L` and the picture drawn at `H`, a request for 800px served **935px** — 135px out, against a snap tolerance of one module. |
| Status | closed |

## LNK-F-0193

**Three rows in the *Closed* table carry a surplus cell, so the `Closed by` prose of each is dropped by every markdown renderer that reads the header row for the column count**

finding · 2026-08-10

cites: [LNK-M-0075](milestones.md#lnk-m-0075)

cites: [LNK-F-0028](#lnk-f-0028)

cites: [LNK-F-0005](#lnk-f-0005)

cites: [LNK-F-0103](#lnk-f-0103)

cites: [LNK-M-0069](milestones.md#lnk-m-0069)

cites: [LNK-F-0189](#lnk-f-0189)

**Three rows in the *Closed* table carry a surplus cell, so the `Closed by` prose of each is dropped by every markdown renderer that reads the header row for the column count.** The reason those three findings closed is in the file and on no rendered page

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0075 |
| Where | `docs/build-notes/deferred-findings.md`, the F28, F5 and F103 rows — each splits into **nine** cells against an eight-column header. F28's and F5's surplus is an *empty* cell between *Reviewed* and *Closed by*; **F103's is a whole LNK-M-0069 amendment**, and its row carries no trailing pipe, which is what hid it |
| Evidence | Counted mechanically 2026-08-10 while moving LNK-M-0075's seven rows across, by splitting every `^\| F` line on unescaped pipes and comparing the count against its table's header. **That scan reported 192 rows and two mismatches, and it was wrong** — it charged one empty field to each end of the line, which assumes a trailing pipe, so a nine-cell row without one counted as eight. Re-derived 2026-08-10 by the pass now in `scripts/check-links.sh`, over every tracked markdown file rather than this one: **2,100 table rows in 40 files, one mismatch, F103** — the other two having been repaired by the scan that could see them. That figure is the tree as it stood when the scan ran, before this pass added its own rows; the gate prints the live one on every run, which is the point of it being a gate rather than a number in a cell. All three are pre-existing and none was touched by this milestone. GitHub-flavoured markdown **drops** cells past the header count rather than widening the table, so what renders in the *Closed by* column is the empty cell and the prose after it is not shown at all. The same scan is what caught an unescaped `\|\|` in this milestone's own F189 row before it landed, which is the argument for the scan rather than for reading |
| Severity | **Low, and documentation only.** Nothing in the product misbehaves and nothing is lost — the text is in the file, and `git show` or any editor displays it. What it costs is the one thing the *Closed* table exists for: a reader asking why F28 or F5 stopped mattering is shown a blank. Fix note: delete the empty cell from F28 and F5, and fold F103's surplus back into its *Closed by*. Worth more than the three rows is that nothing checks this — `make check-links` reads links and anchors and says nothing about column counts, so the next malformed row is found the same way, by accident, or by a scan that can only see the malformation it has already seen |
| Reviewed | **Reviewed 2026-08-10 — no owner decision needed.** A malformed table is a correction to a record, so workflow.md's standing approval covers it and LNK-M-0075 makes it in this pass rather than deferring it. Dispositioned by the orchestrator under the amended first bullet, which sends rows this milestone's own work files to their own disposition rather than back through the sweep. Raised 2026-08-10 by the column-count scan, out of spec when filed: the rows are pre-existing and no LNK-M-0075 bullet is made false by them. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0075**, 2026-08-10, **in two passes, because the first one closed this row against a scan that was itself defective.** F28's and F5's empty cells went first. F103 was found afterwards, by a reviewer, and it is the row this one was written to catch: nine cells, no trailing pipe, and the surplus holding the entire LNK-M-0069 amendment that says the bound lapses for an account-wide key — so m58.md's bullet requiring F103's row to have been *amended rather than deleted* held in the source and failed on the page. Its amendment is now folded into the *Closed by* cell it belongs to and renders. **The scan is the fix, not the three rows.** It lives in `scripts/check-links.sh`, runs over every tracked markdown file, and counts cells GFM's way — leading pipe optional, trailing pipe optional and *independently* so, `\|` content rather than delimiter. The old one took `split(line, "\|") - 2`, charging an empty field to each end: right for `\| a \| b \|`, one short for `\| a \| b`, which is exactly and only the shape it missed. Proven before F103 was touched — the gate ran red naming `deferred-findings.md:157` while the row was still malformed — and green after. The row's severity cell said nothing checks this automatically; that is no longer true, and `make check-links` fails on the next one. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F193 |

## LNK-F-0195

**F160's suppression is per link and per window, and the sentence it shows is worded as a fact about the instance**

finding · 2026-08-10

cites: [LNK-F-0160](#lnk-f-0160)

cites: [LNK-M-0075](milestones.md#lnk-m-0075)

cites: [LNK-M-0095](milestones.md#lnk-m-0095)

cites: [LNK-D-0415](decisions.md#lnk-d-0415)

cites: [LNK-D-0416](decisions.md#lnk-d-0416)

cites: [LNK-D-0436](decisions.md#lnk-d-0436)

**F160's suppression is per link and per window, and the sentence it shows is worded as a fact about the instance** — so on a GeoIP-less instance holding country history, two links side by side disagree: one draws a full choropleth, the one beside it says *"Geographic data is unavailable: no GeoIP database is configured"*

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0075 |
| Where | `internal/httpx/web_links.go:1148` — `geoShowable := data.GeoAvailable \|\| hasResolvedCountries(stats.Dimensions["country"])`. `GeoAvailable` is instance-level (`Config.Analytics.GeoIPPath != ""`); `stats` is **one link over the selected window** — `loadLinkDetail` reads 7, 30 or 90 days, defaulting to 30, and passes that range to `Stats.LinkStats` |
| Evidence | Read from the predicate and the two things it reads, not driven. The sentence is never *false* where it appears: `!geoShowable` implies `!GeoAvailable`, so no database is configured whenever it is shown. What is wrong is the scope a reader takes from it — it reads as a permanent fact about the instance while widening the window to 90 days can replace it with a map, and while a neighbouring link already shows one. Found 2026-08-10 by the third reviewer run at LNK-M-0075, against the claims that milestone wrote for F160; the claims were corrected across the class in the same pass and the behaviour was not |
| Severity | **Low, and it is a wording-versus-scope defect rather than a wrong figure.** No data is hidden that the window holds, nothing is miscounted, and the ranked list and the map still agree with each other on any one page — the disagreement is between two links, and between two windows of one link. Two fix shapes, and they do not cost the same. The cheap one is free of I/O: a link with **no clicks at all** in the window is an ordinary *no data yet*, and `stats.Totals.Clicks` is already in hand, so the sentence would be kept for the state it describes — clicks that arrived and could not be resolved. The thorough one asks whether this link has *ever* resolved a country, which costs a query and breaks `fillLinkAnalytics`'s stated seam that it performs no I/O and cannot fail |

**The release-notes extraction explains itself with a false premise, and the premise is which of its two exits matters.** `release.yml` says *"The newest version is always the last section in CHANGELOG.md"*. | --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0075 |
| Where | `.github/workflows/release.yml:258`, the comment above the `awk` at `:267-272`. Against the file it describes: `## [0.3.0]` at `CHANGELOG.md:32`, `## [0.2.0]` at `:848`, `## [0.1.0]` at `:2652`, and the `[Unreleased]: https://…` definitions last |
| Evidence | True at 0.1.0, when one released section was both newest and last, and never revisited. **The program is correct and is not what this row is about**: it has two exits, the next `## [` heading and the link-reference block (F1), and which fires depends on where the section sits — the F1 exit protects the **oldest** section, and every other version exits on the next heading. The comment presents F1 as this extraction's protection, which for 0.3.0 it is not. Verified read-only 2026-08-10 by running the program from the workflow with `ver="## [0.3.0]"`: 815 lines, exactly the 0.3.0 body (`CHANGELOG.md:33-847`), no second version heading and no reference definitions |

What it costs is the next person who has to reason about the two exits — they will read that the last section is the newest one, conclude the F1 exit is what guards the release they are cutting, and be wrong about which line to change. Fix note: the sentence should say the newest version is the **first** released section, that the next-heading exit is what bounds it, and that F1's exit exists for the oldest |
| Reviewed | **Reviewed 2026-08-11 — routed, and it stays open until the owner applies it.** The correction is written at `ci/proposed/release.yml` with a *Proposed* row at W42, because the path is `.github/workflows/` and nothing here can push it — the token carries no `Workflows` permission and GitHub refuses the push rather than the merge. `make workflow-proposals` reports it pending. **Not closed**: a proposal is not the fix landing, and this row is what says so until it does. Comment-only, so the extraction is untouched byte for byte and was re-run against the 0.3.0 changelog — 815 lines, clean exits. |
| Closed by | **Applied by the owner, `91eeb45`, 2026-08-11** — W42 made. The comment now says which exit guards which end: newest first, so the reference-block exit protects the *oldest* section. `ci/proposed/release.yml` is gone, `make workflow-proposals` reports nothing pending, and the awk is untouched byte for byte, as the proposal promised. |

## LNK-F-0206

**htmx violates the Content-Security-Policy on every page load, in every browser, and the refusal is silent outside a console**

finding · 2026-08-11

cites: [LNK-M-0056](milestones.md#lnk-m-0056)

cites: [LNK-M-0054](milestones.md#lnk-m-0054)

**htmx violates the Content-Security-Policy on every page load, in every browser, and the refusal is silent outside a console.** htmx 2.0.9 ships `includeIndicatorStyles: true`, which injects a `<style>` element for `.htmx-indicator` at load; the app's `style-src 'self'` blocks it. Chromium: *"Applying inline style violates the following Content Security Policy directive 'style-src 'self''… The action has been blocked."*

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0056 *(reopened)* |
| Where | `internal/ui/static/js/htmx.min.js` (`includeIndicatorStyles:true`, `indicatorClass:"htmx-indicator"` in its config block) against `internal/httpx/middleware.go:270`, which sets `style-src 'self'` with no waiver |
| Evidence | Observed 2026-08-11 by driving the running test instance on :8081 with a real browser — the error fires at 13ms on `/login` and again after each swap. **Nothing a user sees is wrong today**: `grep -rn 'hx-indicator'` over `internal/ui/templates/` returns nothing, so the blocked stylesheet is for a feature this product does not use. The CSP is deliberate and correct — `docsCSP` is an explicit `/docs`-only `unsafe-inline` waiver and `test/integration/web_test.go:540` asserts the main policy does not carry one, so **widening the CSP is not the fix** and the inherited *no `unsafe-` waivers* rule forbids it |
| Severity | **Low today, and it has two costs that are not the blocked feature.** First, the **next** template to use `hx-indicator` gets a loading state that silently does nothing, and the failure appears in no test — the template scans read markup and the integration suite reads HTTP. Second, **a permanent console error makes *zero console errors* unusable as an assertion**, which is one of the cheapest checks a browser harness can make, and this repository is adopting one. Fix note: `<meta name="htmx-config" content='{"includeIndicatorStyles":false}'>` is CSP-safe because it is a meta tag rather than inline script; the alternative is shipping the indicator rules in `app.css` and turning the injection off, which is the same meta tag plus three lines of CSS |
| Reviewed | **Approved as work 2026-08-11** into LNK-M-0054, having first been approved into LNK-M-0056. The owner's ground was that the console must be clean before anything asserts against it; the plan review then established LNK-M-0054 runs **first** and names a clean console as one of the two things its kept spec may assert, so the fix moved to satisfy the reason it was approved for. Widening the CSP is not available: the inherited rule forbids `unsafe-` waivers and `test/integration/web_test.go:593-594` asserts the main policy carries none. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0054**, 2026-08-11 — the layout now carries `<meta name="htmx-config" content='{"includeIndicatorStyles":false}'>`, so htmx injects nothing for the CSP to refuse. The kept spec `tools/agent-browser/specs/clean-console.spec.mjs` was born red on the exact refusal this row quotes — run before the fix was deployed it failed, printing *"Applying inline style violates the following Content Security Policy directive 'style-src 'self''"* — and is green since the fix. `make verify-ui` re-asks it against the running test instance. Owner-approved into LNK-M-0054, so this is approved work rather than step 1's in-spec exception |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F206 |

## LNK-F-0209

**The workspace switcher's opened state is the native select popup, which nothing in the product can govern — and the owner named four symptoms on sight**

finding · 2026-08-11

cites: [LNK-M-0055](milestones.md#lnk-m-0055)

cites: [LNK-M-0057](milestones.md#lnk-m-0057)

cites: [LNK-D-0024](decisions.md#lnk-d-0024)

**The workspace switcher's opened state is the native select popup, which nothing in the product can govern — and the owner named four symptoms on sight.** (1) The popup is not right-aligned with the fused control; it anchors where the engine puts it. (2) It opens showing the empty placeholder row — a blank option that cannot be selected, the cost the LNK-M-0055 amendment recorded, now rejected on sight. (3) Selecting a workspace paints the option's text into the `w-8` closed face, partially visible left of the chevron, until the redirect lands. (4) The popup is OS-rendered and matches nothing — *"looks like a bolted on after thought"*

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | — *(owner-reported, post-LNK-M-0057)* |
| Where | `internal/ui/templates/partials/nav.html` — `workspace_switch`'s `<select>` (`6deb8fa`); the closed face is `w-8` so any selected text overflows it |
| Evidence | Owner-reported 2026-08-11 against the running product. All four share one cause: a native select's popup cannot be positioned, styled, or purged of its placeholder cross-engine (`hidden` on `<option>` is ignored by WebKit), and its closed face renders the selected option's text by design — so no fix inside the `<select>` reaches any of the four. The shell already carries the governed alternative: both header menus are the Popover API (`button popovertarget` + `popover="auto"`, D24), styled in-product and right-aligned by the recorded viewport idiom. Symptom 3 transiently falsifies LNK-M-0055's shipped claim that *the closed face is the chevron alone* |
| Severity | **Moderate by ownership, not by breakage**: nothing loses data and the switch works, but the control the owner just approved from wireframes misdraws in the one state the wireframes could not show — a native popup cannot be wireframed. One edit closes all four: rebuild the opened state on the header-menu popover pattern, each workspace a submit button in the existing form, no placeholder row to draw, no select text to flash. Costs: `workspace_test.go:68-71`'s disabled-placeholder assertion encodes an owner answer whose premise (a select must display something) dissolves with the select; a11y shifts from combobox to button+group, the same recorded trade (D24) the other two menus made |
| Reviewed | **Reported by the owner 2026-08-11**, which is review, and **approved as work the same day into LNK-M-0055's reopening** — symptom 3 falsifies the shipped chevron-only claim, which is what reopening exists for, and the owner chose it over deferral to Phase 4. The reopened contract names the popover pattern and the retired assertion |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0055, reopened**, 2026-08-11. The opened state is rebuilt on the header menus’ Popover API pattern (D24): the chevron is a `button popovertarget` invoker, the panel is `popover="auto"` styled in the control’s own border and radius idiom, and each workspace is a submit button in the existing form — no placeholder row exists to draw, nothing can flash, the switch handler and hidden `next` untouched. Right alignment is **CSS anchor positioning**: the fused container carries `anchor-name` and the panel’s right inset is `anchor(right)` behind `@supports`, probed the same day in all three pinned engines (chromium-1234, firefox-1538, webkit-2336) — all three land the panel’s right edge exactly on the control’s; engines without it fall back to the menus’ shared-edge literal. The panel’s left inset clamps at 1rem with its width resolved from the two insets, because the kept spec’s first run caught a fixed-width panel anchored to a mid-bar control overflowing the 360px viewport’s left edge. All four symptoms are asserted where they lived: `tools/agent-browser/specs/workspace-control.spec.mjs` opens the panel, measures its right edge against the control’s, refuses any blank row, and drives a switch there and back proving the invoker’s face never carries text; the template and integration suites hold the markup, the disabled-placeholder assertion retired as approved and replaced by no-blank-entry assertions. The mechanism record is the LNK-M-0055 reopening entry in decisions.md |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F209 |

| --- | --- |

| Evidence | Reproduced and cause isolated 2026-08-11: querying the rendered SVG for paths wider than 900 of the 1000-unit viewBox returns exactly two — **Fiji (width 1000, y≈278) and Russia (width 1000.00, y≈8)**. Both countries cross the antimeridian; mapgen emits their rings unsplit, so the path wraps 180→-180 and the fill sweeps the full map width as a band at that latitude range. Faint at 1280px, obvious at 1920 — which is why it survived every 1280-wide look since LNK-M-0042 shipped the map |
| Severity | **Moderate**: the map is wrong on every instance for every reader whose window is wide enough, and a Russia with clicks would paint its band in accent. The fix is mechanical — split rings at the antimeridian in mapgen and regenerate `countries_gen.go` — and testable: no country path's bbox may span the full viewBox width |

| Closed by | **LNK-M-0042, reopened**, 2026-08-11. mapgen unwraps any ring whose consecutive longitudes jump more than 180°, clips it against the 180° meridian, and emits one ring per side flush on the frame edges; rings that do not cross pass through untouched, so the regenerated `countries_gen.go` changes exactly two lines — FJ and RU. The test the fix note asked for exists at the unit that can carry it: **per ring, not per country**, because a correctly split Russia still touches both frame edges (mainland to x=1000, Chukotka from x=0) and its per-path box legitimately spans the frame — measured so on the rendered page after the fix, both elements at width 1000 with the widest *ring* at 424.2. Written first and run against the shipped file, the test failed on **three** rings, one more than this row measured: Fiji, Russia's mainland, and Wrangel Island (996.9), whose band hid inside the mainland's. Looked at rendered at 1920×1080 on the rebuilt instance: both bands gone, console clean, `make verify-ui` green. The mechanism record is the LNK-M-0042 rebuild entry |

The number itself is in the size control two lines below, and that a `links.read` viewer no longer sees it is F229.)* (b) `qr.FitSize` pins the quiet zone at `DefaultMargin` and the whole remainder lands on the drawn size, where the snap notice already reports it — D179, with the two alternatives rejected on the record. | Evidence | Found while adding the QR preview's frame at LNK-M-0059's reopening. The frame's own classes went into the template deliberately *because* of this — a template is scanned — which is what surfaced the question about the one class that is not. Verified 2026-08-12: `grep -rn 'h-24' internal/ui/templates/ internal/ui/funcs.go internal/ui/choropleth.go` returns the breakdown partial and nothing else |
| Severity | **Low today, and silent when it bites.** Nothing is broken now; the failure mode is a future edit to an unrelated file changing a measured layout with every gate green. The fix is one `@source` line, and the question that makes it a row rather than an edit is whether the answer is that line or a rule that Go files never name utilities — `funcs.go` and `choropleth.go` are already exceptions to it |

Driven — a class written only in `internal/link/service.go`, named on no `@source` line, is generated; and with breakdown.html's `h-24 w-24` removed *and* `ui.go` unsourced, `.h-24` is still in `app.css`. The `@source` line written for this row was **reverted**, because a redundant entry carrying a comment that asserts a false mechanism is worse than no entry. The three existing `@source` lines are left alone: unused is not evidence, and whether they should stay is a question about explicitness rather than about this defect. |
