## LNK-F-0333

**`make verify-ui` signs in more times than the login limiter admits, so the kept browser gate fails on its own shape rather than on the product**

finding · 2026-08-25

cites: [LNK-M-0089](milestones.md#lnk-m-0089)

cites: [LNK-M-0040](milestones.md#lnk-m-0040)

cites: [LNK-M-0095](milestones.md#lnk-m-0095)

cites: [LNK-D-0415](decisions.md#lnk-d-0415)

cites: [LNK-D-0416](decisions.md#lnk-d-0416)

cites: [LNK-D-0435](decisions.md#lnk-d-0435)

**`make verify-ui` signs in more times than the login limiter admits, so the kept browser gate fails on its own shape rather than on the product.** Every spec signs in as the same address, the suite is twenty specs, and `LINKCTRL_LOGIN_RATE_PER_MIN` is ten per address per minute — so the tail of a full run is refused at `/login` and reports *sign-in did not reach /dashboard*, which reads as a broken instance. Parallel workers make it worse and land the refusals on different specs each time, so the gate is non-deterministic about which of its claims it is failing to check

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0089 |
| Where | `.env.example:298` (`LINKCTRL_LOGIN_RATE_PER_MIN=10`) against `tools/agent-browser/specs/` — twenty tests, each calling its own `signIn`; `tools/agent-browser/playwright.config.mjs` sets no `workers`, so the default is CPU-derived |
| Evidence | Measured on 2026-08-25 while running LNK-M-0089's browser gate. `--workers=1` over a freshly seeded test instance: **19 passed, 1 failed**, the failure being `qr-logo.spec.mjs` with *sign-in did not reach /dashboard*; the same spec run alone seventy-five seconds later passed in 933ms. The default worker count fails eight, all of them on the same sign-in message |
| Severity | **Low, and it is tooling rather than product.** The limiter is doing what LNK-M-0040 asks of it and the specs are not an attacker; what it costs is that the one gate the phase-loop's review obligation names cannot be run green in one pass. It is a row rather than an edit because the fix is a choice with three shapes and none is obviously right: one signed-in context reused across the suite (fastest, and it stops each spec asserting its own sign-in), a per-spec address (needs a seeder that makes twenty accounts), or raising the budget on the test instance (masks the limiter on the one instance that exercises it). LNK-M-0089 is where it was measured, not where it started — the suite has been over budget since it passed ten specs |
| Reviewed | **Reviewed 2026-09-04**, LNK-M-0095's triage — Tier B, approved for the close (D415, D416). The previous state is what the triage read. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0095, D435.** A `globalSetup` signs in once and every spec starts from that storage state; the six identical private copies of `credentials()` become one module. Sign-ins per run: **20 → 2**. **The decision's shape had a race it did not weigh, found by running the suite three times**: `workspace-control.spec.mjs` drives a real workspace switch and its own comment promises that leaves other specs unaffected — true while each had its own session, false when they share one and run in parallel, because another spec reads `/links` inside the window. Run 1 green, run 2 red, same tree. That spec now takes an empty storage state and signs in for itself, which is the second sign-in; three consecutive runs green afterwards. Two smaller traps are recorded in the code: `storageState: undefined` does not override the config's value, and a captured state holding no cookies made every spec run signed out while failing about whatever it touched first — the setup now refuses to write one. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F333 |

## LNK-F-0334

**An add-on cannot make an outbound network request, so the OIDC add-on this phase was built to prove cannot be written**

finding · 2026-08-25

cites: [LNK-M-0092](milestones.md#lnk-m-0092)

cites: [LNK-D-0362](decisions.md#lnk-d-0362)

cites: [LNK-M-0030](milestones.md#lnk-m-0030)

cites: [LNK-M-0088](milestones.md#lnk-m-0088)

cites: [LNK-M-0090](milestones.md#lnk-m-0090)

cites: [LNK-D-0364](decisions.md#lnk-d-0364)

cites: [LNK-D-0367](decisions.md#lnk-d-0367)

**An add-on cannot make an outbound network request, so the OIDC add-on this phase was built to prove cannot be written.** The ABI has sixteen functions and none reaches the network; the permission vocabulary has eight tokens and none names egress; `guestModuleConfig` grants a name, a start function, a random source and two clocks, and no filesystem, no sockets, no preopens. An OIDC **relying party** needs three outbound calls that are not optional: the discovery document, the **token exchange** that turns an authorization code into an ID token, and the JWKS fetch that verifies its signature. m69.md requires *authorization-code flow with PKCE against a real IdP implementation in CI*, and the token exchange is precisely the step that flow adds over the implicit one the OAuth 2.0 Security BCP deprecates. There is no arrangement of the current sixteen functions that performs it

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0092 |
| Where | `internal/addon/abi/functions.go` — the whole `Functions` list, none network-shaped; `internal/addon/abi/permissions.go` — eight tokens, `config.read`, `storage.own_schema`, `routes.own_prefix`, `session.context`, `session.mint`, `redirect.observe`, `redirect.inline`, `redirect.rewrite_query`; `internal/addon/host.go:169-179` (`guestModuleConfig`). `grep -rn 'http.Client\|net.Dial\|WithFS\|sock_' internal/addon --include='*.go'` outside tests returns nothing, and `docs/addon-abi.md` contains neither *outbound* nor *egress* |
| Evidence | Found 2026-08-25 at LNK-M-0092's step 1, by the orchestrator, while writing the add-on's `go.mod` after the owner directed the add-on be built (D362). **This is the acceptance test working**, not failing: m69.md's own framing is *if the OIDC add-on cannot be built, the foundation is wrong*, and this is that sentence's answer arriving before a line of the add-on was written rather than after |
| Severity | **The highest severity this phase has produced, and it is a gap rather than a defect.** Nothing shipped is false — no document claims an add-on can reach the network — so no milestone is reopened by it. What it blocks is LNK-M-0092 entirely, and behind LNK-M-0092 the phase's remaining two rows. The fix is a new capability and it is the sharpest one this ABI could gain: **this product refuses SSRF everywhere**, at a single validator call site held by test (LNK-M-0030) and again at LNK-M-0088's *nothing is fetched from a URL*, and an add-on making outbound requests is that same risk arriving through a door the validator does not watch. Any answer has to bound it — hosts declared in the manifest and resolved at install, no redirects to private addresses, a size cap, a timeout — and that is a milestone's worth of design, not a function signature. **Owner-scheduled: the loop stopped and asked** |
| Reviewed | **Reviewed and re-homed 2026-08-25.** The owner's answer is LNK-M-0090 — an add-on declares that it needs egress and the operator names the origins, per D364 — placed before LNK-M-0092, which now carries a hard edge on it. This row stays open until that milestone lands and closes it. |
| Closed by | **Closed by LNK-M-0090, 2026-08-26.** The capability exists: `network.fetch` is the ninth permission, `network_fetch` the seventeenth ABI function, and an add-on's outbound request goes to an origin **the operator named in a setting** — the manifest declares the need and is refused if it names a host anywhere. The bounds this row asked for are all built and each is a test rather than a sentence: https only, `GET` or form-encoded `POST`, no request header the add-on chose, every resolved address checked **at dial time** so loopback, link-local, unique-local and the private ranges are refused however the name got there, no redirect off the origin, a 256 KiB cap and a 3s timeout. **The row's own framing of the fix was not what landed**, and the difference is worth naming: it proposed *hosts declared in the manifest and resolved at install*, and the owner's answer (D364) rules that shape out — a manifest allowlist lets an add-on's author widen its own reach, and resolving at install is a check that expires the moment DNS answers differently. Both redirect classes are refused outright, so the door this row worried about does not reach the path the destination validator guards; D367 records the four shapes the answer took and what was deliberately left out. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F334 |

The cause is in D368 and the repair is LNK-M-0088's.)* **`TestRepeatedInstallAndRemovalDoesNotGrowResidentMemory` fails under the coverage instrumentation `make check` runs it with, and it fails on `main` too.** The test measures this process's resident set across ten install/remove cycles against a 16 MiB tolerance, and the run is not repeatable

| Where | `internal/addon/lifecycle_test.go:625-666` and `heldBytes` at `:679` |

## LNK-F-0336

**A stored setting value becomes an egress destination when a new version of the add-on marks it `origin`, and no operator act named it one**

finding · 2026-08-26

cites: [LNK-F-0332](#lnk-f-0332)

cites: [LNK-M-0090](milestones.md#lnk-m-0090)

cites: [LNK-F-0330](#lnk-f-0330)

cites: [LNK-D-0347](decisions.md#lnk-d-0347)

cites: [LNK-D-0371](decisions.md#lnk-d-0371)

cites: [LNK-M-0094](milestones.md#lnk-m-0094)

**A stored setting value becomes an egress destination when a new version of the add-on marks it `origin`, and no operator act named it one.** `originsFor` pairs the flag off the **manifest in hand** with a value out of `addon_settings` (or the process environment), and neither source records what the setting *was* when the value was written. So v1 declares `homepage` as plain text, the operator fills it in, v2 declares `network.fetch` and marks that same setting `origin: true` — and on the next load this host dials it. The operator sees the new permission and not that an existing value became a destination. F332 is the same defect reached from removal rather than from upgrade: rows survive an add-on and are inherited by whatever installs under the name

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0090 |
| Where | `internal/addon/fetch.go:703-733` (`originsFor`, reading `decl.Origin` off the current manifest against `s.values`), `internal/addon/settings.go:281-301` (`mergeSettings`, which flattens both sources to `map[string]config.Secret` and keeps no provenance) and `internal/store/migrations/04800_addon_settings.sql:58-76`, whose `secret` column is the same idea already built for the same reason |
| Evidence | Raised by LNK-M-0090's third reviewer, 2026-08-26, reading `docs/SECURITY.md`'s *a new version cannot quietly reach somewhere the old one did not* against the code. **The claim half was fixed in spec** — that sentence said something the tree does not enforce, so SECURITY.md and CHANGELOG.md now claim only what the manifest schema guarantees and both name the upgrade case as something to read the settings for. What is filed is the half that is behaviour |
| Severity | **Low, and it is not an escalation** — F330's and F332's reason. Installing a version costs `addons.manage`, non-delegable, and that principal could name any origin they liked; and for the deception to be worth anything the attacker needs the operator to have already typed an *attacker-controlled* URL into a setting, at which point v1 could simply have flagged it. It is a row rather than an edit because the obvious fix is **partial**, and shipping half a mechanism is worse than naming the gap: an `origin` column on `addon_settings` mirroring `secret` would invalidate a stored value on the flag transition, but **the environment half cannot be covered at all** — `LINKCTRL_ADDON_<NAME>_<SETTING>` has no save moment to stamp, and `SettingView.Editable()` is false for it, so an env-sourced origin could never be re-affirmed and would be permanently refused. Deciding what an env-sourced origin means is D347's precedence rule, which is the owner's. D371 records the choice and what the other answer would have bought. **A second consequence, added at LNK-M-0094:** the same missing provenance puts a stored `secret`'s value **in the log**, verbatim — driven, `"an add-on's origin setting holds something that is not an origin … \"sk-live-51H9xQxRtOpAqZ\" is a path"`. Bare tokens, base64 and AWS-key shapes, hex and values with spaces all echo in full; only a value that parses as an origin, or whose colon defeats `url.Parse`, does not. Reached through `internal/addon/fetch.go:907`'s `Reveal()` and `:918-923` logging `err.Error()`, past the same manifest swap this row already describes. It matters separately because a log is a different sink with different retention, readable by people with no database access, while the page withholds the value — `internal/addon/settings.go:358`, asserted by `TestAStoredSecretIsNotUnmaskedByALaterManifest`. The fix above closes it |
| Reviewed | **Unreviewed.** |
| Status | open |

## LNK-F-0337

**Azure's WireServer, `168.63.129.16`, is inside globally-routable unicast space and is not carved out, so the address policy will dial it**

finding · 2026-08-26

cites: [LNK-M-0090](milestones.md#lnk-m-0090)

cites: [LNK-D-0375](decisions.md#lnk-d-0375)

cites: [LNK-M-0091](milestones.md#lnk-m-0091)

cites: [LNK-D-0383](decisions.md#lnk-d-0383)

**Azure's WireServer, `168.63.129.16`, is inside globally-routable unicast space and is not carved out, so the address policy will dial it.** It is a real instance-metadata and host-agent endpoint reachable from every Azure VM, and unlike `169.254.169.254` it does not sit in link-local space — Microsoft allocated it out of public IPv4 and it is refused by nothing in `carvedOut`. **This is outside the stated policy rather than a gap in it** under LNK-M-0090: D375 refuses everything unrouted, and reaching a routable address still costs an operator naming it as an origin in a setting. It is filed because LNK-M-0091 reuses the same `refuseAddress` under a **much weaker** origin policy — a URL the operator typed — where *the operator named it* stops being the bound it is here

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0090 |
| Where | `internal/addon/fetch.go`'s `routableSpace` and `carvedOut` (the two lists `refuseAddress` decides from), and the address table in `internal/addon/fetch_test.go` that asserts those two lists alone reach the policy's verdict for every row |
| Evidence | Raised as an observation by LNK-M-0090's fifth reviewer, 2026-08-26, and explicitly **not** a finding against this milestone — the orchestrator's disposition, recorded here so the fact is not lost. Verified against the two lists: `168.63.129.16` is inside `1.0.0.0/8`–`223.255.255.255` cover and matches no carve-out |
| Severity | **Low here, and it is LNK-M-0091 that decides how low.** Nothing this milestone ships reaches it without an operator writing it into a setting. Whether the address belongs in `carvedOut` is a question about which cloud metadata endpoints this product refuses by name — GCP and AWS share `169.254.169.254`, which link-local already covers; Azure's second endpoint is the one that does not fall out of a range — and it is worth answering once, for both doors, rather than twice |
| Reviewed | **Unreviewed**, and closed without review under phase-loop.md's deferred-overlap rule rather than by approval: LNK-M-0091 is the door the row itself named as the one that would decide it, and its claim — *every bound LNK-M-0090 asserts applies here unchanged* — is false while a routable address that is not a destination is dialled. The exception is named in that milestone's commit message |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0091**, 2026-08-26. `168.63.129.16/32` is in `carvedOut`, with two rows in `fetch_test.go`'s address table: the address, and its neighbour `168.63.129.15`, which is somebody's ordinary host and stays reachable — so the carve-out is asserted to be a `/32` rather than a range. The alternative was to argue that the digest and `addons.manage` are enough, and it fails on what the harm is: the digest decides whether a *response* becomes a module, and the harm at a metadata endpoint is the *request*. D383 |
| Status | closed |

## LNK-F-0338

**The malformed-origin warning is guest-drivable at CPU speed, which is the criterion D378 used to move three others to Debug**

finding · 2026-08-26

cites: [LNK-D-0378](decisions.md#lnk-d-0378)

cites: [LNK-M-0090](milestones.md#lnk-m-0090)

cites: [LNK-M-0095](milestones.md#lnk-m-0095)

cites: [LNK-D-0415](decisions.md#lnk-d-0415)

cites: [LNK-D-0416](decisions.md#lnk-d-0416)

**The malformed-origin warning is guest-drivable at CPU speed, which is the criterion D378 used to move three others to Debug.** `hostState.originsFor` warns once per malformed entry (`internal/addon/fetch.go`, the `refusedFetch` neighbourhood), and `doFetch` calls it **before** the origin gate, so a guest looping `invalid_request` or `origin_refused` — neither of which dials — emits one `Warn` per call, across every instance slot, for the whole route deadline, on a page anybody can reach. One bad entry in an origin setting is the only precondition, and the code deliberately keeps the setting working for its good entries, so that state is persistent rather than transient

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0090 |
| Where | `internal/addon/fetch.go`'s `originsFor` warn site against `internal/addon/hostabi.go`'s `doFetch`, which calls it ahead of the origin check; the level decision is D378 and `TestTheConfigurationShapedRefusalsDoNotWarn` asserts this one line stays at `Warn`, so it is a decision rather than an oversight |
| Evidence | Raised by LNK-M-0090's sixth review, 2026-08-26, applying D378's own test to the line D378 exempted. The defence written beside it — *needs an operator's typo to exist at all* — establishes the precondition and not the rate, which is the gap |
| Severity | **Low, and it is log volume rather than a breach.** It needs an operator to have mistyped an origin, and what it costs is disk and noise rather than reach. It is a row rather than an edit because *make it Debug* is the wrong fix: nothing else carries the fact that an entry is malformed, so the answer is log-once-per-load or a counter, and choosing between those is a design call about how a configuration error reaches an operator |
| Reviewed | **Reviewed 2026-09-04**, LNK-M-0095's triage — Tier A, approved for the close (D415, D416). The previous state is what the triage read. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0095.** The malformed-origin warning is once per load per bad entry, through a shared `originWarnLog` held behind a pointer because `forRequest` copies the state per invocation. Dropping it to Debug stays refused, for the reason this row gives: nothing else carries the fact that an entry is malformed. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F338 |

## LNK-F-0340

**HTTP's own compression layer sits under the bundle reader and has none of its bounds**

finding · 2026-08-27

cites: [LNK-M-0091](milestones.md#lnk-m-0091)

cites: [LNK-D-0385](decisions.md#lnk-d-0385)

cites: [LNK-M-0090](milestones.md#lnk-m-0090)

cites: [LNK-M-0095](milestones.md#lnk-m-0095)

cites: [LNK-D-0415](decisions.md#lnk-d-0415)

cites: [LNK-D-0416](decisions.md#lnk-d-0416)

**HTTP's own compression layer sits under the bundle reader and has none of its bounds.** `internal/addon/fetch.go` sets `Accept` and `User-Agent` and no `Accept-Encoding`, so `net/http`'s transport adds `Accept-Encoding: gzip` itself and transparently inflates a `Content-Encoding: gzip` response before the caller sees a byte. Two things follow for LNK-M-0091, which has just argued a ratio bound at the container layer. **The digest stops covering the file the operator hashed**: an origin that serves a `.tar` with `Content-Encoding: gzip` delivers it inflated, so the sha256 is taken over bytes that are not the ones on the release page, and the operator meets `digest_mismatch` with nothing telling them the transfer encoding is what did it. **And the transport's inflation is bounded absolutely but not by ratio**: `f.maxBytes` caps what is read, so a bomb cannot exceed 32 MiB — but the fifty-times refusal D385 argues for at the container layer does not exist one layer down, where the same request is

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0091 |
| Where | `internal/addon/fetch.go:701-702` (the only two headers set on the outbound request) against `:726`, which reads `resp.Body` — the decoded stream — through `io.LimitReader(resp.Body, f.maxBytes+1)`. `net/http.Transport`'s documented behaviour is the other half: it adds the header and decompresses unless the caller sets `Accept-Encoding` itself |
| Evidence | Found while building LNK-M-0091's container bounds, by asking what the ratio bound does *not* cover. Verified by reading the request construction: no `Accept-Encoding` is set on either fetcher, so both doors — an add-on's own fetch and an operator's install — inherit it. It is not a defect LNK-M-0090 shipped either: the add-on path fetches JSON, where transparent decoding is what a caller wants |
| Severity | **Low, and it fails closed in the direction that matters.** Nothing is executed: a decoded bundle hashes to something the operator did not type and is refused before it is parsed, and the absolute cap holds against a transport-layer bomb. What it costs is a refusal an operator cannot diagnose, and one honest gap between what `docs/SECURITY.md` now claims about bounding compression twice and where the first inflation actually happens. It is a row rather than an edit because the fix is a choice for both doors at once — `Accept-Encoding: identity` on the install request makes the digest cover the wire bytes and gives up transparent decoding for the add-on path if applied there too, and saying nothing is also defensible for JSON *(**The confined fix was identified 2026-08-27 by LNK-M-0091's third reviewer**, so whoever takes this row does not re-derive it: `Accept-Encoding: identity` on the **install** fetcher's request closes it without touching the add-on path, which wants transparent decoding because what it fetches is JSON. That is what makes this a choice rather than a one-liner — the two doors want opposite defaults, and the row exists to decide that once. The reviewer also named the second-order effect: a legitimate origin serving the `.tar` with `Content-Encoding: gzip` yields `digest_mismatch`, sending an operator to check a digest that is correct, which is exactly the *refusal names the wrong bound* failure the code vocabulary exists to prevent.)* |
| Reviewed | **Reviewed 2026-09-04**, LNK-M-0095's triage — Tier A, approved for the close (D415, D416). The previous state is what the triage read. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0095.** `fetchRequest.Identity`, set by the install fetcher and deliberately not by the add-on path, so the transport stops negotiating compression and the digest covers the bytes on the wire. This is the confined fix LNK-M-0091's third reviewer identified, taken unchanged. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F340 |

## LNK-F-0341

**A route-serving add-on cannot learn its own URL, so every OAuth add-on will make an operator re-type something the host already knows**

finding · 2026-08-27

cites: [LNK-M-0083](milestones.md#lnk-m-0083)

cites: [LNK-M-0092](milestones.md#lnk-m-0092)

cites: [LNK-M-0080](milestones.md#lnk-m-0080)

**A route-serving add-on cannot learn its own URL, so every OAuth add-on will make an operator re-type something the host already knows.** No record the ABI hands a route invocation carries a scheme or a host — `HTTPRequest.path` is prefix-relative by design (LNK-M-0083) — so an add-on that must send an absolute `redirect_uri` to a provider has to take it from a setting. That value is `LINKCTRL_APP_BASE_URL` with the add-on's route glued on, which the host has and the guest cannot see, and an operator who mistypes it gets a provider-side error rather than anything this product can word

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0092 |
| Where | The ABI's record list in `internal/addon/abi/functions.go` — no field on `HTTPRequest` or `SessionContext` carries an origin; `internal/httpx/addons.go` mounts the prefix the guest is told about and nothing more |
| Evidence | Found 2026-08-27 while building the OIDC add-on against the published SDK, the exercise LNK-M-0092 exists to run. It is the first thing that build had to design around |
| Severity | **Low as a defect and near-certain as a recurrence.** Nothing is wrong; a capability is absent, and every add-on that talks to an external service it must return from meets it. **It leaks nothing** — unlike a client address, an instance's own base URL is what the instance publishes — so the argument LNK-M-0080 used to keep the client address out does not reach it. The shape is a field on `SessionContext` or a small record of its own, additive under LNK-M-0080's policy |
| Reviewed | **Unreviewed.** |
| Status | open |
| LinkCtrl | F341 |

## LNK-F-0342

**There is no way for an add-on to read a row and consume it atomically, so single-use state has to be spelled as a deliberate primary-key collision**

finding · 2026-08-27

cites: [LNK-M-0092](milestones.md#lnk-m-0092)

**There is no way for an add-on to read a row and consume it atomically, so single-use state has to be spelled as a deliberate primary-key collision.** `storage_exec` returns neither a row count nor `RETURNING`, and `storage_query` runs `READ ONLY`, so *take this authorization-code flow if nobody else has* cannot be expressed. The OIDC add-on spells it as an insert into a second table whose primary key is the flow's handle, and reads a collision as consumption — which works, and which comes back as an undifferentiated `ErrInvalid` because a Postgres message never crosses the boundary, so **a unique violation and a syntax error are the same status to the guest**

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0092 |
| Where | `internal/addon/abi/functions.go` — `storage_exec` has no out-parameter, `storage_query` is documented `READ ONLY`; the status vocabulary is the ABI's five, none of which distinguishes a constraint violation |
| Evidence | Found 2026-08-27 building the OIDC add-on. The add-on's author called it the sharpest thing they had to design around, and it is single-use nonce handling — the part of an authorization-code flow where getting it wrong is a replay |
| Severity | **Low today because the workaround is correct, and worth a row because the workaround is not obvious.** The next add-on needing single-use state will either rediscover this or get it wrong, and *get it wrong* here means a flow that can be replayed. Two candidate shapes, and picking one is why this is a row: a row count out of `storage_exec`, which is small and additive; or a distinguishable constraint-violation status, which is a change to the status vocabulary and therefore to every function |
| Reviewed | **Unreviewed.** |
| Status | open |
| LinkCtrl | F342 |

## LNK-F-0343

**A route-serving module cannot tell a load-time initialization from a request, so it pays its setup on every request forever**

finding · 2026-08-27

cites: [LNK-M-0087](milestones.md#lnk-m-0087)

cites: [LNK-M-0092](milestones.md#lnk-m-0092)

cites: [LNK-F-0341](#lnk-f-0341)

**A route-serving module cannot tell a load-time initialization from a request, so it pays its setup on every request forever.** `http_request_read` answers `ErrNotFound` both at load and outside a request, so there is no once-per-load hook a route add-on can hang DDL or cache warming on. `examples/addons/pageviews` does its DDL in `init` because a redirect-class instance is pooled and initialization is amortized; a route instance is built per request (LNK-M-0087 deliberately does not pool the route path), so the same shape costs a statement per request. The OIDC add-on probes-then-creates instead

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0092 |
| Where | `internal/addon/abi/functions.go`'s `http_request_read`, whose absence is the only signal a guest has; `internal/addon/http.go` instantiates per request |
| Evidence | Found 2026-08-27 building the OIDC add-on |
| Severity | **Low, and it is a performance and clarity gap rather than a correctness one.** One extra statement per request against a schema the add-on owns. It is a row because the durable answer is a *lifecycle* question the ABI has never had to answer — whether a guest is told which kind of invocation it is in — and that is the same question F341 asks from the other end |
| Reviewed | **Unreviewed.** |
| Status | open |
| LinkCtrl | F343 |

## LNK-F-0344

**An add-on that ships migrations cannot be installed by any route this product offers, and the host's own migration runner is unreachable to exactly the add-ons that would keep *DDL is additive* true**

finding · 2026-08-27

cites: [LNK-M-0091](milestones.md#lnk-m-0091)

cites: [LNK-M-0088](milestones.md#lnk-m-0088)

cites: [LNK-F-0328](#lnk-f-0328)

cites: [LNK-M-0092](milestones.md#lnk-m-0092)

cites: [LNK-M-0082](milestones.md#lnk-m-0082)

cites: [LNK-D-0384](decisions.md#lnk-d-0384)

**An add-on that ships migrations cannot be installed by any route this product offers, and the host's own migration runner is unreachable to exactly the add-ons that would keep *DDL is additive* true.** LNK-M-0091's bundle is exactly two files and LNK-M-0088's upload carries the same pair, so a `migrations/` directory has nowhere to travel — such an add-on is hand-install only, into the boot directory. This is F328 reached from the other side and it now has a second instance: `examples/addons/pageviews` makes the same trade, and the OIDC add-on made it a third time

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0092 |
| Where | `internal/addon/bundle.go`'s member rule (two plain files, bare names) against `internal/addon/migrations.go`, which runs an add-on's `.sql` files when they are present in the directory |
| Evidence | Found 2026-08-27 building the OIDC add-on, which wanted a migration and did DDL from the guest instead |
| Severity | **Moderate, and it is two rules that were each right and were never reconciled.** LNK-M-0082 built a migration runner so an add-on's schema changes are the host's problem rather than the guest's; LNK-M-0088 and LNK-M-0091 built install paths that cannot carry one. Every storage add-on therefore does DDL from inside the guest, which is the thing the runner exists to avoid, and nothing says so. The durable fix is a bundle that can carry a directory — which is exactly the depth limit D384 set at zero, so reopening it is a decision and not an edit |

**An add-on that can mint a session cannot put a sign-in control anywhere a person will see it.** `template_render` is `ErrNotAvailable` on every released host, an add-on's route may not answer `text/html`, and the host escapes and wraps what a guest returns — so *Sign in with your provider* is a URL somebody has to be told, not a button on the sign-in page. LNK-M-0085 gave an add-on the power to authenticate a person and LNK-M-0083 gave it a page; neither gave it the one link that makes the pair usable

| Where | `internal/addon/abi/functions.go`'s `template_render` (declared, not live) and the content-type bound in `internal/addon/http.go`; the sign-in page is `internal/ui/templates/pages/login.html`, which knows nothing about add-ons |

What is missing is that nobody can start it without being handed a URL. **It falsifies nothing** — no document claims a sign-in control — which is why it is a row rather than a reopening, and it is squarely the kind of gap LNK-M-0092 exists to surface. The fix is a decision about the host's own sign-in page rather than about the ABI: whether a `session.mint` add-on may contribute a link to it, and what bounds the text |
| Reviewed | **Approved and built as LNK-M-0093, owner-answered 2026-08-27** — the scope was decided at the plan review, not deferred to LNK-M-0095. The row's own question, *whether a `session.mint` add-on may contribute a link and what bounds the text*, is what that milestone answers: it may, by declaring a label and a relative path, and the text is bounded at 64 bytes with no control characters |
| Closed by | LNK-M-0093 — `internal/addon/signin.go` composes the href from the add-on's own route prefix and asserts the result stays under it; `Manifest.Validate` refuses a leading `/`, a `..`, a scheme, a query and a fragment; the operator agrees through the `sign_in_link` toggle on LNK-M-0089's manager page, which is off until they do (D398); the link is drawn from what the host **loaded** rather than what a directory claims (D399); and a stock instance renders `login.html` byte for byte as before |
| Status | closed |

## LNK-F-0346

**Every outbound request an add-on makes whose response is over 512 bytes is sent to the other end twice**

finding · 2026-08-27

cites: [LNK-M-0092](milestones.md#lnk-m-0092)

cites: [LNK-D-0391](decisions.md#lnk-d-0391)

cites: [LNK-M-0090](milestones.md#lnk-m-0090)

**Every outbound request an add-on makes whose response is over 512 bytes is sent to the other end twice.** The ABI's out-parameter convention answers a buffer too small with the size to retry at and writes nothing, and the SDK retries — so `network_fetch` re-entered `hostState.doFetch` and put a second request on the wire. For a document that is invisible. For anything the other end counts it is not: the OIDC add-on's authorization-code exchange went out twice and the second answered `invalid_grant`, so **sign-in failed for every real token response**. The convention's own rule — *a function that changes something checks the buffer before it changes it* — named `session_mint` as the only such function, and this is the second one

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0092 |
| Where | `internal/addon/hostabi.go`'s `network_fetch` entry against `sdk/runtime_wasip1.go:17` (`initialBuffer = 512`); the convention is `docs/addon-abi.md`'s calling-convention list |
| Evidence | Found 2026-08-27 by LNK-M-0092's acceptance test, which is the first thing in this repository ever to drive a real authorization-code flow. Reproduced through a logging proxy in front of the provider: two identical `POST /dex/token` bodies, `200` then `400 invalid_grant`. `TestAFetchTheGuestCouldNotHoldIsNotMadeTwice` is the regression, sabotage-verified |
| Severity | **High while it stood.** It is not a bound being wrong, it is a request being made twice, and every non-idempotent thing an add-on could ever do through this door — a token exchange, a payment, a webhook somebody counts — was affected. It affected no shipped release: `network_fetch` arrives in 0.4.0, which is untagged |
| Reviewed | **Fixed in spec under LNK-M-0092**, per workflow.md's *a defect that makes the current milestone's claim false is in spec whatever it looks like* — the milestone's claim is a sign-in through OIDC and there was none. The host now holds the response and answers the retry from it (D391) |
| Closed by | LNK-M-0092 — and **whether it also reopens LNK-M-0090** is scheduling and therefore the owner's. *(**Attribution corrected 2026-08-27 by LNK-M-0092's reviewer**: this row first said LNK-M-0090's file says *one outbound request*. It does not — that sentence is `internal/addon/abi/functions.go` and `docs/addon-abi.md`. What LNK-M-0090 actually got wrong is its **budget arithmetic**, at `internal/addon/fetch.go` and `internal/config/config.go`: *three fetches at DefaultFetchTimeout, which is what an authorization-code flow costs — nine of the ten seconds*. Measured against the running provider, discovery is 1234 B, JWKS 525 B and the token response ~2 KiB — every one over the SDK's 512-byte first buffer — so before this fix the flow cost **six** requests and up to eighteen seconds against a ten-second route deadline. That is the number setting two shipped defaults, computed against half the real traffic. **The reviewer's answer on reopening is no**, and the reasoning is that the claim is true of the tree as it now stands: found in spec, fixed in spec, sabotage-verified, ABI bumped, and the whole trail under one number — which is the arrangement reopening exists to produce, and splitting it would undo.)* |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F346 |

## LNK-F-0347

**`holdFetch` drops its hold when the guest hands back a bad pointer, so the retry it exists to prevent makes the request again**

finding · 2026-08-27

cites: [LNK-F-0346](#lnk-f-0346)

cites: [LNK-D-0391](decisions.md#lnk-d-0391)

cites: [LNK-M-0092](milestones.md#lnk-m-0092)

cites: [LNK-M-0095](milestones.md#lnk-m-0095)

cites: [LNK-D-0415](decisions.md#lnk-d-0415)

cites: [LNK-D-0416](decisions.md#lnk-d-0416)

cites: [LNK-D-0437](decisions.md#lnk-d-0437)

**`holdFetch` drops its hold when the guest hands back a bad pointer, so the retry it exists to prevent makes the request again.** The whole purpose of the hold (F346, D391) is that an outbound request goes out once however many times the guest retries for a bigger buffer; `holdFetch` releases it when `writeOut` answers `StatusInvalid`, which is the guest passing a pointer the host cannot write to. The next call re-enters `doFetch` and the request is made a second time — the exact shape F346 was, reachable through a different door

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0092 |
| Where | `internal/addon/hostabi.go`'s `holdFetch`, on the `StatusInvalid` limb, against `internal/addon/fetch.go`'s `doFetch`, which the retry re-enters |
| Evidence | Raised by LNK-M-0092's reviewer, 2026-08-27, reading the fix for the defect the acceptance test found. Narrow, and it is the guest's own fault to reach |
| Severity | **Low, and it is a guest harming itself rather than a bound failing.** A module that hands the host an unwritable pointer is broken, and the harm is its own token exchange going out twice. It is a row rather than an edit because the fix is a choice about what the hold's lifetime is keyed to — the invocation, or the last well-formed retry — and answering that decides what happens to a hold nobody ever collects. Related: `scripts/oidc-fixture.sh` verifies only the `.wasm` digest on its early-exit path while re-reading `addon.json`, `go.mod` and `LICENSE` unverified, and two tests assert against those |
| Reviewed | **Reviewed 2026-09-04**, LNK-M-0095's triage — Tier A, approved for the close (D415, D416). The previous state is what the triage read. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0095, D437.** `holdFetch`'s condition is delivery rather than fit, so a guest handing back an unwritable pointer no longer releases the hold and re-enters `doFetch`. The hold's lifetime is the invocation; the cost — a hold nobody collects pinning response bytes for the rest of a deadline — is stated at the call site. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F347 |

## LNK-F-0349

**The stock sign-in page's byte-identity golden embeds the stylesheet's cache-busting fingerprint, so it fails whenever the stylesheet changes — which is every UI milestone**

finding · 2026-08-29

cites: [LNK-M-0093](milestones.md#lnk-m-0093)

cites: [LNK-D-0402](decisions.md#lnk-d-0402)

cites: [LNK-D-0404](decisions.md#lnk-d-0404)

**The stock sign-in page's byte-identity golden embeds the stylesheet's cache-busting fingerprint, so it fails whenever the stylesheet changes — which is every UI milestone.** `TestAStockSignInPageIsUnchanged` compares the whole rendered page against `internal/ui/testdata/login_stock.html`, and that page carries `?v=<hash of app.css>`. `app.css` is gitignored and built by `make css`, so the golden asserts a property of one build of one machine alongside the thing it means to assert. It was captured against a **stale** app.css and CI's fresh build disagreed on the first run

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0093 |
| Where | `internal/ui/login_test.go:47`'s comparison against `internal/ui/testdata/login_stock.html`; the fingerprint is written by the layout's `?v=` on `/static/css/app.css`; `.gitignore:25` ignores the file it hashes |
| Evidence | CI run [33224040287](https://github.com/DevOfPie/LinkCtrl/actions/runs/33224040287), job *Build and unit tests*: all three subtests red, `?v=pnpIg4DzEwg` wanted against `?v=_1USZKa0dtQ` got, and nothing else in the page differing. **Reproduced locally**: `make css` then the test, and it fails here with CI's exact hash |
| Severity | **High, and it is the milestone's own bullet that cannot hold.** LNK-M-0093 says a stock instance renders `login.html` byte for byte as before, *asserted by a template test*, and the test cannot pass anywhere the stylesheet was built. The fix is a choice: compare with the fingerprint normalized out, compare the body only, or rebuild the stylesheet before capturing — the last hides it again rather than fixing it |
| Reviewed | **Fixed in spec under LNK-M-0093, which the owner reopened for it on 2026-08-29** rather than deferring it: the milestone's own *nothing appears on a stock instance* bullet claims a template test asserts byte-identity, and that test could not pass anywhere the stylesheet had been built — including in CI, which is where it did not. The owner also bounded the answer: normalize or compare the body, **not** recapture against a fresh stylesheet, and the result must still fail when an add-on link leaks onto a stock page |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0093**, 2026-08-29, under D402. The one token is normalized out of the comparison on **both** sides and nothing else is: `builtStylesheetURL` in `internal/ui/login_test.go` matches `/static/css/app.css?v=…` alone, and the golden carries the literal `?v=FINGERPRINT` in that position so the substitution is visible to a reader of the testdata file. The favicon, htmx, `qr-size.js` and `addon-select.js` fingerprints all hash **committed** files and stay compared byte for byte. **The count, not the pattern, is the fix's guard**: `withoutStylesheetFingerprint` fails unless it finds exactly one match, so a layout that stopped emitting the fingerprint — or a pattern that stopped matching it — is a failure rather than a silent no-op that leaves the test passing on less than it claims. **Driven from three directions.** Forwards: appending a comment to `app.css` so it hashes differently now leaves the test green, which is the property that was missing. Backwards, twice, because a just-loosened golden is the test to distrust — making `login.html`'s guard unconditional so the empty offer block renders on a stock page is red on all three subtests, and adding a literal `<li><a href="/addons/oidc/start">Sign in with Contoso</a></li>` to the stock page is red on all three subtests. Sideways: deleting `layout.html`'s stylesheet link trips the count guard — *the page carries 0 fingerprinted stylesheet URLs, want exactly 1*. Every sabotage restored by counter-edit and diffed back to byte-identical. The two declined answers are in D402: *compare the body only* throws away four deterministic fingerprints and a `<meta>` tag to fix a one-token defect, and *recapture against a fresh stylesheet* is what the owner ruled out, since it goes red again at the next milestone that touches a template. `phase-details/m69.5.md`'s bullet is amended to say so (D404) |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F349 |

## LNK-F-0351

**A pooled add-on instance resets the guest's linear memory and nothing else, so a mutable WebAssembly global or a funcref table carries one invocation's state into the next — across visitors and acros…**

finding · 2026-09-13

cites: [LNK-M-0094](milestones.md#lnk-m-0094)

cites: [LNK-M-0091](milestones.md#lnk-m-0091)

cites: [LNK-M-0087](milestones.md#lnk-m-0087)

**A pooled add-on instance resets the guest's linear memory and nothing else, so a mutable WebAssembly global or a funcref table carries one invocation's state into the next — across visitors and across workspaces.** The pool is keyed `(add-on, class)` and by nothing else

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Dated | on import: the row carries no date |
| Found in | LNK-M-0094 |
| Where | `internal/addon/pool.go`'s `releaseInstance` restores the memory image taken after `_initialize`; nothing touches globals or tables. `internal/addon/set.go:97-112` builds one pool per add-on and class, for both the inline and the observing class |
| Evidence | Reproduced at LNK-M-0094 by driving hand-assembled modules through `Host.Inline`, the production entry point: `visitor-a -> ?g=0&m=0`, `visitor-b -> ?g=1&m=0`, `visitor-c -> ?g=2&m=0` — memory resets, the global does not — and across workspaces, carrying a byte of the **previous** invocation's `RedirectDecision`. A funcref table survives the reset too. Readable through the shipped ABI: `redirect_answer_write` is in `abi.InlineSafe` and its query lands in the destination the visitor's browser is sent to. **Two finders and a refuter agreed the SDK cannot produce such a module** — Go gives a program no way to place its own state in a wasm global, and the built fixtures carry eight, none exported — but LNK-M-0091 installs arbitrary bytes from a URL |
| Severity | **Medium.** It falsifies four sentences, all corrected under LNK-M-0094: `pool.go`'s *the whole of an instance's mutable state lives in one linear memory*, m66.5.md's *either the guest's state is reset or the pool is per-something that makes sharing safe*, `docs/SECURITY.md`'s *enforced instead*, and `docs/configuration.md`'s *reuse cannot leak one visitor's state to the next*. What it buys an attacker is aggregation across invocations and **influence on another tenant's redirect**, not access to data the module could not already read per invocation — but the **observe** class is pooled by the same code and `RedirectEvent` carries `VisitorHash`, `Country`, `Device`, `Browser`, `OS`, `Language`, `ReferrerHost`. **The remedy is a design choice, which is why this is a row**: re-instantiating reverses LNK-M-0087 (11.05ms onto a 20ms path, p99 44.89ms); *refuse modules carrying mutable globals* refuses every add-on the SDK builds and misses tables entirely; the two that survive scrutiny are rewriting the module's bytes at load to export its globals so they can be snapshotted beside the memory image, or refusing to **pool** a module whose shape the host cannot prove inert, keeping LNK-M-0087's win for every real add-on |
| Reviewed | **Unreviewed.** |
| Status | open |
| LinkCtrl | F351 |

## LNK-F-0353

**A failed add-on install never closes the compiled module, so every failed attempt leaks it for the life of the process**

finding · 2026-09-04

cites: [LNK-M-0094](milestones.md#lnk-m-0094)

cites: [LNK-M-0095](milestones.md#lnk-m-0095)

cites: [LNK-D-0415](decisions.md#lnk-d-0415)

cites: [LNK-D-0416](decisions.md#lnk-d-0416)

**A failed add-on install never closes the compiled module, so every failed attempt leaks it for the life of the process**

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0094 |
| Where | `internal/addon/host.go` drops `compiled` on three post-compile returns — `:1392` (`OutcomeStorageFailed`), `:1439` (instantiate timeout) and `:1442` (instantiate failed) — while `Host.unload` closes it on the success path at `internal/addon/lifecycle.go:665`. `internal/addon/install_url.go:206` is a second surface reaching the same limbs |
| Evidence | Measured at LNK-M-0094 by summing anonymous `r-xp` mappings from `/proc/self/maps`, which counts wazevo's compiled code and is immune to page reclaim: failed-install windows of `+34220 KiB` then `+34220 KiB` — equal to the KiB — against `+0` on the success path. Dropping every Go reference without closing freed 0 bytes, because wazevo holds `e.compiledModules[m.ID]` strongly and only `engine.Close` nils the map, so the comment at `host.go:1413` (*the compiled form is owned by the runtime and closed with it*) is true only of process shutdown. Identical bytes replayed cost `+0` — `AssignModuleID` hashes the binary — so a naive replay is capped at one copy; an operator rebuilding a module that will not start produces distinct bytes every time |
| Severity | **Low, and robustness rather than security.** ~10 MiB RSS per failed install, 6.7 MiB of it mapped executable. *(The first measurement said 26 MiB; that was the race detector's shadow memory, and the refutation pass corrected it.)* Only the instance principal can reach it — `PermAddonsManage` is not in `InstanceGrantable` and is in `NonDelegableScopes` — and that principal can already put working code in the process. The threat model is an operator's debug loop, where the leak is invisible and irreversible short of a restart |
| Reviewed | **Reviewed 2026-09-04**, LNK-M-0095's triage — Tier A, approved for the close (D415, D416). The previous state is what the triage read. |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0095.** `loadOne` closes the compiled module on every post-compile failure return, through a deferred flag rather than three `Close` calls — the defect is a return that forgot, and a fourth added later would forget the same way. The comment claiming the runtime owns the compiled form is corrected: true only at process shutdown. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F353 |

**A guest's `time.Sleep` is a busy-loop: `guestModuleConfig` installs the real wall and monotonic clocks and leaves wazero's fake nanosleep in place, so a well-behaved add-on burns a CPU and one of the sixteen slots for its whole deadline**

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Dated | on import: the row carries no date |
| Found in | LNK-M-0094 |
| Where | `internal/addon/host.go:169-179` sets `WithSysWalltime()` and `WithSysNanotime()` and never `WithNanosleep`, so `platform.FakeNanosleep` — `func(int64){}` — is what `poll_oneoff` calls for a clock subscription |
| Evidence | Measured at LNK-M-0094 with `getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF)` through `guestModuleConfig` itself: `sleep_two shipped config wall=2s cpu=2.01s cpu/wall=1.01`, against `+WithSysNanosleep wall=2s cpu=0s cpu/wall=0.00`, with a busy-loop baseline at 1.00. `time.Sleep` does **not** return early — it returns after the correct duration; `poll_oneoff` returns instantly and the Go runtime re-arms against the real nanotime and spins |
| Severity | **Low, and the obvious fix is a trap** — which is the reason to file it rather than patch it. `WithSysNanosleep` maps to a host `time.Sleep` with no context: measured, a guest sleeping 20s under a 25ms deadline is closed with the right error but **`fn.Call` does not return for 20 seconds**, so the deadline stops bounding wall-clock time, the visitor waits 20s, and `live` is held past `removeGrace` — which opens F355 on shipped defaults. Any real repair is a *capped* nanosleep. The availability envelope does not widen: the host already accepts a guest at 100% CPU for its budget. What changes is that a well-behaved add-on pays the malicious cost, on the redirect path (25ms) and on the page path, where `DefaultRouteDeadline` is 10s and pages share the same sixteen slots — measured at 10.04s of CPU per sleeping page request |
| Reviewed | **Unreviewed.** |
| Status | open |

## LNK-F-0364

**`TestRepeatedInstallAndRemovalDoesNotGrowResidentMemory` decides a claim about a trend from one sample, and its tolerance collapses exactly when the sample is worst**

finding · 2026-09-06

cites: [LNK-M-0095](milestones.md#lnk-m-0095)

cites: [LNK-F-0303](#lnk-f-0303)

**`TestRepeatedInstallAndRemovalDoesNotGrowResidentMemory` decides a claim about a trend from one sample, and its tolerance collapses exactly when the sample is worst.** The bound is `max(early/4, floor)`, so a first window that does not grow — which is the ordinary outcome once the host is warm — drops it to the 8 MiB floor, and ordinary allocator jitter in the second window then reads as a leak. The floor was chosen as *above the noise, under one leaked cycle*, and the noise turned out to reach 10.4 MiB against a leaked cycle of 25 MiB

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0095 |
| Where | `internal/addon/lifecycle_test.go`, the `bound := max(early/4, floor)` line and the single `late > bound` comparison under it |
| Evidence | **Found by CI refusing the release commit.** Run 34048847352 on `315e07b`: `5 cycles a window: 497888 KiB held, -1628 KiB across the first, +10616 KiB across the second, bound 8192 KiB`. **No production Go code changed between that commit and the green run before it** — the diff is a changelog, documentation and one test file in another package — so a memory-growth regression was not available as an explanation. Reproduced locally in the other direction: three runs green, three green under `-race`, and one under four spinning cores where the *first* window read +98,112 KiB, which is the same instability seen from the other side |
| Severity | **None for the product, moderate for the gate.** It is a false red in the one gate a release cannot go round, and this is F303's class in a second place — a measurement asserting an equality between two readings that the machine does not hold still for |
| Reviewed | **Reviewed 2026-09-06**, at the release. In spec for LNK-M-0095 under workflow.md's in-spec rule: m70.md's bullet is that the release PR carries the CI gate's green answer, and a gate that goes red on jitter makes that unobtainable |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0095.** The second window is no longer the verdict. When it exceeds the bound a **third** is taken and the failure needs both later windows past it — a leak grows every window and jitter does not. Costs five extra cycles on a red run and nothing on a green one. **Sensitivity unchanged, sabotage-verified**: removing `l.compiled.Close` gives +52,464 KiB and +52,316 KiB across the two later windows against a 14,052 KiB bound, so the leak this test exists for is still caught twice over. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F364 |

## LNK-F-0375

**A narrowing documented as non-fatal was implemented as fatal**

finding · 2026-09-08

cites: [LNK-M-0082](milestones.md#lnk-m-0082)

cites: [LNK-M-0095](milestones.md#lnk-m-0095)

**A narrowing documented as non-fatal was implemented as fatal.** The call site said *its outcome is logged rather than fatal* and the function said *failure is therefore logged and not fatal*; the next line was `return "", err`. `restrictDatabaseTemp` propagated its `REVOKE`, `GRANT` and `has_database_privilege` errors out of `EnsureAddonSchema`, aborting the load transaction

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Found in | LNK-M-0082 |
| Where | `internal/store/addons.go:324` and `:517` |
| Evidence | **Found by the code review of PR #11** (review 5131991986), which read the production diff in seven passes and verified every finding against the source, wazero v1.12.0 and goose v3.27.3. The non-owner case survived only because Postgres answers it with a WARNING; any genuine failure failed the add-on's load, and for a `required` one stopped the instance. The only actually-non-fatal path was the `log.Warn` at `:543` |
| Severity | **Medium.** Three sentences of documentation describing behaviour the code did not have, on a path whose failure mode is an instance that will not start |
| Reviewed | **Reviewed 2026-09-08**, at the phase PR. In spec for LNK-M-0095 under workflow.md's rule that a defect making the current milestone's claim false is in spec: the phase PR is LNK-M-0095's own deliverable and it does not land carrying a review's findings unanswered |
| Closed by | **LNK-M-0095.** The function returns nothing at all, and its work runs inside a nested transaction — pgx emits `SAVEPOINT` — so a failure rolls back to it and is logged. Discarding the error alone would not have been enough: Postgres aborts a transaction at the failing statement, so everything after it in the load would have failed on the aborted state. **Fenced on the signature rather than end to end, and the limit is named**: provoking a real REVOKE failure needs a role that is neither the owner nor a superuser, and the integration fixture's role is a superuser, which bypasses the check — so the failure is unreachable from there. `TestTheTemporaryNarrowingCannotFailALoad` reads the source instead, in cascade_test.go's idiom, and re-adding a return breaks the build before it reaches the test. |
| Status | closed |
| LinkCtrl | F375 |

## MUS-F-0026

**Registration never required a discoverable passkey, so an account could hold one nobody could sign in with**

finding · 2026-08-25

BeginRegistration set no AuthenticatorSelection, so residentKey was unset and the authenticator decided. What makes this a finding rather than four is the shape: every instance was recorded, two owner answers were given on the same subject (MUS-Q-0010, MUS-Q-0034), and the rate went up. A record that is read after the fact is not a safeguard, and the remedy is not another paragraph in the file that already says this. ## MUS-F-0028

**Revoking a token does not close a stream already open under it**

finding · 2026-08-25

found in: [MUS-W-0021](work-units/MUS-W-0021.md#mus-w-0021)

Revocation is enforced per request: ByToken reads the row rather than a cache, so the next call carrying a revoked token is refused on the running server with no restart. A standalone SSE stream opened before the revocation is not torn down, and was measured still open three seconds after. The impact is bounded rather than absent. That stream is server-to-client only, so no tool call can travel it and nothing can be read through it that was not already being sent; every new request is refused. But 'stops working immediately' is true of calls and not of an already-open connection, and the difference is worth writing down rather than discovering.

Fixed by asking the question for as long as the request lasts. The guard read the credential once, which is the whole truth for a call that answers and stops and no truth at all for one that does not end. It now re-reads it on a ticker while the request is still running and cancels the request's own context the first time the answer changes; the SDK's streamable handler watches that context, so cancelling it is what closes the connection.

Two things chosen rather than fallen into. The recheck calls ByToken rather than a narrower query, so revoked and expired stay one rule with one implementation instead of two that drift. And the interval is two seconds, picked against what revocation promises rather than against load — a person who has just revoked a token is watching a terminal — at a cost of one indexed read of a single row in a local file, and only while a request is still running. For everything but the stream this exists for, that is no time at all: a POST returns before the first tick.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Where | internal/web/guard.go |
| Evidence | A held request under a live token, revoked while running: it ends. With the cancellation removed the same test reports the stream outliving its token after two seconds, which is the defect as found. A token nobody revoked holds its stream across many ticks, which is the half a recheck could quietly break. |
| Status | fixed |

## MUS-F-0029

**No passkey from a password manager could ever sign in, because the backup flags were never stored**

finding · 2026-08-26

found in: [MUS-W-0020](work-units/MUS-W-0020.md#mus-w-0020)

and: [MUS-W-0021](work-units/MUS-W-0021.md#mus-w-0021)

The owner registered a passkey on a phone through Bitwarden, then tried to sign in from a laptop and was told the passkey was not recognised. Registration had worked: the account existed, with one credential, sixteen-byte id and a seventy-seven byte ES256 key. Sign-in could never have worked. WebAuthn asks the relying party to notice if a credential's backup-eligible flag changes between registration and use, and go-webauthn enforces it at login. Mustur stored no flags at all, so the credential it rebuilt to check the assertion claimed BE=0 while the assertion carried BE=1, and the library refused with 'Backup Eligible flag inconsistency detected during login validation'. That is not an edge case. Every synced credential manager sets BE=1 — Bitwarden, iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password — so every passkey a person would realistically use could be registered and then never used. Only a credential welded to hardware, which sets BE=0, would have worked, and only because zero happened to match the flag that was never written. It shipped through a three-reviewer pass because the virtual authenticator written for milestone 5b modelled only the hardware case. The double agreed with the bug, which is worse than having no double: the suite was evidence pointing the wrong way. The diagnosis was also harder than it needed to be. The server tells a browser nothing about why a passkey was refused, which is right and deliberate; it also told the operator nothing, which was an omission rather than a decision. The reason had to be reconstructed from an empty ceremony table and the library's source.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Where | internal/store/schema.sql, internal/account/account.go, internal/web/auth.go, internal/web/authenticator_test.go |
| Status | fixed |

## MUS-F-0033

**A long field value made the records page wider than the phone, and the tab bar went with it**

finding · 2026-08-26

found by: [MUS-F-0032](#mus-f-0032)

The owner reported that the records tab was wider than the others on a phone, leaving only three of the four tabs reachable without scrolling sideways. Measured at 390px: the document was 601px wide. A field row is a flex line with a fixed 9rem key and a flexible value, and a flex child will not shrink below its content unless it is told it may — so a value with no break opportunities, which a work unit's 'Done means' has plenty of, pushed the row 211px past the screen. The tab bar is a consequence rather than the cause. It is fixed to the viewport, but a page wider than the viewport is a page a phone lets you pan, and the bar pans with the layout. Fixing the overflow fixes the bar. min-width:0 is the declaration that does the work; flex-wrap and overflow-wrap do nothing without it, which is the same thing that kept the session view's output pane from scrolling.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Where | internal/web/records.go |
| Evidence | 390px viewport, document 601px before and 390px after; measured in a headless browser rather than reasoned about. |
| Status | fixed |

The shell capped the page at 100dvh and let the output pane scroll inside it, which measures correctly at every viewport size tried here — five phone sizes, none of them reproducing the fault. A column only holds its shape while the browser agrees about how tall the viewport is, and that is the assumption the report contradicts. The output runs behind it, as asked, and reserves its height so the newest line still comes to rest above it rather than under it. The height is measured by the script because the composer grows as it is typed into and CSS cannot measure a sibling. Not reproduced before it was fixed, which is worth writing down: the fix is the shape the owner asked for and is robust to the cause rather than aimed at it.

## MUS-F-0037

**A stored photo kept the metadata its camera wrote into it**

finding · 2026-08-26

found in: [IDW-F-0003](#idw-f-0003)

contradicts: [MUS-D-0119](decisions.md#mus-d-0119)

The first real upload from the owner's phone arrived carrying EXIF, including the exact device build it was taken on. Nothing stripped it, so it sat in the store and would have been handed to anyone the record surface was opened to. This contradicted a decision taken in the same change. The sender's filename is deliberately not stored, on the reasoning that a filename carries a date, a device and often the content of the picture. EXIF carries all three more explicitly, and it was kept — the rule was written and then applied to the smaller of the two carriers.

Fixed as the bytes are stored rather than as they are served, so a thing nobody wanted is never written down at all: the APPn application segments and the comment segment come off a JPEG, and the text, time and colour-profile chunks off a PNG. Byte surgery rather than a re-encode, because decoding and re-encoding would lose quality on somebody's evidence in order to remove a header. GIF and WebP carry their own metadata and are deliberately left alone rather than half-handled — an unstripped format named as such is a smaller lie than one silently believed to be clean.

Recorded late. The fix shipped with the change that found it and this record was left saying open for two days, which is its own small instance of the thing the queue exists to stop.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Where | internal/store/attach.go |
| Evidence | A JPEG with an Exif segment spliced in after the SOI goes into the store and comes back out with no Exif block and a decodable image. The GIF and WebP cases are asserted as passing through untouched, so the limit is measured rather than assumed. |
| Status | fixed |

from: [MUS-D-0121](decisions.md#mus-d-0121)

The owner asked for search if it were an easy add. It is not, and the reason is worth writing down before somebody tries it and discovers the cost halfway. The intake surface carries no script and never has. Filtering a list of options needs one, so a search box makes it the seventh scripted surface — and MUS-Q-0053 settled that the count is of script tags and that a seventh is a decision the owner takes, not a consequence of building something. That is the first route and it is a prompt, not a task. The script-free route is a datalist behind a text input, and it fails on something simpler than rendering: with `input list=`, the input's value is the option's value, so choosing 'Mustur' leaves MUS-P-0001 sitting in the box. Routing by display name instead would work only while no two destinations share one, which is a constraint on the routing records rather than on the control. A check of how the two browsers render a datalist popup was attempted and proved nothing — it read the values out of the DOM, which is what was put in, not what a browser draws. The popup is native chrome and is not in the page. Recorded because a measurement that answers the wrong question is worse than none. What the padding did answer: a native select does not grow with its list. Sixteen options rendered in the same 358px on a phone and 640px on a laptop as six did, in Chrome and Firefox both. The closed control is not the problem; the opened popup is, and that is what a search box would be for.

Put to the owner with both routes costed, and their answer was to leave it (MUS-Q-0062): the closed control is not the problem and the list is four long. Not closed as wrong — closed as not worth either price yet. What would reopen it is the list growing long enough that the opened popup is actually unpleasant, which is a thing to notice rather than a number to wait for.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Where | internal/web/intake.go |
| Evidence | Sixteen options measured at 358px and 640px, unchanged from six, in Chromium and Firefox at 390x844 and 1366x768. Intake carries zero script tags today. |
| Status | not now |

## MUS-F-0040

**The account page was the one surface with no way back to a session**

finding · 2026-08-26

Filed by the owner: can't move from the account page to the session screen.

Every other surface carries the same four-tab nav. The account page carried three — Records, Decisions, Intake — and no Sessions tab at all, so an owner who reached their account from a running session had no way back to it but the browser's own history. The header link into the account page goes one way.

It was not a missing condition but a missing field: Accounts had no ShowSessions at all, where every other surface takes one, so there was nothing to render the tab from even when the server was serving sessions. Fixed by carrying the flag and setting it in render() rather than at the two call sites, which is the same shape sessions.go uses and for the same reason — a page built without it renders a nav that is quietly wrong.

Gated on the flag like everywhere else, because a build served without --sessions has no such surface and a dead tab is worse than an absent one (MUS-Q-0052).

## MUS-F-0041

**The session page was the only surface that let itself be cached, so its markup could outlive its script**

finding · 2026-08-26

broke: [MUS-F-0038](#mus-f-0038)

Reported by the owner: clicking a sub-agent row on the deployed session view opened nothing, hours after MUS-F-0038 shipped the sheet that a row is supposed to open.

The session view was the only surface in this binary that did not send Cache-Control on its page. Intake, compose, account, sign-in and records all send no-store; this one sent nothing at all, and the script beside it sends no-cache and is therefore revalidated on every load. So the two halves of a page that have to agree with each other were delivered under different rules, and a deploy could leave a reader holding markup from before it next to a script from after it. Rows drawn by the old markup carry no identifier attribute; the delegated handler looks for one, finds nothing, and does nothing — silently, which is why it presents as a dead control rather than an error.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Where | internal/web/sessions.go |
| Evidence | internal/web/sessions.go render() set Content-Type and nothing else; every sibling surface sets no-store. Against the deployed binary, a real mouse click at the centre of a row — not element.click(), which skips hit-testing — opened the sheet in Chrome and Firefox at 390x844 and 1366x768, with the row under the pointer and no page errors. So the code as deployed works and something about the delivered page did not. Fixed by sending Cache-Control: no-store from render(). no-store rather than no-cache because it also keeps the page out of the back/forward cache, which restores a whole live document including script state, and is what a phone returning to a backgrounded tab meets. Not proven to be the cause the owner hit: their browser's cache state could not be reproduced here. A hard refresh would confirm it. |
| Status | fixed |

## MUS-F-0042

**The quiet timer measured the age of the tab, in three separate ways**

finding · 2026-08-27

Filed by the owner, and reported still broken after the first fix. It had three causes and the first fix reached one.

One: the socket handler declared 'quiet := 0', never assigned it, and sent it. Fixed by calling Stream.Quiet, which had existed since the stream did and had never been called.

Two: Stream.lastAt is set when output is appended, so a reader that has just opened has seen nothing and reports zero. That is the case the timer exists for — the first viewer of a session quiet since Sunday — and the test written for the first fix echoed immediately, so it measured the mechanism working and never the case. Fixed by seeding lastAt from tmux's session_activity, which List already reads for the route row's default.

Three: the scrollback capture-pane hands over at the start was appended as output with a timestamp of now, on the server and again on the client. So attaching to a silent session announced that it had just spoken, twice. Fixed by separating replay from output at both ends: Stream.replay leaves lastAt alone, Update and the socket frame carry a Replay flag, and the client does not treat a replayed chunk as activity.

The shape worth remembering is that a value can be threaded correctly through every layer and still be wrong at the source, and that a test which sets up the happy case cannot tell you which.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Where | internal/session/stream.go, internal/web/sessions.go, internal/web/assets/session.js |
| Evidence | On a session started 29s earlier and silent since, the first paint reads 'quiet 29s' and climbs, in Chrome and Firefox. Before: 'quiet 0s' on every load. Three tests: the first viewer is told the truth, the replayed scrollback does not reset it, and the backlog frame is marked as replay. |
| Status | fixed |

## MUS-F-0046

**A submit button nobody drew, hidden by script, stacked by a selector written for another form**

finding · 2026-08-26

on: [MUS-D-0123](decisions.md#mus-d-0123)

It was on no wireframe because it was added without being drawn. A GET form cannot build a path segment, so the picker posts a query to /sessions and the server turns it into a path; the button was there to submit it with scripting off. The reasoning was sound and it was still a control the approved drawings did not contain.

It was visible because the first version drew it always and removed it from the script. A control the server draws and the script takes away is a control that can fail visible, and it did: the owner met a stale page carrying new markup beside old script. Clearing cookies made it go away, which is MUS-F-0041's cache mismatch rather than a fix for anything.

It was under the dropdown rather than beside it, and full height, because of a bare element selector. form { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap; padding } was written for the composer, and a bare element selector reshapes every form added after it. Fixed on the owner's instruction that the button should appear only with scripting disabled. It lives in a noscript element rather than being hidden, so the browser decides at parse time and a page whose script is stale, blocked or missing still gets exactly the control it needs. The noscript is given display: contents so the button rather than the wrapper is the flex item, and .pick resets flex-direction and padding.

The picker's submit button lives in a noscript so the browser decides whether it is there. To make the button a flex item of the row rather than the noscript being one, the noscript was given display: contents — and that override also cancels the rule every browser applies with scripting enabled, noscript { display: none }. ## MUS-F-0052

**Frames left nothing to scroll back through, because an agent pane has no scrollback at all**

finding · 2026-08-27

from: [MUS-D-0132](decisions.md#mus-d-0132)

Reported by the owner as soon as frames shipped: the session could no longer be scrolled back.

The frame was set to carry 120 lines of history above the visible screen, and that number was measured on the wrong thing. It came from a plain shell pane, where history exists. An agent CLI runs on the alternate screen — measured: alternate_on=1, history_size=0 — and tmux keeps no scrollback for one. Not a little: none. So capture-pane -S -120 returned twenty-four rows however deep it was asked to go, and had done since the first frame shipped.

That was visible in the very first measurement, which reported the same twenty-four lines at every depth from 0 to 2000. It was read as 'this session has little history' and not chased.

Fixed by making the pane tall rather than by reconstructing a transcript. The CLI redraws its whole conversation into whatever height it is given, and a capture costs what the content costs rather than what the height is: 60 rows was 4.8KB, 200 rows 6.9KB and 300 rows 7.0KB on the same session, because the difference is blank padding that gets trimmed. Sessions Mustur starts are now 100x300.

The cost, named rather than discovered later: window-size is manual, so somebody attaching to one of these with tmux gets a 300-row window rather than one sized to their terminal.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Where | internal/session/session.go, internal/session/screen.go |
| Evidence | tmux display-message on both live sessions: alternate_on=1, history_size=0, history_limit=2000. After the resize, Demo renders 120 scrollable lines from its startup banner to its last output where it had 24. |
| Status | fixed |

## MUS-F-0055

**amend replaces a record whole, and the command that exists to correct records has been quietly gutting them**

finding · 2026-08-28

answered by: [MUS-Q-0063](questions.md#mus-q-0063)

`mustur amend ID --title "..."` — changing nothing but the title — returned the identifier, exited 0, and left a record with no body, no citations and no fields. Everything the caller did not restate was gone, and nothing in the output said so.

It was deliberate, which is the part worth keeping. The code carried its own argument: an amendment states the record afresh, because carrying fields forward silently would make `amend --title` keep data the writer never saw, and the log holds the earlier version anyway. Both halves are true. It still lost to the evidence — the reasoning was about a writer who might be surprised by what survived, and the actual writers were surprised by what did not.

The help line read `correct one, without losing what it said`. There is a reading on which that was true: the log is insert-only, so nothing is unrecoverable. It is not the reading somebody types the command under.

Found by looking for the least-tested code rather than by anything failing. `cmd/mustur` was at 2.8% statement coverage, the lowest in the tree by a factor of sixteen, and it is the half the owner actually types.

The damage was already here. Fifteen amendments across this store dropped content. Most were deliberate — a jot's intake scaffolding coming off at triage, a field reworked into the body — but eight records were still missing citations two days later, including MUS-F-0031 and MUS-F-0049, which are the same defect and had stopped pointing at each other. MUS-M-0010 lost its entire 630-character body to one amendment and took three more to rebuild it; nobody wrote that down at the time.

The eight were repaired, and the method is the point: each amendment was rebuilt from the record's own stored payload and re-sent with the missing citations added. Retyping the content by hand is how it was lost, so no part of the repair retyped anything.

Fixed by merging, which the owner chose on MUS-Q-0063. What is passed replaces its counterpart; what is not passed survives; `--drop` removes one on purpose and `--replace` still states a record afresh for the rare time that is wanted. A field passed again keeps the place it already had, because fields render in order and a correction that shuffles them is a diff nobody asked for. Citations are identified by both halves rather than by their key, because a record can be found in two work units and cite them under the same word.

It also closes a smaller trap in the same command. `--at` defaults to today, so every correction restamped the record's date with the date of the correction — which moved three records' dates earlier today before it was noticed. An amendment that keeps what it did not mention keeps the date too.

This record was itself amended with the new behaviour, passing only a body and a status, and its evidence and citations survived unmentioned.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Where | cmd/mustur/main.go |
| Evidence | A finding created with a body, one citation and two fields, amended with --title alone, comes back as a bare title: exit 0, output the identifier. Across record_event, 15 amends dropped content and 8 records were still missing citations today; MUS-M-0010 went 630 characters of body to zero and back over four amends. |
| Status | fixed |
